lessons.title: How the digital SAT adapts (and what it means for you)
lessons.body: The digital SAT has two sections, Reading and Writing and Math, and each is split into two modules. Your first module contains a mix of easy, medium and hard questions. How you do on it decides whether your second module is the harder or the easier version, and only the harder version opens the path to top scores. Practical consequences: first, module 1 matters a lot, so do not rush it to bank time for later. Second, a hard-feeling module 2 is usually good news, not a sign you are failing. Third, there is no penalty for wrong answers, so never leave a question blank; flag it, guess, and return if time allows. Inside a module you can move back and forth freely, so use the mark-for-review tool. A simple pacing rule: Reading and Writing gives you about 71 seconds per question (32 minutes for 27), Math about 95 seconds (35 minutes for 22). Mini-example: you hit a long data question at question 6 of a math module. Make your best guess, flag it, finish the quick ones, then return. Ten easy points beat one stubborn puzzle.

lessons.title: Reading and Writing: answering from the text, not from opinion
lessons.body: Each Reading and Writing question pairs one short passage with one question, so precision beats speed-reading. Start with the question stem, because it tells you what to look for: the main purpose, a word in context, the claim a quotation would support, or the logical completion of a text. Then read the whole passage once, carefully. Before looking at the options, predict an answer in your own words. Wrong options usually fall into three traps: too extreme ("always", "proves"), true in real life but not stated in the passage, or the right topic with the wrong relationship (cause instead of correlation). Mini-example: a passage says a researcher "found that bees visited blue flowers more often in two of three trials." An option claiming bees "prefer blue flowers in all conditions" is too extreme; one saying the results "offer partial support" for a blue preference matches the evidence. For words in context, plug your own simple word into the blank first, then pick the option closest in meaning and tone. If two options seem right, return to the exact sentence and ask which one the text actually commits to.

lessons.title: Standard English conventions: the rules that show up most
lessons.body: Conventions questions test a small, predictable set of rules. Learn them and these become your fastest points. (1) Sentence boundaries: two complete sentences cannot be joined with only a comma; use a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a FANBOYS conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). (2) Colons follow a complete sentence and introduce a list, explanation or example. (3) Subject-verb agreement: find the true subject and ignore the prepositional phrase in between: "The collection of rare maps IS on display." (4) Pronouns must match their noun in number: a company is "it", not "they". (5) Modifiers: an opening descriptive phrase must describe the noun that comes right after the comma. "Walking to school, the rain soaked Maria" is wrong; "Walking to school, Maria was soaked by the rain" is right. (6) No comma between a subject and its verb, or between a verb and its object. Mini-example: "The scientists' findings, published last spring ___ challenged earlier models." The phrase "published last spring" is an interrupter opened by a comma, so it must be closed by a comma: "spring, challenged".

lessons.title: Transitions and rhetorical synthesis
lessons.body: Transition questions ask for the logical link between two sentences. Cover the options, read the sentence before and after the blank, and label the relationship: contrast (however, nevertheless), continuation (moreover, additionally), cause and effect (therefore, consequently), example (for instance), or sequence (subsequently, finally). Only then check which option carries that label. Example: "The new bridge cut commute times by half. ___, local shops along the old route lost customers." The second idea is an unwanted consequence that contrasts with the good news, so "However" fits, while "Therefore" would wrongly suggest the shops were meant to lose business. Rhetorical synthesis questions give you bullet-point notes and a goal, such as "emphasize a difference" or "introduce the study to an unfamiliar audience". The correct answer is the option that achieves that exact goal, even if other options contain more true details. Underline the goal words, then eliminate every option that does a different job. An answer that compares two items cannot satisfy a goal to "describe one item's method".

lessons.title: Math: linear equations, systems and the built-in calculator
lessons.body: Linear relationships are the largest math domain on the SAT. Be fluent in three forms: slope-intercept y = mx + b, point-slope, and standard Ax + By = C. In word problems the slope is a rate (dollars per hour) and the y-intercept is a starting value (a fixed fee). For systems of equations, decide the method by the numbers: if a variable already has matching coefficients, eliminate; if one variable is isolated, substitute; if the question asks "how many solutions", compare slopes: different slopes give one solution, same slope with different intercepts gives none, identical lines give infinitely many. The Bluebook app includes a graphing calculator (Desmos). Use it to graph both equations and read the intersection instead of grinding algebra, and to check answers. Mini-example: a plumber charges a $60 visit fee plus $45 per hour. Cost = 45h + 60. For a $240 bill, 45h = 180, so h = 4 hours. Common trap: answering with an intermediate value (180) instead of what was asked. Always reread the last line of the question before you choose.

lessons.title: Math: percentages, data and the final-week plan
lessons.body: Problem-solving and data analysis questions reward clean setups. Percent change = (new - old) / old. A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease is not a return to the start: 100 becomes 120, then 96. For tables, read the row and column labels twice; most errors come from using the total of the wrong group. For "what proportion of the participants who..." questions, the denominator is the group named after "of". Mini-example: of 200 surveyed students, 80 play a sport, and 30 of those also play an instrument. The fraction of athletes who play an instrument is 30/80 = 37.5%, not 30/200. Final-week plan: take one full Bluebook practice test under real timing, review every miss by category (conventions, inference, linear, percent, geometry), and drill the two weakest categories in the official question bank or on Khan Academy. The night before, stop studying early, charge your device, and confirm that Bluebook is installed and your admission ticket is ready.

lessons.title: The enhanced ACT: structure and pacing
lessons.body: The current ACT has three core tests that make up your Composite score: English (50 questions, 35 minutes), Math (45 questions, 50 minutes) and Reading (36 questions, 40 minutes). Science (40 questions, 40 minutes) and Writing are optional add-ons reported separately. Check whether your target colleges want Science or Writing before you register. Pacing per question: English about 42 seconds, Math about 67 seconds, Reading about 67 seconds. Unlike the SAT, the ACT is not adaptive, so every question is worth the same and difficulty does not rise in a fixed pattern. That means the best strategy is "two passes": answer everything you can do quickly, mark the slow ones, and come back. There is no penalty for guessing, so every bubble or click should be filled before time is called. Mini-example: at minute 30 of Math you have 10 questions left. Spend 60 seconds scanning for any you can solve in under a minute, do those, then make educated guesses on the rest by eliminating impossible values. Pick a "letter of the day" for blind guesses so you never waste time deciding.

lessons.title: English: concise, correct, consistent
lessons.body: ACT English questions sit inside passages and test grammar plus writing choices. Three habits raise scores fast. First, when options differ only in length and all are grammatical, the shortest one that keeps the meaning is usually right; the ACT punishes redundancy such as "annual yearly festival". Second, test punctuation with the "complete sentence" check: a semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides; a colon needs a full sentence before it. Third, keep verb tense and pronouns consistent with the rest of the paragraph. Questions that ask whether to add or delete a sentence want you to judge relevance: does it support the paragraph's specific point? Answer yes or no first, then choose the reason that is actually true. Mini-example: "The museum, which opened in 1995, it attracts thousands of visitors." The pronoun "it" duplicates the subject "The museum", so delete it: "The museum, which opened in 1995, attracts thousands of visitors." Watch for "NO CHANGE": it is correct about as often as any other option, so do not avoid it out of suspicion.

lessons.title: Math: what to know cold
lessons.body: ACT Math covers topics through early grade 12, now with four answer choices per question. Memorize formulas the test does not give you: slope (y2 - y1)/(x2 - x1), the distance and midpoint formulas, area of a circle (pi r squared) and circumference (2 pi r), the Pythagorean theorem, SOHCAHTOA, and the quadratic formula. Questions are roughly ordered easier to harder, so bank time early but never get careless on the first 20. Use backsolving when the answers are numbers: plug the options into the question, starting with a middle value, and see which works. Use picking numbers when the answers contain variables: choose simple values like x = 2, compute the target, and test each option. Mini-example: "If a shirt costs $40 after a 20% discount, what was the original price?" Backsolve: $50 x 0.8 = $40, so $50 is correct. The trap answer is $48 (adding 20% of 40), which ignores that the discount was 20% of the original. A calculator is permitted; check your model is on the approved list.

lessons.title: Reading and Science: locate, do not memorize
lessons.body: ACT Reading and Science reward finding information fast. For Reading, skim each passage for structure in about two to three minutes: who is speaking, what each paragraph does, and where the tone shifts. Then answer line-reference and detail questions first, and leave broad "main idea" questions for the end of each passage, when you know it better. Correct answers are paraphrases of the text; wrong ones often reuse exact words from the wrong place. For the optional Science test, you rarely need outside knowledge. Go straight to the figures: read axis labels, units and legends, then answer. In "conflicting viewpoints" passages, write a three-word summary of each scientist's position before reading the questions. Mini-example: a graph shows plant height rising with fertilizer from 0 to 20 grams and falling after 20 grams. A question asks what happens at 25 grams; the trend says height decreases, even though more fertilizer "sounds" better. Trust the data shown over intuition.

lessons.title: The 2025 ACT format and how to plan around it
lessons.body:
Since spring 2025 (online) and September 2025 (paper), the ACT has used a shorter format. The core test is English (50 questions, 35 minutes), Math (45 questions, 50 minutes) and Reading (36 questions, 40 minutes), about two hours and five minutes of testing. Your Composite score, from 1 to 36, is the average of those three tests only. Science (40 questions, 40 minutes) is now an optional add-on, and so is the Writing essay (40 minutes). Neither affects the Composite. If you take Science, you also receive a STEM score that combines Math and Science.

Three practical changes matter for your preparation. First, Math questions now have four answer choices instead of five, so elimination pays off faster: removing two choices leaves a coin flip. Second, passages and sections are shorter, which raises the time per question. English gives you about 42 seconds per question, Math about 67 seconds, Reading about 67 seconds and Science about 60 seconds. Third, Science is no longer automatic, so you must decide before registering whether to add it.

How to decide on Science: check the testing policy of every college on your list. If any of them, or any scholarship you want, asks for Science or a STEM score, add it. If you are applying to engineering, nursing or science programs, adding Science is often a sensible signal even when it is not required. Otherwise, you can spend that preparation time raising the three tests that build your Composite.

A simple plan for eight weeks: take one full timed practice test from ACT's official materials in week one to set a baseline. Spend weeks two to six on your two weakest tests, three sessions a week, using an error log that records the topic and the reason for each miss (content gap, misread, or time). In weeks seven and eight, take two more timed tests and review every question you missed or guessed.

Mini-example: a student scores English 27, Math 22, Reading 26 (Composite 25). Raising Math to 26 lifts the Composite to 26, because the average rounds to the nearest whole number. Target the test with the most room to grow.

lessons.title: English: the punctuation rules that decide most points
lessons.body:
A large share of ACT English questions test the Conventions of Standard English: sentence structure, punctuation and usage. The good news is that a short list of rules covers most of them.

1. Independent clauses. Two complete sentences can be joined by a period, a semicolon, or a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). A comma alone between them is a comma splice. Example: "The bus was late, so we walked" is correct; "The bus was late, we walked" is not.

2. Colons. A colon must follow a complete sentence. What comes after it explains or lists. "She packed three things: a map, water and a jacket" works because "She packed three things" stands alone. "She packed: a map" does not.

3. Nonessential elements. Information that can be removed without changing the core meaning is set off by a matching pair of commas, dashes or parentheses. Mixing a comma with a dash, or forgetting the closing comma, is a classic trap. If the information identifies which one you mean, it is essential and takes no commas.

4. No comma between a subject and its verb, between a verb and its object, or right after a conjunction such as "and" in a list.

5. Apostrophes. Singular possessive: the dog's bowl. Plural possessive: the dogs' bowls. "Its" is possessive; "it's" means "it is."

6. Agreement. Find the true subject by crossing out prepositional phrases. In "The box of old letters sits on the shelf," the subject is "box," so the verb is "sits."

7. Pronoun case. Remove the other person to test: "The coach thanked Ana and me" is correct because you would say "thanked me."

Strategy: when the answer choices differ only in punctuation, read the sentence and decide which rule applies before looking at the choices. When the choices differ in length and all are grammatical, the ACT usually rewards the shortest one that keeps the meaning. Keep NO CHANGE in play: it is correct about as often as any other choice.

lessons.title: English: add, delete, move and purpose questions
lessons.body:
Production of Writing questions ask you to think like an editor rather than a grammarian. They fall into a few repeating patterns, and each pattern has a reliable method.

Add or delete. The question gives a sentence and asks whether the writer should add it (or keep it). The answer choices pair Yes or No with a reason. Decide Yes or No first by asking one question: does this sentence support the main point of this specific paragraph? Then choose the reason that is accurate. A common trap is a choice with the right Yes or No but a false reason, for example claiming the sentence contradicts something it does not.

What would be lost. If the writer deleted a phrase, what would the paragraph lose? Describe the phrase's function in your own words, such as "a specific example" or "the second piece of evidence," and match it.

Transitions. Read the sentence before and the sentence with the transition. Classify the relationship: contrast (however, yet), cause and effect (therefore, as a result), addition (also, moreover), or example (for instance). Two choices with the same meaning cannot both be right, so they usually both are wrong.

Sentence and paragraph order. Look for clues inside the sentence: pronouns such as "this" or "these" need something earlier to point to, and words such as "first," "next" and "finally" signal sequence. Test your chosen spot by reading the sentences around it.

Writer's goal. A question may ask whether the essay fulfills a purpose such as "to explain how a process works." Summarize the essay's real focus in one sentence and compare. Answers that overstate the essay ("argues that all cities should...") are usually wrong.

Style and tone. Choose words that match the passage's level of formality and that are precise. Slang in a formal essay or vague words like "stuff" are wrong. Redundant phrases, such as "collaborated together," are wrong because they repeat meaning.

Mini-example: a paragraph describes how bees signal the direction of food. A proposed sentence about the color of the hive is off-topic, so the answer is No, with the reason that it distracts from the paragraph's focus.

lessons.title: Math: the algebra and functions toolkit
lessons.body:
The ACT Math test reports a category called Preparing for Higher Math, which includes Number and Quantity, Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Statistics and Probability, plus Integrating Essential Skills, which covers rates, percentages, proportions and multi-step everyday problems. Algebra and functions appear throughout, so make these tools automatic.

Linear equations and systems. Distribute, collect like terms, isolate. For a system, use elimination when coefficients line up and substitution when one variable is already alone. A system has no solution when the lines are parallel (same slope, different intercept) and infinitely many when the equations are multiples of each other.

Inequalities. Solve like equations but flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative number. Check with a test value: if you get x < -4, plug in -5 and confirm it works.

Quadratics. Factor when you can, use the quadratic formula when you cannot, and remember the vertex of y = ax^2 + bx + c is at x = -b/(2a). The vertex gives the minimum value when a is positive. Sum of roots is -b/a and product is c/a.

Functions. f(-2) means substitute -2 everywhere, with parentheses: f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1 gives 2(4) + 6 + 1 = 15. For composite functions, work from the inside out. Rational functions have vertical asymptotes where the denominator is zero after canceling common factors; a canceled factor leaves a hole instead.

Exponents and logarithms. log_b(x) = y means b^y = x, and log(a) + log(b) = log(ab). Always check that solutions keep the argument of every logarithm positive.

Exponential growth. A quantity growing r percent per period is P(1 + r)^t. Linear growth adds the same amount each period; exponential growth multiplies.

Time strategy: with about 67 seconds per question and only four choices, backsolving is powerful. If the choices are numbers, start with a middle value, test it, and move up or down. If the problem uses variables, pick a simple number for each variable, compute the target, and test the choices.

Mini-example: if 2^(x+3) = 32, write 32 as 2^5, so x + 3 = 5 and x = 2.

lessons.title: Math: geometry, trigonometry, matrices and probability
lessons.body:
Many students lose points on ACT Math not because topics are hard but because they forget formulas. The ACT does not give you a formula sheet, so memorize these.

Geometry. Area of a triangle is half base times height; of a trapezoid, half the sum of the bases times height; of a circle, pi r^2, with circumference 2 pi r. The Pythagorean theorem a^2 + b^2 = c^2 and the triples 3-4-5, 5-12-13 and 8-15-17 (and their multiples) save time. In a 45-45-90 triangle the sides are x, x, x times the square root of 2; in a 30-60-90 triangle they are x, x times the square root of 3, 2x. A circle written as (x - h)^2 + (y - k)^2 = r^2 has center (h, k) and radius r; complete the square when the equation is expanded.

Trigonometry. SOH-CAH-TOA for right triangles. Know the signs by quadrant: in Quadrant II only sine is positive, so if sin of theta is 5/13 and theta is obtuse, cosine is -12/13 and tangent is -5/12. Also know sin^2 + cos^2 = 1.

Matrices and complex numbers. The determinant of a 2 by 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]] is ad - bc. Multiplying a 2 by 2 matrix by k multiplies its determinant by k^2. For complex numbers, i^2 = -1; multiply like binomials and replace i^2.

Statistics and probability. Mean is the sum divided by the count, so a missing value is found from the total: mean times count. The median is the middle value of the sorted list. Probability is favorable outcomes over total outcomes; for "without replacement," the denominator shrinks after each draw. For two dice, list the 36 outcomes when in doubt.

Integrating Essential Skills. Percent change is (new - old)/old. Successive percentages multiply: a 25 percent discount followed by 5 percent tax is 0.75 times 1.05 of the original. Unit rates and proportions solve most recipe, map and speed questions.

Mini-example: a rectangle has perimeter 46 and length 15. The width is 46/2 - 15 = 8, so the area is 120. The common mistake is using 46 - 15 as the width.

lessons.title: Reading and optional Science: a passage method that saves time
lessons.body:
Reading and Science both reward finding information quickly rather than memorizing it. The same core method works for both, with small changes.

Reading (36 questions, 40 minutes). The enhanced ACT uses shorter passages, including literary narratives, informational texts in social science, humanities and natural science, and paired passages. Questions fall into three reporting categories: Key Ideas and Details (main ideas, details, inferences, relationships), Craft and Structure (word meaning, purpose, point of view, structure) and Integration of Knowledge and Ideas (arguments, evidence, and connections between texts). Method: read the passage once, at a steady pace, and write a five-word summary of each paragraph in your head or on scratch paper. Then answer questions, returning to the text for every answer. Correct answers are supported by specific words in the passage; wrong answers are often too strong ("always," "entirely"), true but off-topic, or the opposite of what the text says. For paired passages, answer questions on Text 1, then Text 2, then the questions comparing both.

Science (optional, 40 questions, 40 minutes). Science measures Interpretation of Data, Scientific Investigation, and Evaluation of Models, Inferences, and Experimental Results. You see three kinds of passages: data representations (tables and graphs), research summaries (several related experiments) and conflicting viewpoints (two or more explanations of one phenomenon). For data passages, skip the introduction at first and go straight to the questions; read the axis labels and units of the table they point to. For research summaries, identify what was changed (independent variable), what was measured (dependent variable) and what was held constant in each experiment. For conflicting viewpoints, write one sentence summarizing each scientist's claim and note where they agree.

Trends and interpolation. Many questions ask for a value between or beyond the data. Find the pattern first (increasing, decreasing, leveling off) and choose the answer that continues it. Look at how big the changes are, not only their direction.

Mini-example: if dissolved oxygen is 9.1 mg/L at 20 degrees C and 7.6 mg/L at 30 degrees C, a reasonable estimate at 25 degrees C is about 8.3 mg/L, roughly halfway between.

practice.prompt: Choose the best version: "The library extended its hours ___ students could study late during finals."
practice.explanation: "so" (without a comma here) correctly joins the clause of purpose. A comma alone creates a comma splice; a semicolon before "so" is incorrect; the fourth option creates a fragment.

practice.prompt: Choose the best version: "The team made a final decision at the end of the meeting to postpone the launch."
options: made a final, conclusive decision at the end of the meeting
made a decision that was final at the end of the meeting
finally made a final decision at the meeting's end
made a final decision at the end of the meeting
practice.explanation: The original is clear and not redundant. The other options add repetition ("finally ... final", "final, conclusive") or wordiness.

practice.prompt: Choose the best version: "The list of approved field trips for the spring semester ___ posted outside the main office."
practice.explanation: The subject is "list" (singular); "of approved field trips" is a prepositional phrase that does not change the subject. So the singular verb "is" is correct.

practice.prompt: If 3x - 7 = 2x + 5, what is the value of x?
practice.explanation: Subtract 2x from both sides: x - 7 = 5, so x = 12. Check: 3(12) - 7 = 29 and 2(12) + 5 = 29.

practice.prompt: A line passes through the points (1, 4) and (3, 10). What is its y-intercept?
practice.explanation: Slope = (10 - 4)/(3 - 1) = 3. Using (1, 4): 4 = 3(1) + b, so b = 1. The trap answer 3 is the slope.

practice.prompt: After a 20% discount, a jacket costs $40. What was the original price?
practice.explanation: Original price x 0.80 = 40, so the original price is 40 / 0.80 = $50. $48 comes from wrongly adding 20% of the sale price.

practice.prompt: A bag holds 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green marbles. Two marbles are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are blue?
practice.explanation: P = (5/10) x (4/9) = 20/90 = 2/9. The answer 1/4 assumes replacement (5/10 x 5/10).

practice.prompt: If f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 1, what is f(-2)?

practice.passage: Urban beekeeping has grown quickly over the past decade, and many city dwellers assume that more hives always mean more help for pollinators. Ecologists studying several European cities have found a more complicated picture. Where honeybee hives became dense, wild bee species, which often pollinate native plants more effectively, had less pollen and nectar available to them. The researchers do not argue that city hives should be banned; instead, they recommend planting more flowering species and setting limits on hive density in neighborhoods with few green spaces.
practice.prompt: Which statement best summarizes the passage?
options: Dense urban hives can compete with wild bees, so researchers suggest more flowers and hive limits.
Urban beekeeping should be banned to protect wild bees.
Wild bees are less effective pollinators than honeybees.
More honeybee hives in cities always benefit pollinators.
practice.explanation: The passage presents competition as the problem and flowers plus density limits as the recommendation. It explicitly rejects a ban and says wild bees are often more effective, so the other options contradict it.

practice.passage: Urban beekeeping has grown quickly over the past decade, and many city dwellers assume that more hives always mean more help for pollinators. Ecologists studying several European cities have found a more complicated picture. Where honeybee hives became dense, wild bee species, which often pollinate native plants more effectively, had less pollen and nectar available to them. The researchers do not argue that city hives should be banned; instead, they recommend planting more flowering species and setting limits on hive density in neighborhoods with few green spaces.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, hive limits are recommended especially in neighborhoods that
practice.explanation: The final sentence names "neighborhoods with few green spaces".

practice.passage: In an experiment, students grew bean plants with different amounts of fertilizer for 4 weeks. Average final heights: 0 g: 12 cm; 10 g: 18 cm; 20 g: 22 cm; 30 g: 19 cm; 40 g: 15 cm.
practice.prompt: Based on the results, which fertilizer amount would most likely produce the tallest plants?
practice.explanation: Height peaks at 20 g (22 cm) and declines with more fertilizer, so 20 g is best among the tested amounts.

practice.passage: In an experiment, students grew bean plants with different amounts of fertilizer for 4 weeks. Average final heights: 0 g: 12 cm; 10 g: 18 cm; 20 g: 22 cm; 30 g: 19 cm; 40 g: 15 cm.
practice.prompt: If a plant received 50 g of fertilizer, its expected average height would most likely be
practice.explanation: Above 20 g, height falls by 3-4 cm per 10 g (22, 19, 15). Continuing the trend past 40 g gives a value below 15 cm.

practice.passage: The museum's newest exhibit features [artifacts that, were] recovered from a shipwreck off the coast of Maine. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: "That were recovered from a shipwreck" is an essential clause identifying which artifacts, so no commas are used. A comma before "that" or after "were" wrongly separates parts of the clause.

practice.passage: Maya trained for the marathon for six [months, she] finished the race in under four hours. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: Two independent clauses need a comma plus a coordinating conjunction (or a period or semicolon). The original is a comma splice, and removing the comma creates a run-on.

practice.passage: The collection of letters written by the poet's sisters [reveals] how closely the family followed her early career. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: The subject is "collection," which is singular, so the singular verb "reveals" is correct. The plural verbs agree with "letters" or "sisters," which are inside the modifying phrases.

practice.passage: Last spring, the city council [votes] to convert the empty lot into a community garden. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: "Last spring" marks a completed past action, so the simple past "voted" is needed. "Has voted" (present perfect) does not pair with a specific finished time.

practice.passage: The orchestra had rehearsed the symphony for weeks. On opening night, the [orchestras'] conductor raised her baton, and the hall fell silent. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: The passage refers to one orchestra, so the singular possessive "orchestra's" is correct. "Orchestras'" is the plural possessive and would mean several orchestras share one conductor.

practice.passage: The two scientists [collaborated together jointly] on a study of urban heat islands. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: To collaborate already means to work together, so "together" and "jointly" are redundant. The single word "collaborated" is the most concise correct choice.

practice.passage: Volunteers at the Eastside Community Garden grow vegetables for the neighborhood food pantry. Last year they harvested more than two tons of produce. [Proposed sentence here] The pantry distributed the vegetables to roughly 300 families.
practice.prompt: The writer is considering adding the following sentence at this point: "The garden's tool shed was painted blue in 2019." Should the writer make this addition?
options: Yes, because it adds a vivid visual detail about the garden.
Yes, because it explains how the volunteers stored their harvest.
No, because it introduces a detail unrelated to the paragraph's focus on the harvest and its use.
No, because it contradicts the claim that volunteers grow vegetables.
practice.explanation: The paragraph is about how much the volunteers harvested and where the food went; the shed's color is irrelevant. The second option gives a false reason, since the sentence says nothing about storage.

practice.passage: Electric buses cost more to buy than diesel buses. [Therefore,] they are cheaper to fuel and maintain, so many cities save money over a bus's lifetime. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: The first sentence says electric buses cost more to buy; the next says they are cheaper to run. That is a contrast, so "However" fits. "Therefore" wrongly presents the lower running cost as a result of the higher price.

practice.passage: The recipe calls for only three [ingredients: flour,] water, and salt. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: A colon correctly follows a complete clause ("The recipe calls for only three ingredients") and introduces the list. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, and a colon should not follow "such as."

practice.passage: [Walking through the old library, the smell of paper] reminded him of his grandfather's study. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: While walking through the old library, the smell of paper
The smell of paper, walking through the old library,
Walking through the old library, Leo noticed that the smell of paper
practice.explanation: The opening phrase "Walking through the old library" must describe the person walking, so "Leo" must follow the comma. The other choices make "the smell of paper" the one walking, a dangling modifier.

practice.passage: The award was shared by the two lab partners, and the professor congratulated [Priya and I] in front of the class. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: The pronoun is the object of "congratulated," so the objective case "me" is required; test by removing Priya: "congratulated me." "Myself" is reflexive and needs "I" as the subject.

practice.passage: Sally Ride[, who joined NASA in 1978, became] the first American woman in space in 1983. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: , who joined NASA in 1978, she became
practice.explanation: The clause "who joined NASA in 1978" is nonessential and must be enclosed by a pair of commas, as in the original. Dropping either comma breaks the pair, and adding "she" gives the verb a second subject.

practice.passage: The new bell schedule had a noticeable [affect] on attendance during first period. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: After the article "a" and the adjective "noticeable," a noun is needed: "effect" means a result. "Affect" is normally a verb meaning to influence.

practice.passage: [1] First, she sanded the old table down to bare wood. [2] Finally, she sealed the surface with two coats of clear varnish. [3] Next, she applied a dark walnut stain and let it dry overnight. [4] The table, once a garage-sale reject, now sits proudly in her dining room.
practice.prompt: For the sake of logic and cohesion, Sentence 2 should be placed:
practice.explanation: The steps follow the signal words First, Next, Finally, so the sentence beginning "Finally" belongs after the "Next" step, Sentence 3. Placing it after Sentence 4 would put a process step after the paragraph's concluding result.

practice.passage: When the last passenger train left Millbrook in 1971, the brick depot stood empty for decades. In 2018, residents voted to fund its conversion into a public library. Workers kept the original ticket windows, now used as the checkout desk, and turned the freight room into a children's reading area. Today the depot welcomes more visitors each week than it did in its final years as a station.
practice.prompt: Suppose the writer's primary purpose had been to explain how a historic building can be adapted for a new public use. Would this essay accomplish that purpose?
options: Yes, because it describes how the town converted its railway depot into a public library.
Yes, because it argues that every historic building should be turned into a library.
No, because it focuses only on the history of passenger rail travel.
No, because it describes a building that was eventually demolished.
practice.explanation: The essay shows the depot being reused, with specific details such as ticket windows becoming the checkout desk. The second option overstates the essay, which never argues that every historic building should become a library.

practice.passage: Before leaving the trailhead, the hikers packed [water, trail mix, and, a first-aid kit]. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
options: water trail mix, and a first-aid kit
water, trail mix, and a first-aid kit
water, trail, mix and a first-aid kit
practice.explanation: Items in a series are separated by commas, with no comma after the final "and." The original puts an extra comma after "and," and the second choice omits the comma after "water."

practice.passage: After reviewing the budget figures, the planning committee found the proposal [super awesome] and approved it unanimously. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: The passage is a formal report, so the precise, formal word "persuasive" fits. The other choices are informal slang that clashes with the tone.

practice.passage: The internship taught her to write grant proposals, to manage a budget, and [presenting] research to donors. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: The list uses infinitives ("to write," "to manage"), so the third item must also be an infinitive: "to present." The original breaks the parallel structure with an -ing form.

practice.passage: Of the two routes to the lake, the coastal road is the [most scenic]. The bracketed portion of the sentence is the part being tested.
practice.prompt: Which choice is best for the bracketed portion?
practice.explanation: When comparing exactly two things, use the comparative form: "more scenic." The superlative "most" is for three or more.

practice.passage: Honeybees communicate the location of food through a movement called the waggle dance. [The angle of the dance relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food relative to the sun.] The duration of the waggle portion signals how far away the food is.
practice.prompt: If the writer deleted the bracketed sentence, the paragraph would primarily lose:
options: an explanation of how the dance conveys direction, one of the two pieces of information the paragraph describes.
a detail that contradicts the sentence that follows it.
an example of how bees locate sources of water.
a transition that introduces a new topic.
practice.explanation: The paragraph says the dance communicates location; the bracketed sentence covers direction and the next covers distance. Without it, half the explanation is missing. It does not contradict the next sentence, which adds a second piece of information.

practice.prompt: If 5(x - 2) = 3x + 8, what is the value of x?
practice.explanation: Distribute: 5x - 10 = 3x + 8, so 2x = 18 and x = 9. Choosing 3 usually comes from forgetting to distribute the 5 to the -2.

practice.prompt: A shirt regularly priced at $36 is on sale for 25% off. A 5% sales tax is applied to the sale price. What is the total cost?
practice.explanation: Sale price = 0.75 x 36 = $27.00; with tax, 27 x 1.05 = $28.35. Answering $27.00 forgets the tax, and $25.65 subtracts the tax instead of adding it.

practice.prompt: What is the value of |-7 + 3| - |2 - 9|?
practice.explanation: |-7 + 3| = |-4| = 4 and |2 - 9| = |-7| = 7, so 4 - 7 = -3. Answering 3 drops the sign of the final subtraction.

practice.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 46 centimeters and a length of 15 centimeters. What is its area, in square centimeters?
practice.explanation: Length plus width is 46 / 2 = 23, so the width is 8 and the area is 15 x 8 = 120. Using 23 as the width gives 345.

practice.prompt: What is the mean of the data set 4, 7, 7, 9, 13?
practice.explanation: The sum is 40 and there are 5 values, so the mean is 8. The value 7 is both the median and the mode, a common mix-up.

practice.prompt: If f(x) = 2x^2 - 3x + 1, what is f(-2)?
practice.explanation: f(-2) = 2(4) - 3(-2) + 1 = 8 + 6 + 1 = 15. Getting 3 comes from treating -3(-2) as -6.

practice.prompt: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 2 cups of milk. How many cups of milk are needed for 7.5 cups of flour?
practice.explanation: Milk = 7.5 x (2/3) = 5 cups. The answer 11.25 multiplies by 3/2, inverting the ratio.

practice.prompt: If 2x + 3y = 12 and x - y = 1, what is the value of x + y?
practice.explanation: From x = y + 1, 2(y + 1) + 3y = 12 gives y = 2 and x = 3, so x + y = 5. Check: 2(3) + 3(2) = 12.

practice.prompt: What is the minimum value of g(x) = x^2 - 6x + 5?
practice.explanation: The vertex is at x = -(-6)/2 = 3, and g(3) = 9 - 18 + 5 = -4. The answer 3 is the x-coordinate of the vertex, not the minimum value.

practice.prompt: A right triangle has legs of length 9 and 12. What is the length of the altitude drawn from the right angle to the hypotenuse?
practice.explanation: The hypotenuse is 15 and the area is (9 x 12)/2 = 54. Using the hypotenuse as the base, 54 = (15 x h)/2, so h = 7.2. The answer 7.5 is half the hypotenuse, which is the median, not the altitude.

practice.prompt: Two fair six-sided dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 8?
practice.explanation: The pairs (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) give 5 outcomes out of 36. The answer 1/6 is the probability of a sum of 7, which has 6 outcomes.

practice.prompt: Which of the following is equal to (2 + 3i)(1 - i), where i^2 = -1?
practice.explanation: Expand: 2 - 2i + 3i - 3i^2 = 2 + i + 3 = 5 + i. Choosing -1 + i treats -3i^2 as -3.

practice.prompt: What is the radius of the circle with equation x^2 + y^2 - 6x + 4y - 12 = 0?
practice.explanation: Completing the square: (x - 3)^2 + (y + 2)^2 = 12 + 9 + 4 = 25, so r = 5. The answer 25 is r^2, and 2√3 ignores the completed-square terms.

practice.prompt: A phone plan costs $25 per month plus $0.10 for each text message beyond the first 200. If a monthly bill is $41.50, how many text messages were sent that month?
practice.explanation: The extra charge is $16.50, which is 165 texts beyond 200, so 365 texts in total. The answer 165 forgets the 200 included texts.

practice.prompt: A town's population of 1,200 grows by 5% per year. To the nearest whole number, what is the population after 3 years?
practice.explanation: Exponential growth: 1,200(1.05)^3 = 1,389.15, which rounds to 1,389. The answer 1,380 adds 60 people per year, treating the growth as linear.

practice.prompt: Which of the following is the solution set of -3x + 7 > 19?
practice.explanation: Subtract 7 to get -3x > 12, then divide by -3 and reverse the inequality: x < -4. Forgetting to reverse the sign gives x > -4.

practice.prompt: The graph of f(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x^2 - x - 6) has which vertical asymptote(s)?
practice.explanation: f(x) = (x - 3)(x + 3)/((x - 3)(x + 2)). The factor (x - 3) cancels, leaving a hole at x = 3, so the only vertical asymptote is x = -2. Choosing both values ignores the cancellation.

practice.prompt: If sin θ = 5/13 and 90° < θ < 180°, what is the value of tan θ?
practice.explanation: cos θ = -√(1 - 25/169) = -12/13 because cosine is negative in Quadrant II, so tan θ = (5/13)/(-12/13) = -5/12. The answer 5/12 ignores the quadrant.

practice.prompt: For what value of k does the system kx + 4y = 8 and 3x + 6y = 5 have no solution?
practice.explanation: No solution requires equal slopes and different intercepts: -k/4 = -3/6 gives k = 2. Then the equations become x + 2y = 4 and x + 2y = 5/3, which are parallel and distinct.

practice.prompt: The mean of 8 test scores is 82. When the highest and lowest scores are removed, the mean of the remaining scores is 83. If the highest score is 97, what is the lowest score?
practice.explanation: Total of 8 scores = 656; total of the remaining 6 = 498. The two removed scores sum to 158, so the lowest is 158 - 97 = 61.

practice.prompt: Matrix A has rows [2 1] and [3 4]. What is the determinant of 2A?
practice.explanation: det A = 2(4) - 1(3) = 5. Doubling a 2 by 2 matrix doubles both rows, multiplying the determinant by 2^2 = 4, so det(2A) = 20. The answer 10 doubles only once.

practice.prompt: What is the solution set of log_2(x) + log_2(x - 2) = 3?
practice.explanation: Combine: log_2(x(x - 2)) = 3, so x^2 - 2x = 8 and x = 4 or x = -2. Since log_2(-2) is undefined, only x = 4 works.

practice.passage:
Literary narrative. The ferry left at seven, and by six-forty Nadia was already on the dock, her suitcase upright beside her like a patient dog. Her grandmother had insisted on coming, though the wind off the harbor made her cough, and now she stood a careful step behind Nadia, as if to make clear that the leaving was Nadia's idea and not hers.

"You packed the blue sweater," her grandmother said. It was not a question. Nadia had packed it twice, once when she first filled the suitcase and again at midnight, after taking it out to make room for books and then deciding the books could wait.

For nineteen years the island had been the whole size of the world. Nadia knew which fisherman's dog would follow you to the post office and which would not; she knew that the church bell ran four minutes fast and that no one had fixed it because everyone had learned to subtract. In the city, she supposed, the clocks would be right, and no one would know they had ever been wrong.

When the ferry horn sounded, her grandmother finally stepped forward and pressed something into Nadia's palm: a brass key, warm from her pocket. "The front door," she said. "In case you forget which one it is."

Nadia laughed, and then, to her surprise, could not stop her eyes from stinging. There was only one front door on the whole lane that had ever been hers.
practice.prompt: Which choice best describes the main focus of the passage?
options: A grandmother's attempt to persuade her granddaughter not to leave
The history of a small island's ferry service
A young woman's departure from her home island and her complicated feelings about leaving
A young woman's simple excitement about moving to a city
practice.explanation: The passage centers on Nadia leaving, her memories of the island, and her unexpected emotion at the end. The grandmother never argues against the departure, so the second choice is unsupported.

distrusted the church and its officials.

practice.prompt: The final sentence most strongly implies that Nadia:
options: worries that she will lose the key in the city.

is merely amused that her grandmother thinks she might forget the door.

practice.passage:
Social science. Walk across almost any college campus and you will find them: narrow strips of bare dirt cutting diagonally across lawns where no sidewalk was planned. Urban planners call these "desire paths," and for decades they were treated as a maintenance problem. Groundskeepers fenced them off, replanted the grass, and posted signs asking pedestrians to stay on the pavement. The paths usually came back within a season.

More recently, some planners have begun to treat desire paths as data. If hundreds of people choose the same shortcut, the reasoning goes, the shortcut reveals something the original designers missed, perhaps a bus stop that was added later or a building entrance that shifted. A few universities now delay paving new walkways until a year after a building opens, allowing foot traffic to show where sidewalks are actually needed before any concrete is poured.

The approach has critics. Some landscape architects point out that a desire path reflects the preferences of people who already use a space, not those who might use it if it were designed differently. A path worn by students hurrying to a lecture hall, for example, says little about where an elderly visitor or a person using a wheelchair would want to go. Others note that shortcuts are often only marginally shorter; people may take them out of habit rather than real need.

Still, even skeptics tend to agree on one point: a path that keeps reappearing after being fenced off is a signal worth investigating rather than ignoring.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, how did groundskeepers traditionally respond to desire paths?
options: They fenced them off and replanted the grass.
They paved them into official sidewalks.
They used them to plan new buildings.
They left them alone as harmless.
practice.explanation: The first paragraph says groundskeepers "fenced them off, replanted the grass, and posted signs." Paving them is the newer approach described later, not the traditional one.

A path worn by students hurrying to a lecture hall, for example, says little about where an elderly visitor or a person using a wheelchair would want to go. Others note that shortcuts are often only marginally shorter; people may take them out of habit rather than real need.

Still, even skeptics tend to agree on one point: a path that keeps reappearing after being fenced off is a signal worth investigating rather than ignoring.
practice.prompt: It can reasonably be inferred that some universities wait a year after a building opens to pave walkways so that they can:
options: save money by postponing construction costs.
see where people actually walk before building permanent sidewalks.
give newly planted grass time to grow.
allow critics to review the building's design.
practice.explanation: The passage says delaying lets "foot traffic show where sidewalks are actually needed before any concrete is poured." Saving money may be a side effect, but the passage does not mention it.

practice.passage:
Text 1
Many gardeners believe that talking to plants helps them grow, and a handful of small experiments have been cited in support. The more likely explanation is mundane: gardeners who talk to their plants tend to spend more time near them, noticing wilting leaves, pests, and dry soil sooner. The benefit, in other words, comes from attention, not from sound.

Text 2
Plants do respond to vibration. Studies have shown that the roots of some species grow toward the sound of running water, and certain flowers produce sweeter nectar within minutes of being exposed to the buzz of a pollinating bee. None of this proves that conversation benefits a houseplant, but it suggests that dismissing sound as irrelevant to plant biology would be premature.

options: Plants grow toward the sound of human voices.
Gardeners who talk to plants also spend more time watching and caring for them.
The carbon dioxide in human breath feeds the plants.
Plants produce sweeter nectar when they hear speech.
practice.explanation: Text 1 credits attention: these gardeners notice wilting, pests and dry soil sooner. The nectar detail comes from Text 2 and concerns bee buzzing, not speech.

Conflicting viewpoints. A metal spoon and a wooden spoon have been lying on the same table in a room at 22°C for several hours. When a student touches them, the metal spoon feels colder.

Student 1: The metal spoon really is at a lower temperature than the wooden spoon. Metals absorb cold from the surrounding air, so the metal spoon has cooled below room temperature, while wood does not absorb cold.

Student 2: Both spoons are at room temperature. Metal conducts heat much faster than wood, so when a warm hand touches the metal spoon, heat flows from the hand into the metal quickly. The skin cools faster, so the metal feels colder even though both spoons are at 22°C.

the same temperature for both spoons.
a lower temperature for the wooden spoon.
practice.explanation: Student 2 says both spoons are at room temperature, 22°C. A lower reading for the metal spoon is Student 1's prediction.

lessons.title: IELTS Academic at a glance: bands and what examiners want
lessons.body: IELTS Academic has four parts: Listening (about 30 minutes, 40 questions), Reading (60 minutes, 40 questions, three long passages), Writing (60 minutes, two tasks) and Speaking (11-14 minutes with an examiner). The total is about 2 hours 45 minutes, and the format is the same on paper, on computer, and online. Each skill gets a band from 0 to 9, and the overall band is their average, rounded to the nearest half band. Listening and Reading raw scores out of 40 are converted to bands, while Writing and Speaking are judged against public band descriptors. For Writing these are Task Achievement or Response, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy; Speaking uses Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammar, and Pronunciation. Mini-example: Listening 7.0, Reading 6.5, Writing 6.0 and Speaking 6.5 average 6.5, so the overall band is 6.5. Universities often require a minimum in each skill as well as overall, so check the exact requirements and focus on your weakest skill first.

lessons.title: Reading: True / False / Not Given without the panic
lessons.body: True/False/Not Given questions test whether a statement matches the information in the passage. True means the passage states the same idea, usually in different words. False means the passage directly contradicts it. Not Given means the passage does not say either way. The classic mistake is answering from general knowledge or from what seems logical. Method: underline the key words in the statement, especially qualifiers such as "all", "only", "always" and "more than", and numbers. Scan for the matching part of the passage; questions follow the passage order. Then compare meaning precisely. Mini-example: the passage says "Most participants preferred the new design." Statement A, "All participants preferred the new design", is False because "most" contradicts "all". Statement B, "The new design was cheaper to produce", is Not Given if cost is never mentioned. Do not spend more than about 90 seconds hunting for one answer; if you truly cannot find the information anywhere, that itself is a clue toward Not Given.

lessons.title: Reading: headings, completion tasks and the 20-minute rule
lessons.body: You have 60 minutes for three passages that get harder, so aim for about 17, 20 and 23 minutes, and transfer answers as you go; there is no extra transfer time on Reading. For matching headings, read each paragraph's first and last sentences and ask what the whole paragraph is about, not what one sentence mentions. Distractor headings often repeat a word from the paragraph while describing a minor detail. For sentence, summary and table completion, check the word limit: if the instructions say "NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS", a three-word answer is wrong even if the meaning is right. Copy spelling exactly from the passage, and check that your answer fits the grammar of the gap. Mini-example: "The researchers measured the ______ of each sample." If the passage says "they recorded how acidic each sample was" and later "the acidity levels", the answer is "acidity", a noun, because "the ___ of" needs a noun. Build speed by doing one full passage daily under a timer and reviewing every wrong answer.

lessons.title: Listening: predict, follow, and beware of changes of mind
lessons.body: The four Listening parts move from everyday conversation to an academic lecture, and you hear each recording only once. Use the short pause before each part to read the questions and predict the type of answer: a number, a date, a name, a noun. In completion tasks, the speaker often gives a wrong option before correcting it: "We meet on Tuesday, oh no, sorry, it moved to Thursday." The answer is the final version. Spelling counts, so practise names and addresses that are spelled aloud, and learn how people say dates and numbers, for example "double seven" for 77. Multiple-choice questions usually mention all the options, so listen for the one the speaker actually chooses or confirms. Mini-example: the question asks for "the cost per person". You hear "The full group rate is 300 pounds, which works out at 25 each." The answer is 25, not 300. If you miss an answer, let it go immediately and listen for the next one; chasing it costs two more.

lessons.title: Writing Task 1 and Task 2: structures that score
lessons.body: Task 1 (at least 150 words, about 20 minutes) asks you to describe a chart, table, map or process. Write an introduction that paraphrases the prompt, an overview of the two or three main trends without detailed numbers, which examiners look for specifically, and two body paragraphs that group and compare key data. Do not give opinions or causes. Task 2 (at least 250 words, about 40 minutes) counts for more, so never leave it short. Answer every part of the question: "discuss both views and give your opinion" requires both views and a clear opinion. Use four paragraphs: introduction with position, two body paragraphs each with one main idea, an explanation, and an example, and a conclusion. Mini-example overview for a chart of energy use: "Overall, coal use declined steadily while solar and wind grew, and by 2025 renewables had overtaken coal." Avoid memorised phrases such as "in this day and age"; examiners recognise them. Accuracy matters more than complexity: a correct compound sentence beats a broken complex one.

lessons.title: Speaking: extend, structure and self-correct
lessons.body: Speaking has three parts. Part 1 asks familiar questions about home, work or study and interests; give two or three sentences, not one word. Part 2 gives you a task card and one minute to prepare a talk of up to two minutes. Use the minute to note three or four keywords, not full sentences, covering each prompt on the card, and keep speaking until the examiner stops you. Part 3 is a discussion of more abstract ideas linked to Part 2. Here use a simple pattern: answer, reason, example, and a contrast or qualification. Mini-example: "Should cities ban cars from the centre?" "To some extent, yes. Fewer cars mean cleaner air, and when my city closed its main square to traffic, cafes there got busier. That said, older people and delivery drivers still need some access." Fluency does not mean speed; natural pauses are fine. If you make a mistake, correct it briefly and continue, which shows control. Practise by recording yourself and checking for repeated words, and learn topic vocabulary in phrases.

lessons.title: Listening Parts 1 and 2: forms, spelling and map tasks
lessons.body: Parts 1 and 2 of IELTS Listening are the everyday-context sections: Part 1 is a conversation between two people (often a booking, an enquiry or a registration) and Part 2 is a monologue such as a guided tour or an information talk. Each of the four parts has 10 questions, and you hear each recording once only, so these early parts are where you collect safe marks. Before the audio starts, use the reading time to predict the type of answer for every gap. "Date of arrival: ____" needs a date; "Cost per night: ____" needs a number with a currency; "Name of street: ____" will probably be spelled out letter by letter. Write a tiny note next to each gap (N for number, D for date, S for spelling) so your brain is ready. Spelling counts. A correct idea spelled wrongly is marked wrong, so practise the alphabet aloud until letters that sound alike (A/E/I, G/J, B/P/V, M/N) are automatic. Learn how speakers say "double" letters ("double R") and how British and Australian speakers read phone numbers in groups ("oh-seven-nine-four-five", "three-one-eight"). Always check the word limit in the instructions: if it says ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER, then "the Garden Studio" written in full may break the limit, while "Garden Studio" fits. Expect distractors. Speakers often give an answer and then change it: "The Tuesday group is full, but we have opened a Thursday group." The first information is a trap. Words like "actually", "sorry, I mean", "it used to be" and "that has changed" signal a correction. For map and plan labelling in Part 2, find your starting point first ("You are at the visitor centre at the southern entrance"), then follow the speaker with your pencil. Direction words matter: "on your left as you face the lake", "directly opposite", "beyond", "at the far end". Do not jump ahead if you miss one label; the questions follow the order of the talk, so let it go and catch the next. At the end, use the transfer or check time (paper tests allow extra transfer time; on computer you have a short review period) to fix capital letters for names, plural endings and units.

lessons.title: Listening Parts 3 and 4: discussions and lectures
lessons.body: Parts 3 and 4 move into academic settings. Part 3 is usually a discussion between two or more speakers, such as students and a tutor planning a project. Part 4 is a lecture by one speaker with no break in the middle, and it is usually tested with note, table, summary or flow-chart completion. Part 3: track who says what. Multiple-choice and matching questions often ask about one speaker's opinion. When Maya suggests an idea and Tom replies "I'm not sure that would solve the problem", the question "What does Tom think about the idea?" is testing that reaction, not the original suggestion. Listen for agreement and disagreement signals: "that's a fair point", "I take your point, but", "I'd go further", "that's exactly what I was worried about". A tutor's final instruction ("Do both, and record where each response came from") is a favourite target for the last question in a set. With three or four options, read the stem and underline the key idea, then mark options as you hear them mentioned. Every option is often mentioned; the correct one is the one the speaker actually chooses or concludes. Part 4: use the headings. Notes are organised like the lecture itself: "Measuring past climate", "Dating the layers", "Storage". The speaker usually signposts each section: "Let's turn now to...", "How do researchers date the layers?", "Finally, a practical point." When you hear a signpost, move your eyes to the matching heading even if you missed an earlier gap. Predict grammar and meaning. In "Air bubbles are used to measure past levels of ____", the gap needs a noun, probably a gas or substance. In "Deep layers are too ____ to count", you need an adjective. The answer usually uses the speaker's exact words, while the notes paraphrase the surrounding sentence ("compressed so thin" in the audio may appear as "too ____ to count"). Expect cautious language. Lecturers often hedge: "results are still being analysed", "this may be partly explained by". Options that turn a hedge into a certainty are wrong. Practice routine: play a recorded lecture, write notes under three headings, then write a 3-sentence summary from memory. This trains you to follow structure rather than individual words.

lessons.title: Reading: matching information, features and sentence endings
lessons.body: Matching tasks reward a different reading strategy from True/False/Not Given, because the answers usually do NOT follow the order of the passage. Matching information asks which paragraph contains a specific piece of information, such as "a reference to a limitation of a study" or "an example of an official decision". The key is to recognise the type of information, not just topic words. "A limitation of a study" might appear as "although the sample was small" or "the authors cautioned that". "An official decision" might be "the island made the language a compulsory school subject". Read the list of statements first, convert each into a type ("a warning", "a date", "a comparison", "a criticism"), then read the passage paragraph by paragraph and tick statements as they match. Some paragraphs may be used more than once, and some not at all, so check the instructions. Matching features gives you a list of people, places or dates and asks you to match statements to them. Circle every name in the passage first so you can find them quickly. Then read the sentences around each name carefully: researchers are often contrasted ("by contrast", "a third researcher"), and the statement will paraphrase what each one found. Watch for a statement that combines two people's ideas; it belongs to whoever is actually responsible for the specific claim. Matching sentence endings asks you to join sentence beginnings to endings. Two checks make this reliable. First, grammar: the ending must continue the beginning grammatically ("In tonal languages, whistlers mainly..." needs a verb phrase such as "follow the melody of the tones"). Second, meaning: there are always more endings than beginnings, and the extra endings often use real words from the passage but belong to a different subject. For example, "imitate vowel sounds as higher and lower notes" is true in the passage, but for non-tonal languages, not tonal ones. Time management: give matching tasks a firm limit. With about 20 minutes per passage, aim to finish any easy completion questions first, then do matching, which takes longer because you must search the whole text. If you are stuck on one statement, eliminate the paragraphs you have already used confidently and make an informed guess; there is no penalty for wrong answers.

lessons.title: Writing Task 1: overview, grouping and accurate comparison
lessons.body: In Academic Writing Task 1 you describe visual information such as a graph, table, chart, process or map in at least 150 words, and you are advised to spend about 20 minutes on it. You are assessed on Task Achievement, Coherence and Cohesion, Lexical Resource, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. The single most important sentence is the overview: a summary of the main trends or most striking features without detailed numbers. Without a clear overview it is very hard to reach the higher bands for Task Achievement. A strong overview for a table of household heating sources in 2005 and 2025 might read: "Overall, gas remained the most common heating source despite a fall in its share, while heat pumps saw by far the largest increase." Notice that it compares, it selects, and it contains no figures. Next, group the data. Instead of describing each category in turn (gas, then electricity, then heat pumps, then oil), organise two body paragraphs around patterns: sources that grew (heat pumps, electricity, other) and sources that declined (gas, oil). Grouping shows the examiner that you can select key features rather than list everything. Be precise with numbers. If the share using electricity moved from 20% to 22%, it rose by 2 percentage points, which is a 10% increase in relative terms. Writing "rose by 2%" is inaccurate. Useful accurate patterns include: "rose from 2% to 17%", "more than eightfold", "fell by 14 percentage points", "was overtaken by", "remained the second most common", "accounted for just under half". Do not explain causes. Task 1 asks you to report what the data shows. Sentences such as "This is because people care more about the environment" add information that is not in the chart and can distract from the task. Vary your language without forcing it. Mix noun phrases ("a sharp decline in oil use") with verb phrases ("oil use declined sharply"), and use comparatives ("heat pumps were nearly as common as oil had been in 2005"). A simple timed plan: 2 minutes to find the 2-3 key features, 1 introduction sentence that paraphrases the title, 1-2 overview sentences, two grouped body paragraphs, and 2 minutes to check numbers against the chart.

lessons.title: Writing Task 2: question types, planning and paragraphs that develop
lessons.body: Task 2 is an essay of at least 250 words and carries more weight than Task 1, so give it about 40 minutes. Start by identifying exactly what the question asks, because Task Response depends on answering every part. Common question types: "To what extent do you agree or disagree?" requires a clear position, maintained throughout. "Discuss both views and give your own opinion" requires a fair treatment of each view plus your opinion. "What are the causes of this problem and what solutions can you suggest?" has two parts, and both need roughly equal development. "Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?" requires a judgement, not just two lists. Spend about 5 minutes planning. Write your position in one sentence before writing anything else, then note two main ideas, each with an explanation and an example. For "Some people think cities should make public transport free. To what extent do you agree?", a plan might be: Position: mostly agree, with conditions. Idea 1: reduces car use and congestion; example: a city that removed bus fares and saw more bus passengers. Idea 2: costs must be covered; explain how a congestion charge could fund it. Build each body paragraph in four moves: a topic sentence that states the point, an explanation of why it is true, a specific example, and a link back to the question. A weak paragraph lists three ideas in three sentences; a strong paragraph develops one idea fully. Examiners reward relevant, extended and supported ideas. Cohesion is more than linking words. Use referencing ("this policy", "such costs") and paragraph-level organisation. Overusing "Moreover" and "Furthermore" at the start of every sentence can lower your Coherence and Cohesion score. Choose linkers by meaning: "However" for contrast, "As a result" for consequence, "For instance" for examples. For Lexical Resource, prefer precise collocations to vague ones: "a pressing concern" rather than "a big problem", "ease congestion" rather than "make traffic less". For grammar, aim for a mix of simple and complex sentences, and keep 3-4 minutes at the end to check subject-verb agreement, articles and plural endings, which are the most frequent errors.

lessons.title: Speaking Parts 2 and 3: the long turn and the discussion
lessons.body: The Speaking test is a face-to-face interview with an examiner lasting 11 to 14 minutes. Part 1 is short questions about familiar topics, Part 2 is the long turn, and Part 3 is a discussion of more abstract ideas linked to the Part 2 topic. You are assessed on Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation. Part 2: you receive a task card with a topic and several prompts, one minute to prepare, and you speak for one to two minutes. The examiner will stop you if you go beyond two minutes. Use the minute well: write 2-3 keywords for each prompt, not sentences. For "Describe a skill you learned outside school", notes might be: "pottery - evening class - neighbour", "first bowl collapsed", "patience - mistakes are normal". Then add one story-telling detail, because a short anecdote makes it easy to keep talking naturally. If you run out of ideas before two minutes, do not stop. Extend with time ("At first... later..."), feelings ("What surprised me was..."), comparison ("Compared with learning at school...") or the future ("I would like to..."). Silence wastes your opportunity to show language. Part 3: the questions are broader. "Why do some people prefer learning skills online?" is not asking about your personal habits; it is asking about people in general. A strong answer gives a direct opinion, a reason, an example and, ideally, a contrast: "I think the main reason is flexibility. Someone with a full-time job can watch a lesson at midnight. That said, practical skills like cooking are harder to learn without feedback." Use speculative and hedging language naturally: "It's likely that...", "I'd imagine...", "This may depend on...". If you do not understand a Part 3 question, you can ask the examiner to rephrase it: "Could you put that another way?" This is better than guessing and answering a different question. Pronunciation is about being easy to understand, not about a particular accent. Practise word stress on common topic words (environment, technology, economy), chunk your speech into meaningful groups, and let your intonation rise and fall to show what is important. Record yourself answering a Part 3 question and listen for long pauses or flat delivery.

practice.passage: Cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, a phenomenon known as the urban heat island effect. Dark surfaces such as asphalt and roofing absorb sunlight during the day and release heat slowly at night, which is why the temperature gap is usually largest after sunset. Trees reduce this effect in two ways: their canopies shade the ground, and water evaporating from their leaves cools the surrounding air. A study in one city found that streets with continuous tree cover were up to 5 degrees Celsius cooler at ground level on summer afternoons than nearby streets without trees. However, planting is not a simple solution. Young trees need several years to provide meaningful shade, and in dry regions irrigation can place pressure on water supplies. Some planners therefore combine planting with 'cool roofs', which are coated with reflective materials. Critics note that reflective roofs mainly benefit the building's occupants and do less for people at street level.
practice.prompt: The temperature difference between cities and the countryside tends to be greatest at night.
practice.explanation: The passage says the gap "is usually largest after sunset", which matches the statement.

practice.passage: Before the 1950s, loading a cargo ship was slow and labour-intensive. Goods arrived at ports in sacks, barrels and crates of different sizes, and teams of dockworkers moved each item by hand, a process that could keep a ship in port for a week or more. The standardised steel container changed this. Because every container had the same dimensions and fittings, cranes could lift them directly from trucks or trains onto ships. Loading times fell dramatically, and theft at ports declined because goods remained sealed from factory to destination. The benefits were not evenly shared, however. Many traditional port cities lacked the space for the large container terminals that the new system required, and dock employment fell sharply in some of them. Economists still debate how much of the growth in world trade since the 1960s can be attributed to containers rather than to falling tariffs, but most agree that the reduction in handling costs was substantial.

practice.explanation: The passage says goods arrived in "sacks, barrels and crates of different sizes", which contradicts "uniform size".

practice.passage: Researchers have long suspected that sleep helps the brain consolidate new memories. In a recent experiment, two groups of university students learned a list of unfamiliar word pairs in the evening. One group slept normally, while the other stayed awake under supervision. When tested the next morning, the students who had slept recalled about 20 per cent more pairs. Interestingly, a third group that learned the words in the morning and was tested in the evening of the same day, without sleeping, performed similarly to the group that had stayed awake overnight. The authors suggest this indicates that the benefit came from sleep itself rather than from the time of day of the test. They caution, however, that the participants were all young adults, and that the findings may not apply to older people, whose sleep patterns differ.

practice.passage: Peatlands cover only a small fraction of the world's land surface, yet they store a remarkably large share of soil carbon. Peat forms when waterlogged conditions slow the decay of dead plants, allowing material to accumulate over thousands of years. When peatlands are drained for agriculture or forestry, the peat dries out and the stored carbon begins to escape into the atmosphere as carbon dioxide. Restoration usually begins with blocking drainage ditches so that the water table rises again. Mosses that thrive in wet conditions may then recolonise the site, although full recovery of the ecosystem can take decades. Landowners are sometimes reluctant to restore drained land, because it reduces the area available for grazing or crops. In several countries, governments now offer payments to compensate them.

Transcript:
Guide: Welcome to Marsh End Nature Reserve. You're standing at the visitor centre, which is at the southern entrance. The main path heads north from here, and after about 200 metres it splits in two. If you take the left fork, you'll come to the bird hide, which overlooks the large lake. That's the best spot for herons, especially early in the morning. The right fork crosses the reed beds on a wooden boardwalk, but the boardwalk is closed this month while it's repaired, so please don't try to use it. If you want the woodland trail on the eastern side, come back past the visitor centre and follow the road east for about ten minutes instead. The picnic area is beside the car park, directly west of the visitor centre. There are toilets inside the visitor centre only, not on the trails. One change from our printed leaflet: the cafe used to be beside the lake, but it has moved to the first floor of the visitor centre. Finally, guided walks leave from the visitor centre at ten and at two. The afternoon walk is free for children under twelve; adults pay four pounds for either walk.

On the road east of the visitor centre

At the end of the left fork, beside the large lake
practice.explanation: The guide says the left fork leads to the bird hide overlooking the large lake. The right fork leads over the reed beds, and the area west of the visitor centre is the car park and picnic area.
