practice.passage:
Transcript:
Lecturer: Today I want to look at ice cores as records of past climate. In places like Antarctica and Greenland, the snow that falls each year doesn't melt. Over time it's compressed into ice, and tiny bubbles of air become trapped inside. These bubbles are effectively samples of the ancient atmosphere, so by measuring the gases inside them, scientists can estimate past levels of carbon dioxide.
Temperature is estimated in a different way: not from the bubbles, but from the ice itself. Water containing heavier forms of oxygen condenses more readily, so the ratio of heavy to light oxygen in the snow changes with temperature.
How do researchers date the layers? Near the surface, they can simply count annual layers, rather like tree rings, because summer and winter snow look different. Deeper down, though, the layers are squeezed so thin that counting becomes impossible. Instead, scientists use models of how ice flows, and they check those models against known events. Large volcanic eruptions are especially useful here, because they leave layers of ash and sulphur that can be matched to eruptions dated by other methods.
The longest continuous record so far comes from Antarctica and covers roughly 800,000 years. Several teams are now drilling for ice that may be well over a million years old, though I should stress that results from those projects are still being analysed.
Finally, a practical point. Cores are usually cut along their length, and part of each section is archived without being touched. That's because once ice is melted for analysis, it can never be measured again, and future researchers may have techniques that we don't have today.
practice.prompt: Complete the notes. Air bubbles in the ice are used to measure past levels of ______.
practice.explanation: The lecturer says measuring gases in the bubbles lets scientists estimate past carbon dioxide levels. Oxygen ratios are measured in the ice itself, and ash and sulphur come from volcanic layers.

How do researchers date the layers? Near the surface, they can simply count annual layers, rather like tree rings, because summer and winter snow look different. Deeper down, though, the layers are squeezed so thin that counting becomes impossible. Instead, scientists use models of how ice flows, and they check those models against known events. Large volcanic eruptions are especially useful here, because they leave layers of ash and sulphur that can be matched to eruptions dated by other methods.
The longest continuous record so far comes from Antarctica and covers roughly 800,000 years. Several teams are now drilling for ice that may be well over a million years old, though I should stress that results from those projects are still being analysed.
Finally, a practical point. Cores are usually cut along their length, and part of each section is archived without being touched. That's because once ice is melted for analysis, it can never be measured again, and future researchers may have techniques that we don't have today.

practice.passage:
Rethinking the timetable: should schools start later?
For decades, most secondary schools have opened at roughly the same early hour, a schedule shaped more by bus routes and parents' working days than by any evidence about learning. That evidence now exists, and in my view it is difficult to ignore.
During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later: teenagers typically begin to feel sleepy considerably later in the evening than they did as children. Because their waking time is fixed by the school day, many do not get the amount of sleep that health bodies recommend for their age group.
Several research teams have studied what happens when the start time moves. Dr Lena Okafor followed two districts that moved their opening time from 7:45 to 8:30 and found that students gained, on average, around forty minutes of sleep a night, rather than, as critics had predicted, simply going to bed forty minutes later. Professor Marcus Hale, by contrast, focused on attendance and reported a modest fall in late arrivals in the first term, although the effect had weakened by the end of the year. A third researcher, Dr Priya Nandakumar, examined road safety data and found fewer accidents involving teenage drivers after start times changed, a result she cautioned could partly reflect wider improvements in vehicle safety.
Opponents raise practical objections. A later start can push sports practice and part-time jobs into the evening, and families with younger children may find drop-off times harder to coordinate. These concerns are real, but I believe they are problems of organisation rather than reasons to dismiss the research. Schools that changed successfully usually did so gradually: they first surveyed families, then renegotiated bus contracts, ran the new timetable for a trial term, and only then made it permanent.
What I find least convincing is the claim that teenagers would simply stay up later. The data on this point are fairly consistent, and they suggest otherwise. Still, a later start is no cure-all. Screens in bedrooms, heavy homework loads and anxiety also affect sleep, and no change to the timetable will solve those on its own.
practice.prompt: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer? Current early start times were originally chosen for educational reasons.
practice.explanation: The writer says the schedule was shaped "more by bus routes and parents' working days than by any evidence about learning", which contradicts the idea of educational reasons.

Rethinking the timetable: should schools start later?
For decades, most secondary schools have opened at roughly the same early hour, a schedule shaped more by bus routes and parents' working days than by any evidence about learning. That evidence now exists, and in my view it is difficult to ignore.
During adolescence, the body's internal clock shifts later: teenagers typically begin to feel sleepy considerably later in the evening than they did as children. Because their waking time is fixed by the school day, many do not get the amount of sleep that health bodies recommend for their age group.
Several research teams have studied what happens when the start time moves. Dr Lena Okafor followed two districts that moved their opening time from 7:45 to 8:30 and found that students gained, on average, around forty minutes of sleep a night, rather than, as critics had predicted, simply going to bed forty minutes later. Professor Marcus Hale, by contrast, focused on attendance and reported a modest fall in late arrivals in the first term, although the effect had weakened by the end of the year. A third researcher, Dr Priya Nandakumar, examined road safety data and found fewer accidents involving teenage drivers after start times changed, a result she cautioned could partly reflect wider improvements in vehicle safety.
Opponents raise practical objections. A later start can push sports practice and part-time jobs into the evening, and families with younger children may find drop-off times harder to coordinate. These concerns are real, but I believe they are problems of organisation rather than reasons to dismiss the research. Schools that changed successfully usually did so gradually: they first surveyed families, then renegotiated bus contracts, ran the new timetable for a trial term, and only then made it permanent.
What I find least convincing is the claim that teenagers would simply stay up later. The data on this point are fairly consistent, and they suggest otherwise. Still, a later start is no cure-all. Screens in bedrooms, heavy homework loads and anxiety also affect sleep, and no change to the timetable will solve those on its own.
practice.prompt: Do the following statements agree with the views of the writer? Students who sleep longer achieve higher exam grades.
practice.explanation: The writer discusses sleep, attendance and road safety, but never mentions exam grades. It may seem logical, but the writer gives no view on it, so it is Not Given rather than Yes.

practice.prompt: Which best summarises the writer's overall position?

Later start times should be introduced immediately in every school.

table.caption: Percentage of households using each main heating source in one country

practice.prompt: Which sentence would make the best overview for a Task 1 report on this table?
options: Overall, governments should encourage more households to install heat pumps.
In 2005, 62% of households used gas, compared with 20% for electricity and 12% for oil.
Overall, electricity replaced gas as the most popular heating source over the period.
Overall, gas remained the most common heating source despite a fall in its share, while heat pumps showed by far the largest increase.
practice.explanation: A good overview summarises the main features without detailed figures, and this sentence picks out the two key trends accurately. The figures-only sentence is detail, the electricity claim is inaccurate (gas is still highest), and the last option is an opinion that Task 1 does not ask for.

table.caption: Percentage of households using each main heating source in one country

practice.prompt: Which sentence describes the data accurately?
options: The proportion using electricity rose by 2%.
The proportion of households using heat pumps rose by 15 percentage points.
The proportion using oil more than halved.
The proportion using gas fell by 14%.
practice.explanation: Heat pumps rose from 2% to 17%, a rise of 15 percentage points. Electricity rose by 2 percentage points (a 10% relative increase), gas fell by 14 points (about 23% in relative terms), and oil fell from 12% to 7%, which is less than half.

table.caption: Percentage of households using each main heating source in one country

practice.prompt: A candidate wants to add this sentence to the report: "Heat pumps became popular because people became more worried about climate change." What is the best advice?
options: Keep it, but add a statistic to support it.
Keep it, but move it into the overview.
Leave it out, because Task 1 asks you to report the data, not to explain causes that are not shown.
Keep it, because explaining causes raises the Task Achievement score.
practice.explanation: Task 1 is a report of the visual information. Reasons that are not in the table are speculation and do not help Task Achievement; moving the sentence into the overview would make the overview weaker.

practice.prompt: What are the minimum length and the recommended time for Academic Writing Task 1?
options: At least 150 words in about 20 minutes
At least 150 words in about 40 minutes
At least 250 words in about 40 minutes
At least 100 words in about 15 minutes
practice.explanation: Task 1 requires at least 150 words, and candidates are advised to spend about 20 minutes on it. 250 words and 40 minutes are the figures for Task 2.

practice.prompt: The question says: "Some people think cities should make public transport free. To what extent do you agree or disagree?" What must the essay include?
options: A balanced description of both sides with no personal opinion
A description of public transport in your home city
A clear position on the statement that is maintained throughout
A list of advantages and disadvantages without a conclusion
practice.explanation: "To what extent do you agree or disagree" asks for your own position, clearly stated and consistently developed. An essay that only describes both sides without a view does not fully answer this question type.

practice.prompt: Which thesis statement best answers "Some people believe children should start school at four; others think seven is better. Discuss both views and give your own opinion"?
options: Children start school at different ages in different countries around the world.
While an early start can build social skills, I believe a later start, combined with high-quality preschool play, gives children a stronger foundation.
Starting school at four is clearly the only sensible choice for every family.
This essay will discuss whether children should start school at four or at seven.
practice.explanation: The best thesis acknowledges the other view and gives a clear opinion, which matches both parts of the question. Announcing the topic gives no opinion, and the last option ignores the other view entirely.

practice.prompt: Choose the best linking word. "Free public transport would cut costs for low-income workers. ______, it could reduce traffic in the city centre."
practice.explanation: The second sentence adds another benefit, so an additive linker is needed. "However" and "Nevertheless" signal contrast, and "As a result" wrongly suggests that reduced traffic is caused by cheaper fares for workers.

practice.skill: Writing Task 2: Grammatical range and accuracy
practice.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: The number of people who commutes by car have risen sharply.
Despite of the high cost, many families prefers private cars.
If the government will reduce fares, more people would use buses.
Had the city invested in cycle lanes earlier, fewer residents would depend on cars today.
practice.explanation: The correct option is a mixed conditional with inversion ("Had the city invested ... would depend"). The others contain errors: "commutes/have" should be "commute/has", "despite of" and "prefers" are wrong, and "if ... will" should be "if ... reduced".

practice.prompt: Topic sentence: "Free public transport could significantly reduce congestion." Which next sentence develops this point most effectively?
options: Public transport is also important for tourists who visit the city.
However, some people argue that free transport is too expensive.
When fares are removed, commuters who currently drive short distances have a strong incentive to switch to buses, which take far less road space per passenger.
Congestion is a problem in many cities around the world.
practice.explanation: A developing sentence explains how or why the topic sentence is true. The tourist sentence changes topic, the general statement repeats rather than develops, and the counter-argument moves away before the point is supported.

practice.prompt: Which phrase is the most precise and natural replacement for "a big problem" in "Air pollution is a big problem for city residents"?
practice.explanation: "A pressing concern" is a natural collocation meaning an urgent problem. "Heavy concern" and "strong trouble" are not standard collocations, and "difficulty case" is unnatural; using unnatural collocations can lower Lexical Resource.

practice.prompt: How is the Writing score affected by the two tasks?
options: Only Task 2 is scored; Task 1 is practice.
Task 2 carries more weight than Task 1.
Task 1 carries more weight because it comes first.
Both tasks carry exactly equal weight.
practice.explanation: Task 2 contributes more to the Writing band than Task 1, which is why about 40 of the 60 minutes are recommended for it. Task 1 is still scored, so it should not be skipped.

practice.prompt: The examiner asks: "Do you prefer mornings or evenings?" Which answer is the most effective?
options: In my opinion, there are many advantages and disadvantages of mornings and evenings in modern society.
I prefer mornings or evenings depending on the situation, morning or evening.
Definitely mornings. My mind is clearest before nine, so I usually do my hardest studying then, although I'm useless after about ten at night.
practice.explanation: A good Part 1 answer is direct and then extended with a reason or example in natural language. A one-word reply gives no evidence of language, the repetitive answer shows weak fluency, and the essay-style opening sounds memorised and avoids the question.

practice.prompt: In Part 2 you have one minute to prepare. What is the most useful way to use it?
options: Write out your full answer as complete sentences to read aloud.
Ask the examiner to choose which prompt to talk about.
Write a few keywords for each prompt on the card, plus one example or story to tell.
Sit silently and try to memorise advanced vocabulary.
practice.explanation: Short notes for each prompt give you a route through the talk while keeping your speech natural. Full sentences take too long to write and reading them aloud damages fluency.

practice.prompt: You have spoken for about one minute in Part 2 and run out of planned points. What should you do?
options: Repeat your opening sentence to fill the time.
Keep talking by adding detail, such as how you felt, what happened later or how it compares with something else.
Stop and tell the examiner you have finished.
Ask the examiner for a different topic.
practice.explanation: You can speak for up to two minutes, and the examiner will stop you. Extending with feelings, sequence or comparison shows more language; stopping early or repeating gives the examiner less to assess.

practice.prompt: The examiner asks: "Why do some people find it hard to save money?" Which response best suits Part 3?
options: Because money is hard to save for some people who cannot save it.
I save money every month because my parents taught me to.
I think a big factor is how easy spending has become. With one-click payments, people don't feel the money leaving. Social pressure matters too; if friends are always eating out, it's hard to say no.
practice.explanation: Part 3 asks about people in general, so the best answer gives reasons and examples at a general level. A purely personal anecdote does not answer the question, and the other two are too short or circular.

practice.prompt: You notice that you said "he go" instead of "he went". What is the best thing to do?
options: Correct it quickly ("he went") and continue speaking.
Start your whole answer again from the beginning.
Ignore it and avoid using past tenses for the rest of the test.
Stop and apologise to the examiner for your grammar.
practice.explanation: Brief self-correction shows awareness of grammar without damaging fluency. Avoiding past tenses would narrow your grammatical range, and restarting or apologising breaks the flow of speech.

practice.prompt: In Part 3 you do not understand a word in the examiner's question. What is the best response?
options: Guess what the question might mean and answer a different question.
Say "I don't know" and wait for the next question.
Ask the examiner to rephrase or explain the question, then answer it.
Answer with a memorised paragraph on a related topic.
practice.explanation: In Part 3 the examiner can rephrase questions, so asking for clarification is appropriate and natural. Answering a different question or giving a memorised answer will not show your ability on the actual topic.

practice.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four criteria used to assess IELTS Speaking?
practice.explanation: Speaking is assessed on Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, and Pronunciation. Task Achievement is a Writing Task 1 criterion.

practice.prompt: Which statement best describes what the Pronunciation criterion rewards?
options: Pronouncing every word slowly and separately
Speech that is easy to understand, using features such as word stress, chunking and intonation effectively
Speaking as fast as possible without pauses
A native-like British or American accent
practice.explanation: Pronunciation is judged on how clearly and flexibly you use features like stress, rhythm and intonation, not on a particular accent. Very fast speech can reduce clarity, and word-by-word delivery sounds unnatural.

practice.prompt: The examiner asks: "How might the way people shop change in the next twenty years?" Which answer uses the most appropriate language for speculating?
options: Shopping is changed by internet. It changes. People like it.
I bought some shoes online last week and they were too small.
People will definitely stop going to shops completely in twenty years.
I'd imagine more shopping will be automated; it's quite likely that fridges will reorder basics, although people may still want to see clothes in person.
practice.explanation: The best answer speculates with appropriate hedging ("I'd imagine", "quite likely", "may") and adds a contrast. The first overstates with "definitely", the second is an off-topic personal story, and the last has limited grammar and no development.

exams.name: TOEFL iBT
exams.best_for: Non-native English speakers applying to English-taught universities, especially in the U.S. and Canada, and for some visa and licensing purposes.

sections.name: Reading
sections.notes: Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life, Read an Academic Passage; adaptive.

sections.name: Listening
sections.notes: Listen and Choose a Response, conversations, announcements, academic talks; adaptive.

sections.name: Writing
sections.notes: Build a Sentence, Write an Email, Write for an Academic Discussion.

sections.name: Speaking
sections.notes: Listen and Repeat, Take an Interview.

format.score_scale: 1-6 band scale (half-point steps) per section and overall, aligned to CEFR; a comparable 0-120 total is also reported during the transition period after January 21, 2026
format.delivery: Computer-based at an authorized test center or TOEFL iBT Home Edition; adaptive, so item counts and time can vary. ETS base section times sum to about 90 minutes; ETS advises allowing about 2 hours.

free_resources.title: TOEFL iBT practice tests (official)
TOEFL iBT full-length practice test 1 (paper edition, aligned with the January 2026 test)
TOEFL TestReady prep portal
TOEFL iBT prep hub (incl. free 8-week Test Prep Planner)

lessons.title: The 2026 TOEFL iBT: new tasks and the 1-6 score scale
lessons.body: Since January 21, 2026, the TOEFL iBT uses a shorter, adaptive format. Reading (about 30 minutes) includes Complete the Words, Read in Daily Life and Read an Academic Passage. Listening (about 29 minutes) includes choosing a response, conversations, announcements and academic talks. Writing (about 23 minutes) includes Build a Sentence, Write an Email and Write for an Academic Discussion. Speaking (about 8 minutes) includes Listen and Repeat and Take an Interview. ETS advises allowing about two hours overall. Because Reading and Listening are adaptive, the questions you see depend on your answers, so concentrate fully from the first item. Scores are now reported on a 1-6 scale in half-point steps for each section and overall, aligned to the CEFR, and for a transition period ETS also reports a comparable 0-120 total. Scores are valid for two years. Important rule: you must attempt every section, because skipping a section means none of your sections are scored. Mini-example: if a university asks for "TOEFL 90", ask whether it publishes a 1-6 equivalent, or check that your report shows the comparable 0-120 score.

lessons.title: Complete the Words: grammar plus spelling
lessons.body: In Complete the Words you see a short academic paragraph in which the second half of some words is missing, and you type the missing letters. It tests vocabulary, spelling and grammar together, because the context tells you which form fits. Read the whole paragraph once quickly for meaning before filling anything in. For each gap, ask three questions: what part of speech is needed (noun, verb, adjective)? Does it need an ending such as plural -s, past -ed, or -ly? Does the number of visible letters suggest a common word? Mini-example: "Many plants rely on ins___ to carry pollen between flowers." The sentence needs a plural noun meaning small creatures that carry pollen: "insects". Another: "The results were surpris___ similar across all groups." Before an adjective, you need an adverb, so "surprisingly". Build this skill by reading short science and history texts and practising spelling of high-frequency academic words, such as environment, significant, necessary, process and therefore. Typos cost points, so check each word before moving on.

lessons.title: Reading: daily-life texts and academic passages
lessons.body: Read in Daily Life uses short real-world texts such as emails, notices, menus, schedules and social media posts. Questions ask about purpose, details, and what someone should do next. Read the question first, then scan: the answer is usually a specific detail, such as a date, a condition or an exception introduced by "unless", "except" or "only if". Read an Academic Passage uses a shorter academic text than older TOEFL versions, with questions on main idea, details, inference, vocabulary and the author's purpose. For inference questions, choose what must be true based on the text, not what might be true. For vocabulary questions, substitute each option into the sentence and keep the meaning. Mini-example notice: "The library will close at 6 p.m. on Friday for maintenance. Laptop loans must be returned by 5 p.m. that day." Question: "What must students with borrowed laptops do?" Answer: return them by 5 p.m. Friday, not 6 p.m. The trap option uses the closing time. Underline mentally every time and condition in short texts.

lessons.title: Listening: responses, announcements and academic talks
lessons.body: Listening now includes very short items in which you hear a question or statement and choose the most natural response, plus conversations, campus announcements and academic talks. For response items, think about function: is the speaker asking for help, making an offer, or complaining? The correct response matches the function, not just the topic words. Mini-example: you hear "Do you mind if I borrow your notes from Monday?" "Sure, I'll send them tonight" is natural; "Monday was really cold" repeats a word but does not answer. For longer recordings, take short notes in two columns: main points on the left, examples and details on the right. In academic talks, listen for signposts such as "the key point is", "however", "for example" and "so what this tells us". Questions about why the speaker mentions something test purpose: an example usually supports the point just made. Practise with short podcasts or lectures, pausing every minute to summarise aloud in one sentence.

lessons.title: Writing: Build a Sentence, Email and Academic Discussion
lessons.body: Build a Sentence asks you to arrange words into a correct sentence that answers a conversational prompt. Start by finding the subject and main verb, then attach objects and phrases; question forms place the auxiliary first ("Could you tell me..."), but embedded questions do not invert ("Could you tell me where the lab is?"). Write an Email gives a situation and asks you to write a short message covering specific points. Use a clear structure: greeting, purpose in the first sentence, one or two sentences per required point, a polite closing. Match the tone to the reader: more formal for a professor, friendlier for a classmate. Write for an Academic Discussion shows a professor's question and two student posts; you add your own contribution. State your opinion in the first sentence, give one well-developed reason with an example, and briefly respond to a classmate's idea to show engagement. Mini-example opening: "I agree with Maya that online labs save money, but I think hands-on practice matters more because..." Aim for clear, accurate sentences rather than length alone.

lessons.title: Speaking: Listen and Repeat and the interview
lessons.body: In Listen and Repeat you hear a sentence and repeat it exactly. Accuracy of words and natural pronunciation matter most. Listen for meaning chunks, not single words: "The tutoring center | is open | until eight | on weekdays." Holding three or four chunks is much easier than holding twelve separate words. Keep the speaker's stress and rhythm, and if you lose a word, keep going rather than stopping. In Take an Interview you answer questions from an interviewer about your experiences and opinions, with a short time to respond. Use a quick pattern: direct answer, one reason, one specific detail. Mini-example: "What is a skill you would like to learn?" "I'd like to learn to code, mainly because my economics classes use a lot of data. Last term I spent hours cleaning a spreadsheet by hand, and a short script could have done it in minutes." Practise daily by shadowing short audio clips and recording one-minute answers to everyday questions, then listening back for hesitations and missing word endings.

lessons.title: Build a Sentence: let word order do the work
lessons.body: In Build a Sentence you see a short context, usually a question or a comment from another person, and a set of words or phrases. You arrange them into one grammatical sentence that responds to the context. The task looks simple, but it is designed to test exactly the word-order rules that learners find hardest. Rule 1: find the subject and main verb first. Before you move anything, ask "Who does what?" In the set [usually / it / at nine / opens], the core is "it opens". Then attach the rest: frequency adverbs such as usually, always and often normally go before the main verb ("It usually opens at nine") but after the verb "be" ("It is usually open at nine"). Rule 2: indirect questions use statement order. After phrases like "Could you tell me", "I wonder", "She wanted to know" and "Do you know", the subject comes before the verb and there is no auxiliary "do": "Could you tell me where the advisor's office is?", not "where is the advisor's office". This is the single most common trap in the task, because the wrong order looks like a normal question. Rule 3: "whether" and "if" introduce yes/no reported questions. "Did they extend the deadline?" becomes "I asked whether it had been extended." Watch the tense shift back after a past reporting verb. Rule 4: relative clauses follow the noun they describe. "I missed the bus which I usually take" keeps "which I usually take" directly after "the bus". If a phrase such as "which I usually take" ends up separated from its noun, the sentence is probably wrong. Rule 5: use the context. The context tells you which tense and which pronoun the answer needs. If the context is "Why weren't you at the meeting?", the answer will probably start with "I" and use a past tense. Method under time pressure: (1) read the context, (2) identify subject + verb, (3) place the object or complement, (4) attach adverbs, prepositional phrases and clauses, (5) read the whole sentence silently to check that it sounds natural and answers the context. Every word must be used once. If one word seems not to fit anywhere, you have probably misjudged the structure, so look again for an indirect question or a relative clause.

lessons.title: Write an Email: purpose, points and the right tone
lessons.body: In Write an Email you read a short situation, often from campus or everyday life, and write an email that responds to it. The instructions usually list specific things to include, for example explaining a problem, suggesting a solution and asking a question. Scorers check whether you complete the communicative goal clearly, stay on topic and follow basic writing conventions. Step 1: turn the bullet points into a checklist. If the task says "Explain why you missed the field trip, describe what you did to catch up, and ask how the trip will be graded", write three quick notes before typing. Missing one required point is the most common reason a fluent email still loses credit. Step 2: choose the register from the recipient. A professor, a housing office or an employer needs a polite, semi-formal tone. Open with "Dear Professor Lin," or "Hello Ms Ortiz,". State your purpose in the first sentence: "I am writing to ask whether I could submit the lab report two days late." Avoid very casual language ("Hey, so basically...") and avoid sounding demanding ("You need to give me an extension"). Softeners help: "Would it be possible to...", "I was wondering whether...", "I would really appreciate...". Step 3: give one short paragraph per point. Each paragraph can be two or three sentences: the point, a detail and, where useful, a reason. "I missed Friday's trip because my flight back from a family event was cancelled. I have since read the two assigned articles and borrowed notes from a classmate." Step 4: close politely and clearly. "Thank you for your time. I look forward to hearing from you. Best regards, Sam Lee." If you are asking for action, a short closing line can restate it: "Please let me know if a short make-up assignment would be possible." Common errors to check in your final minute: missing articles ("I borrowed notes from a classmate"), wrong verb forms after modal verbs ("could submit", not "could submitted"), and run-on sentences joined only with commas. A clear, complete, polite email of moderate length usually scores better than a long one that wanders from the task.

lessons.title: Academic Discussion: add something new, briefly and clearly
lessons.body: In Write for an Academic Discussion you see a professor's question posted to an online class discussion and short posts from two classmates. You write your own contribution. Scorers look for a relevant opinion, ideas that are explained and supported, and language that suits an academic but conversational setting. Read the professor's question for its exact focus. If it asks "Should universities require all first-year students to take a public speaking course?", your post must answer that question, not a general one about education. Read both classmates quickly and note their main points. The strongest posts acknowledge the discussion and then contribute a different angle. If Maria argues that public speaking builds confidence and Jamal says the course would take time away from major subjects, you could agree with Maria but add a new reason: employers value presentation skills, and practising them in a low-pressure setting early prevents anxiety later. Simply repeating Maria's point in other words adds little. A reliable structure: 1. Position: "I think a required public speaking course is a good idea, although it should be short." 2. Brief link to a classmate: "Jamal is right that time is limited, but..." 3. New reason with explanation: why your point is true. 4. Specific example: "When I had to present a group project in high school, I realised I had never practised speaking for more than a minute in front of people." 5. Optional closing line that returns to your position. Use precise language for academic tone without becoming stiff. "This would particularly benefit students who..." and "One overlooked advantage is..." are natural. Avoid absolute claims such as "Everyone hates presenting"; hedge with "many students" or "often". Watch the clock. Spend about a minute reading and choosing your angle, most of your time writing, and the last minute fixing errors in verb forms, plurals and articles. A focused post of a solid paragraph that develops one fresh idea with an example is better than a long list of undeveloped points.

lessons.title: Listen and Choose a Response: listen for function, not keywords
lessons.body: In Listen and Choose a Response you hear a short spoken prompt, often one sentence, and choose the most appropriate reply. Because the audio is short, the task tests whether you understand what the speaker is doing: asking for help, complaining, making a suggestion, checking information or expressing surprise. Identify the function. "Would you mind if I borrowed your notes?" is a request for permission. The natural reply grants or refuses permission: "Not at all, I'll send them tonight." "The shuttle's running late again" is a complaint or observation that invites a practical response: "Then let's walk. It's only fifteen minutes." Beware of word-repetition traps. Wrong options often repeat a word from the prompt with a different meaning. If the prompt mentions the shuttle "running late", an option such as "I'm running too" reuses the word but makes no sense as a reply. If the professor "moved the exam up", an option about moving something up the stairs is a trap. Matching sounds is not matching meaning. Handle negative and tag questions carefully. For "Haven't you finished the lab report yet?" an answer that starts "No" must continue with something that confirms it is unfinished: "No, I just need to add the graphs." "No, I finished it yesterday" contradicts itself. With tag questions like "You're presenting first tomorrow, aren't you?", the best reply often corrects or confirms the assumption: "Actually, Priya swapped with me, so I'm going last." Indirect replies are often correct. Natural conversation does not always answer the literal question. "Do you know if the bookstore is still open?" can be answered with "I think it closes at six, so you've got about twenty minutes." This gives the information the speaker really needs. For longer conversations, keep track of the problem and the solution. Questions often ask why the student came to see the professor, what the professor suggests, and what the student will probably do next. A quick note with three words (problem, advice, next step) is usually enough. Listen especially to the end of the conversation, where advice and decisions typically appear.

lessons.title: Academic passages and talks: main idea, purpose and inference
lessons.body: Read an Academic Passage and Listen to an Academic Talk share most question types: main idea, detail, vocabulary in context, purpose ("Why does the author mention...?") and inference. Learning to recognise each type saves time. Main idea. The correct answer covers the whole text, not one paragraph. For a passage about the honeybee waggle dance, "How honeybees communicate the location of food, and how this was confirmed" is better than "The scientist who first described bee dances", which is only one part. Reject options that are too narrow or that add claims the text does not make. Detail. Locate the sentence, then compare meaning carefully. Wrong options often mix two true facts from different parts of the text, for example linking the duration of the dance to direction when the text links duration to distance. Vocabulary in context. Replace the word in the sentence with each option. In "the dance itself might be incidental", the option "of minor importance" fits; "accidental" looks similar but changes the meaning. Purpose questions ask why the writer or speaker includes something, not what it says. A professor who mentions "a common assumption that autumn colours are caused by cold weather" is setting up a misconception to correct. Typical purposes are: to give an example, to introduce a contrast, to correct a misconception, to provide evidence and to explain a cause. Inference questions require one small logical step, never a leap. If a run straight up the comb means "fly toward the sun", you can infer that a run straight down means "fly directly away from the sun". You cannot infer that bees cannot find food on cloudy days, because the text says nothing about it. Listening adds one challenge: you cannot look back. Notes should follow the speaker's structure with signposts: "Today I want to explain...", "Here's the key point", "Red is a different story". Write short labels (yellow = hidden all summer; red = new, sunscreen?) rather than full sentences. Lecturers emphasise key ideas with stress and repetition, and they often signal uncertainty ("one leading idea is") that the correct answer will preserve.

lessons.title: Speaking: accurate repetition and strong interview answers
lessons.body: The Speaking section has two task types. In Listen and Repeat you hear short sentences and repeat each one exactly. In Take an Interview you answer a series of questions about your experiences and opinions, usually on school or campus topics. Both are recorded through your microphone. Listen and Repeat rewards precision. Small changes count: dropping an article ("closed for cleaning on Friday afternoon" becomes "closed for cleaning Friday afternoon"), changing a tense ("will be closed" becomes "is closed") or swapping a word for a synonym ("shut" for "closed") all reduce accuracy. Strategies: listen to the whole sentence as meaning, not as separate words, because meaning is easier to remember than a string of sounds. Mentally group it into chunks: "The chemistry lab / will be closed / for cleaning / on Friday afternoon." Then repeat at a natural speed with the same chunking. If you lose a word, keep going with the rest of the sentence rather than stopping; a near-complete repetition earns more than a broken one. Practise with short recorded sentences: play, pause, repeat, then compare with a transcript. Pay attention to small grammar words (a, the, to, have, been), plural endings and past-tense endings, which learners most often drop. Take an Interview rewards clear, relevant, well-developed answers. A simple frame works for most questions: answer directly, give a reason, add an example, and if time allows, add a contrast or result. For "Do you prefer studying alone or in a group?": "Mostly alone, because I can control the pace. For example, before my history exam I needed to reread one chapter three times, which would have frustrated a group. That said, for problem sets, a group is great for checking answers." Avoid three common problems: very short answers that stop after one sentence, memorised speeches that do not fit the question, and long silences while you plan. A short filler phrase ("That's an interesting question; I'd say...") buys a second or two naturally. If a question asks about something you have not experienced, answer hypothetically: "I haven't done that, but I imagine I would..." Speak at a steady pace with clear word stress; you do not need a particular accent, only speech that is easy to follow.

practice.passage: Many desert plants survive long dry periods by storing water in thick, fleshy tissues. Cacti, for example, can expand their stems after rain and slowly use the stored water over the following months. To limit water loss, many of these plants open their stomata, the small pores used for gas exchange, at night rather than during the day. Cooler night air means less water evaporates through the open pores. The plants take in carbon dioxide in the dark and store it as an acid, then use it for photosynthesis once the sun rises and the pores are closed. This strategy is efficient in hot, dry climates, but it typically produces slower growth than the daytime gas exchange used by most plants in wetter regions.
practice.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why cacti grow faster than other plants
How some desert plants conserve water
practice.explanation: The passage describes water storage and night-time gas exchange as water-saving strategies.

practice.passage: In the nineteenth century, the spread of railways changed how many towns kept time. Before railways, each town usually set its clocks by local solar noon, so the time in one town could differ by several minutes from the time in a town only a short distance to the east or west. For travelers on foot or horseback, these small differences hardly mattered. Railway companies, however, needed timetables that worked across long distances, and inconsistent local times led to confusion and even safety risks. Railway companies therefore adopted standard times for their networks, and over the following decades many governments made similar systems official. Historians note that this shift reflected a broader change: time was increasingly coordinated by institutions rather than by the position of the sun in each community.
practice.prompt: What is the main point of the passage?
options: Railways made travel on horseback faster.
Solar noon is the same in every town.
Railways encouraged a shift from local solar time to standardized time.
practice.explanation: The passage explains how railway needs led to standard time and a broader change in timekeeping.

practice.skill: Reading: Read an Academic Passage (main idea)
practice.passage:
When a honeybee forager discovers a rich source of nectar, she returns to the hive and performs what researchers call the waggle dance. On the vertical surface of the honeycomb, she runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then loops back to her starting point and repeats the run, alternating between left and right loops.
In the 1940s, the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch proposed that this dance contains coded information. The angle of the straight "waggle run" relative to vertical, he argued, represents the direction of the food relative to the sun. A run pointing straight up the comb tells other bees to fly toward the sun; a run angled 40 degrees to the right of vertical indicates a direction 40 degrees to the right of the sun. The duration of the waggle run, meanwhile, corresponds to distance: the longer the run, the farther away the food.
Von Frisch's interpretation was not universally accepted. Some researchers argued that recruited bees found food mainly by following the scent carried on the dancer's body, and that the dance itself might be incidental. The debate continued for decades, until experiments using harmonic radar tracked individual recruits after they left the hive. Many flew directly toward the area the dance indicated, which strongly supported von Frisch's view, although scent appears to help bees locate the exact flowers once they are nearby.
The dance is also remarkably adaptable. Because the sun moves across the sky during the day, a dancer adjusts the angle of her run over time to keep the direction accurate, even after she has spent a long period inside the dark hive. Such observations have made the waggle dance one of the most studied examples of symbolic communication in animals.
practice.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: The life of the scientist Karl von Frisch
Why scent is the main way bees find flowers
How honeybees use a dance to communicate the location of food, and how this idea was supported
practice.explanation: The passage explains what the dance encodes, the debate about it and the evidence that settled it. Von Frisch and radar are parts of that story, and the passage says scent mainly helps only once bees are nearby.

practice.skill: Listening: Listen to an Academic Talk
practice.passage:
Transcript:
Professor: Okay, so last time we talked about photosynthesis, and you'll remember that chlorophyll is the pigment that makes leaves green. Today I want to explain why many leaves change color in the fall. A common assumption is that fall colors appear because the weather turns cold. That's only partly right. As days get shorter, many trees stop producing chlorophyll, and the chlorophyll already in the leaf breaks down. Now here's the key point: the yellow and orange pigments, called carotenoids, were in the leaf all summer. They were simply hidden by the much larger amount of green chlorophyll. So yellow isn't really a new color; it's a revealed color.
Red is a different story. In species such as some maples, the leaf actively produces new red pigments, called anthocyanins, in the fall. Why would a tree spend energy making pigment in a leaf it's about to drop? One leading idea is that anthocyanins act a bit like sunscreen, protecting the leaf while the tree pulls nutrients such as nitrogen back into its branches. That would also help explain why a run of sunny days and cool, but not freezing, nights tends to produce the most brilliant reds.
practice.prompt: What is the talk mainly about?
options: Why leaves change color in the fall
Why trees lose their leaves in winter
practice.explanation: The professor states the topic directly: "Today I want to explain why many leaves change color in the fall." Photosynthesis was last class's topic, and maples are only an example.

practice.prompt: Context: "Where is the study session today?" Arrange the words to make a correct response: [is / in / it / the library]
practice.explanation: A statement answer uses subject + verb + place: "It is in the library." "Is it in the library" is question word order, which does not answer the question.

practice.prompt: Context: "What time does the computer lab open?" Arrange the words: [usually / it / opens / at nine]
practice.explanation: Frequency adverbs such as "usually" normally go before the main verb: "It usually opens at nine." The other orders separate the verb from its subject or split the time phrase.

practice.prompt: Context: "I'm new here." Arrange the words to make a correct question: Could you tell me [the advisor's office / where / is]?
options: Could you tell me the advisor's office where is?
Could you tell me is where the advisor's office?
Could you tell me where is the advisor's office?
Could you tell me where the advisor's office is?
practice.explanation: After "Could you tell me", an indirect question uses statement order: question word + subject + verb. "Where is the advisor's office" is direct question order, the classic trap in this task.

practice.prompt: Context: "Did you ask about the deadline?" Arrange the words: [I / asked / whether / it / had been / extended]
options: I asked whether it had been extended.
I asked whether had it been extended.
I asked it whether had been extended.
Whether I asked it had been extended.
practice.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses "whether" followed by statement order: "whether it had been extended". Inverting "had it" is direct-question order, which is not used after "asked whether".

practice.prompt: Context: "Why were you late this morning?" Arrange the words: [I / missed / the bus / which / I / usually / take]
options: I missed the bus which I usually take.
I missed the bus I which usually take.
I missed the which bus I usually take.
I the bus missed which I usually take.
practice.explanation: The relative clause "which I usually take" must follow the noun it describes, with the relative pronoun first. Placing "which" after "I" or inside the noun phrase breaks the clause.

practice.prompt: Context: "What did the professor ask you after class?" Arrange the words: [she / wanted to know / which topic / we / had chosen]
options: She wanted to know we had chosen which topic.
Which topic she wanted to know we had chosen.
She wanted to know which topic we had chosen.
She wanted to know which topic had we chosen.
practice.explanation: An embedded question after "wanted to know" keeps statement order: "which topic we had chosen". "Which topic had we chosen" uses direct-question inversion, which is incorrect here.

practice.prompt: You are writing to your professor to ask for a two-day extension on a lab report. Which opening is most appropriate?
options: Professor, you must give me two more days for the report.
Hey Prof! Need more time for the report, ok?
Dear Professor Lin, I hope you are well. The weather has been lovely this week.
Dear Professor Lin, I am writing to ask whether I could submit my lab report two days late.
practice.explanation: The best opening is polite and states the purpose in the first sentence. The second is too casual, the third sounds demanding, and the last delays the purpose with unrelated small talk.

practice.prompt: Task: Write to the housing office. Explain a problem with your heating, say what you have already tried, and ask when it can be repaired. Which email body completes ALL three points?
options: The heater in Room 214 is broken. Could you please send me a new key for my room as well?
The heater in Room 214 has not worked since Sunday. I have reset the thermostat and checked the switch, but nothing changed. Could you let me know when someone might be able to repair it?
I have reset the thermostat and checked the switch. Could you let me know when someone might come?
The heater in Room 214 has not worked since Sunday, and the room is very cold at night. It is difficult to study. I hope this can be fixed.
practice.explanation: Only the correct option explains the problem, describes what was tried and asks when it can be repaired. The first never says what was tried or asks a question, the second never states the problem, and the third adds an irrelevant request.

practice.prompt: Which sentence in an email to a manager would most need revising for tone?
options: I would really appreciate it if you could consider this request.
I expect you to change my schedule by tomorrow.
Would it be possible to change my shift on Thursday?
Please let me know if you need any more information.
practice.explanation: "I expect you to..." sounds like a demand and is inappropriate when making a request to a manager. The other sentences use polite request forms that suit a semi-formal email.

practice.skill: Writing: Write for an Academic Discussion
practice.passage:
Professor Kim: This week we are discussing campus life. Some universities require all first-year students to take a short public speaking course. Do you think this requirement is a good idea? Why or why not?
Maria: I think it's a great idea. Many students are nervous about speaking in front of others, and a course would build their confidence.
Jamal: I disagree. First-year students already have heavy schedules, and a required course would take time away from classes in their major.
practice.prompt: Which contribution best adds a NEW idea to the discussion?
options: I think Jamal is right that first-year students have heavy schedules.
Public speaking is a very important topic in many universities.
I agree with Maria, but for a different reason: employers consistently look for presentation skills, and practising them early, when grades are less critical, lowers the stakes of making mistakes.
I agree with Maria because many students are nervous, and a course would build their confidence.
practice.explanation: The best post takes a position and adds a reason neither classmate gave, with a brief explanation. The first two simply restate the classmates' points, and the last is too general to answer the question.

practice.skill: Writing: Write for an Academic Discussion
practice.passage:

Maria: I think it's a great idea. Many students are nervous about speaking in front of others, and a course would build their confidence.
Jamal: I disagree. First-year students already have heavy schedules, and a required course would take time away from classes in their major.
practice.prompt: Which sentence would best support a post arguing that the course should be required but kept short?
options: A six-week module, meeting once a week, would give students regular practice without displacing a full course in their major.
Public speaking has been taught since ancient times.
Everyone hates speaking in public, so the course is essential.
Some students are naturally confident speakers.
practice.explanation: The specific, realistic proposal supports both parts of the claim (required, but short) and responds to Jamal's concern about time. The last option overgeneralises with "everyone", which weakens an academic argument.

practice.prompt: Which approach should you AVOID when writing your response?
options: Briefly referring to a classmate's point
Supporting your opinion with a specific example
Repeating one classmate's argument in slightly different words
practice.explanation: Scorers reward a relevant contribution that develops ideas; repeating a classmate adds nothing new. Stating a clear opinion, referring to others and giving examples are all features of a strong post.

options: The tour of the art museum was moved to the following Tuesday.
The tour of the art museum has been moved to the next Tuesday.

practice.prompt: You miss one word in the middle of a sentence you must repeat. What is the best strategy?
options: Ask the speaker to repeat the sentence.
Replace the whole sentence with your own summary.
Stop and say nothing, so you do not make mistakes.
Repeat the rest of the sentence fluently, keeping the original structure as closely as possible.
practice.explanation: A nearly complete, fluent repetition earns more than silence or a summary, because the task measures how closely you reproduce the sentence. Audio cannot be replayed on request.

practice.prompt: Interviewer: "Do you prefer studying alone or in a group?" Which answer is strongest?
options: Studying is very important for all students in the world today.
I prefer studying alone or in a group, it depends, alone or group.

Mostly alone, because I can control the pace. Before my history exam, for example, I reread one chapter three times, which would have frustrated a group. For problem sets, though, a group helps me check answers.
practice.explanation: The strongest answer responds directly, gives a reason, adds an example and offers a contrast. The others are too short, off-topic or repetitive.

practice.prompt: Interviewer: "Tell me about a time you worked on a team project." You have never done a formal team project. What is the best approach?
options: Say "I have never done that" and stop.
Describe a related experience, such as organising an event with friends, and explain what you learned.
Ask the interviewer to choose a different question.
Give a memorised answer about your hometown.
practice.explanation: Adapting the question to a related real experience keeps your answer relevant and lets you show language. Stopping, changing the topic or refusing gives the scorer little to assess.

practice.prompt: Interviewer: "Should universities offer more online classes?" Which opening gives you time to think while still sounding natural?
options: I don't know anything about universities.
That's an interesting question. I'd say yes, mainly because...
practice.explanation: A short, natural filler followed by a clear position buys a moment of thinking time without long silence. Repeated hesitation sounds and fragments reduce fluency.

practice.prompt: Interviewer: "What change would most improve student life on your campus?" Which answer is best developed?
options: I'd extend library hours during exam periods. Right now it closes at ten, so students who work evening jobs lose their only quiet study time. Even opening until midnight in the last two weeks of term would make a real difference.
The library. It's good. But it could be better maybe.
Many things could improve student life, such as food, housing, library, sports and transport.
I would like to improve student life because it is important to improve student life.
practice.explanation: The best answer chooses one change, explains who benefits and why, and gives a concrete detail. Listing many ideas without development, circular reasoning and fragments are all weaker.

exams.name: Duolingo English Test
exams.best_for: Non-native English speakers applying to the many universities that accept a low-cost, online, on-demand English test.

sections.name: Introduction and onboarding
sections.notes: Equipment checks, ID verification, room scan.

sections.name: Adaptive test
sections.notes: Varied short question types (reading, listening, writing, speaking); difficulty adapts to performance.

sections.name: Writing Sample and Speaking Sample
sections.notes: Extended responses shared with institutions alongside the score.

format.score_scale: 10-160 overall in 5-point increments (average of Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing subscores, each 10-160); aligned to CEFR
format.delivery: Online from home on your own computer, any time, with AI and human proctoring; results in about 2 days (12 hours with faster results).
