lessons.title: How the Duolingo English Test works
lessons.body: The Duolingo English Test takes about one hour, entirely online on your own computer. It has three stages: about 5 minutes of setup (camera, microphone, ID and room checks), about 45 minutes of adaptive questions, and about 10 minutes for a Writing Sample and a Speaking Sample, which are scored and also sent to the institutions you share results with. Many questions are short and timed individually, from 5 seconds for Read and Select up to a few minutes for writing and speaking tasks, so the test moves fast. Your overall score runs from 10 to 160 in 5-point steps and is the average of four subscores: Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing. Several question types are adaptive, so a question that feels hard often means you are doing well. Results usually arrive within two days and are valid for two years. Because the test is proctored by video, rules matter: stay in view, keep your ears visible, do not look away from the screen except when typing, and make sure nobody enters the room. Mini-example: test your setup on the free practice test the day before, at the same desk and time of day.

lessons.title: Read and Select and Fill in the Blanks: fast word recognition
lessons.body: In Read and Select you see one word at a time and have about 5 seconds to decide whether it is a real English word. The fake words are designed to look plausible, often by combining real-looking parts, such as "clundery" or "brastive". Tips: if you clearly know the word, click Yes immediately; if you have never seen it and it does not sound familiar when you say it silently, click No. Watch for real words that look unusual, such as "vellum" or "meander". In Fill in the Blanks, a sentence contains one word whose second half is missing; you type the ending in about 20 seconds and spelling must be exact. First decide the part of speech the sentence needs, then the ending. Mini-example: "The bridge will signif___ reduce travel time." Between "will" and the verb "reduce" you need an adverb: "significantly". Train by reading widely and keeping a list of words you misspell; common traps include double letters (accommodate, occurred) and silent letters (doubt, receipt).

lessons.title: Read and Complete: the paragraph puzzle
lessons.body: Read and Complete shows a paragraph in which several words are missing their second half, and you have about three minutes to type every ending. Each word is scored on its own and must be spelled correctly. Strategy: read the whole paragraph once for meaning before typing anything; context from later sentences often reveals earlier words. Then work in order, checking grammar clues around each gap: an article before the gap suggests a noun, "can" or "will" suggests a base verb, and "more" or "very" suggests an adjective. Mini-example: "Coffee contains caffeine, which can make people feel more al___." After "feel more", you need an adjective describing a state: "alert". "However, drinking too much can make it diff___ to sleep" needs an adjective after "make it": "difficult". If you get stuck, skip the gap and come back, because an unanswered gap is simply wrong, but a later gap you can solve still scores. Leave about 20 seconds at the end to scan for typos such as missing plural -s or wrong verb endings.

lessons.title: Interactive Reading: one passage, many question types
lessons.body: Interactive Reading gives you a passage and a series of linked tasks: Complete the Sentences (choose the best word for each gap), Complete the Passage (choose the sentence that best fills a missing spot), Highlight the Answer (select the words in the text that answer a question), Identify the Idea (choose which idea the passage expresses), and Title the Passage (choose the best title). For word choices, think about meaning and collocation: you "make a decision" but "do research". For the missing sentence, check both directions: the sentence must follow logically from what comes before and lead into what comes after; pronouns such as "this" or "they" must have something to refer to. For Highlight the Answer, select the shortest exact phrase that answers the question, not a whole paragraph. For titles, choose the option that covers the whole passage rather than one detail. Mini-example: a passage about a town that turned an empty lot into a garden, how neighbors share the work, and how fresh produce reaches a food bank. "A Shared Garden That Feeds a Neighborhood" beats "Tomatoes Grow Best in Summer".

lessons.title: Listening: Listen and Type and Interactive Listening
lessons.body: In Listen and Type you hear a sentence and type exactly what you heard; you can play it up to three times, and your answer is scored by how close it is to the original. Use the plays strategically: first play, listen for the overall meaning and start typing the first words; second play, fill the gaps; third play, check small words such as articles, prepositions and endings like -ed and -s, which learners often miss. Interactive Listening simulates a conversation in a campus or everyday setting: you choose the best response at each turn, and at the end you write a short summary of the conversation. For responses, pick the reply that fits the purpose of what was said, such as answering a question or accepting an offer, and the right level of politeness. Mini-example: a classmate says, "I can't make the study session tonight." A natural reply is "No problem, I'll send you the notes", not "The session is in the library", which ignores the speaker's point. For the summary, include who, the problem, and the outcome in two or three sentences.

lessons.title: Writing and speaking tasks: say more, organized
lessons.body: Writing tasks include Write About the Photo (1 minute), Interactive Writing (about 5 minutes for a first answer, then 3 minutes for a follow-up question on the same topic) and the Writing Sample (5 minutes). Speaking tasks include Speak About the Photo, Read Then Speak, Interactive Speaking (a short conversation with several questions) and the Speaking Sample. Responses are judged on content, coherence, grammar and vocabulary, plus fluency and pronunciation for speaking, so length alone is not enough, but very short answers cannot show your range. A simple frame works almost everywhere: main point, two supporting details, a concrete example, and a closing sentence. For photo tasks, move from the big picture to details: who or what, where, what is happening, and what might happen next. Mini-example (photo of a market): "This photo shows a busy outdoor market, probably in the morning. In the foreground, a vendor is weighing apples while a customer holds out a cloth bag..." Keep talking or typing until time is nearly up, and use linking words such as "however", "for example" and "as a result".

lessons.title: Interactive Listening: complete, respond, then summarise
lessons.body: Interactive Listening is built around one short scenario, for example a classmate who wants to plan a presentation with you. It has three parts that always come in the same order: Listen and Complete, Listen and Respond, and Summarize the Conversation. Listen and Complete and Listen and Respond share 6 minutes 30 seconds, and the summary has its own 75 seconds. Listen and Complete: you hear the scenario and see three sentences about it, each with a missing part. You type the missing part. You can replay the scenario as many times as you like, and spelling is not the main thing scored; what matters is that your answer gives the right idea. Keep answers short and exact: if the sentence is "The presentation has been moved to ____", type "Wednesday", not a whole explanation. Listen and Respond: you take part in the conversation. The other person speaks, you choose the best reply from options on screen, and the conversation continues. Each audio clip plays only once, so listen carefully, but you can reread the scenario. Wrong options usually fail for one of these reasons: they do not fit the scenario, they do not match what the other person just said, they use the wrong words or pronouns, they are too formal or too informal, or they add or leave out information. Example: Jordan says the presentation has moved from Friday to Wednesday. "Great, that gives us more time" is wrong because the change gives you less time. After each reply, you see whether you were right, and if not, the correct line. Read it; it keeps you on track for the rest of the conversation. If you have time left at the end, reread the conversation to prepare for the summary. Summarize the Conversation: in 75 seconds, write a short summary in full sentences. It counts toward Writing and also affects Listening, because it shows whether you understood. Cover three things: the situation, the main points, and what happened at the end. You may write in the first person ("Jordan told me...") or the third person ("Two students..."), and you may reuse words from the conversation. A good 3-sentence model: "Jordan told me our history presentation was moved from Friday to Wednesday. We divided the work: Jordan will make the slides and I will do the timeline. We agreed to practise in the library tomorrow at four." Avoid bullet points, and check that every detail (days, names, places) matches what you heard.

lessons.title: Interactive Writing and the Writing Sample
lessons.body: Two longer writing tasks give the Writing subscore much of its evidence: Interactive Writing and the Writing Sample. Both are scored on content, discourse coherence, grammar and lexis. Interactive Writing has two parts on the same topic: 5 minutes for Part 1 and 3 minutes for Part 2, with 30 seconds to plan before Part 1. In Part 1 you answer a question; then a second question asks you to write about an idea you did not cover the first time. Both answers are scored together. Use the 30 seconds to decide your main point and one example. For "Should students have part-time jobs?", you might plan: "Yes, in moderation - teaches time management - my café job." Then write a clear opening sentence that states your view, explain it, and support it with the example. Part 2 often pushes you to the other side or to a new angle, for example "What might be the disadvantages?" Do not repeat Part 1. Start with a signal that you are moving to a new idea ("On the other hand", "A different concern is") and develop it with a reason and an example: "A job can leave students too tired to study, especially when shifts end late at night." The examiner wants to see you handle a second idea, which is exactly what happens in a university seminar when a teacher asks a follow-up question. The Writing Sample is a single 5-minute response with 30 seconds to read and plan. The question asks about something that happened to you or your opinion. Your Writing Sample is sent to the schools that receive your results, so someone in an admissions office may actually read it. Write as you would for a teacher: a clear first sentence, one or two developed paragraphs and a short conclusion. Three habits raise the score in both tasks. First, combine short sentences: "I worked in a café. I learned to manage my time. My grades improved." becomes "Working in a café taught me to manage my time, and as a result, my grades improved." Second, choose strong, precise verbs: "the policy cut waiting times by half" is better than "the policy made waiting times become less". Third, save the last 30 seconds to check spelling, punctuation and verb forms. Length helps only when the extra sentences add relevant ideas.

lessons.title: Photo tasks: Write About the Photo and Speak About the Photo
lessons.body: The test includes photo tasks in both writing and speaking. Write About the Photo appears three times; for each, you have 1 minute to type a description. Speak About the Photo appears once; you have 20 seconds to look at the photo and then up to 90 seconds to speak. The photos are real photos showing people, animals or objects in different situations. Start immediately with the main scene. Guidance from the test makers specifically warns against long, empty introductions such as "This picture shows a situation that might be happening in everyday life." Instead: "An older man and a young girl are kneeling in a vegetable garden." That sentence already tells the reader who, what and where. Then move from the main action to details, using position language: "in the foreground", "in the background", "on the left", "next to", "behind". "The girl is holding a watering can, while the man is pointing at a row of small green plants. Behind them is a wooden fence." Go beyond naming things. After describing what you see, add a reasonable interpretation using cautious language: "It looks as if he is teaching her which plants need water, and the cloudy sky suggests it might rain soon." Interpretation shows more advanced grammar (it looks as if, suggests, might) and gives the scorer more content to assess. Use the present continuous for actions (is holding, are kneeling) and "there is/there are" for objects. Write full sentences with correct punctuation; in 1 minute, three or four accurate, connected sentences are a realistic target. For the speaking version, imagine describing the photo to a friend on the phone who cannot see it. Use the full time. If you do not know the word for something important, do not skip it: describe it with simple words. If you forget "departure board", say "a large screen above the platform showing the times of the trains". This paraphrasing skill is rewarded because it keeps communication going. Practice method: take any photo on your phone, set a 1-minute timer, and type a description; then set a 90-second timer and describe it aloud while recording. Compare: did you mention the main scene first, use position words and add one interpretation?

lessons.title: Interactive Speaking and Read, Then Speak
lessons.body: Two speaking tasks ask you to respond to questions in real time. In Interactive Speaking, a Duolingo character asks you a set of 6 to 8 questions on two different topics, 3 or 4 questions on each. You have 35 seconds to answer each question, and the timer starts when the character finishes asking. You must click Record Now before speaking, and you hear each question only once. The questions adapt: they become harder if you do well. 35 seconds is enough for about four to six sentences. Use a compact pattern: answer, reason, example. For "What do you usually do on weekends?": "On Saturdays I usually play football with friends in the park near my flat. It's the only time in the week when I'm outdoors for hours, and it helps me forget about studying. Last weekend we played for three hours and I could hardly walk afterwards." That answer is direct, specific and uses varied tenses. If you do not fully understand a question, do not stay silent. Say something relevant to the topic you heard. Silence gives the scorer nothing; a partly relevant answer still shows fluency, grammar and vocabulary. Read, Then Speak gives you a written question about your experience or opinion, often with bullet points, 20 seconds to prepare and up to 90 seconds to speak. The question stays on the screen while you speak. Use the 20 seconds to note one idea for each bullet. For "Talk about a place you like to go to relax. Say where it is, what you do there, and why it helps you relax," your notes might be: "riverside path near home - walk, listen to podcasts - quiet, no screens". Then follow the bullets in order, adding detail to each. The bullets are your structure, so you do not need to invent one. In both tasks, scores reflect content, discourse coherence, fluency, grammar, lexis and pronunciation. Connect ideas with simple linkers (because, so, for example, that's why, but), vary your sentence beginnings, and speak at a steady, natural pace. Short fillers such as "Let me think" or "That's a good question" can buy a second of thinking time, but avoid long chains of "umm". Recording yourself and listening back is the fastest way to notice repetition and long pauses.

lessons.title: Read and Select and Fill in the Blanks: word knowledge at speed
lessons.body: Read and Select and Fill in the Blanks are fast vocabulary tasks that feed the Reading subscore. In Read and Select you see one word at a time and click Yes if it is a real English word or No if it is not; you have 5 seconds per word, and there are 15 to 18 words. A word left unanswered after 5 seconds is marked wrong. The fake words are designed to look like real words. Strategies for Read and Select: say the word silently; real words usually "sound" familiar. Click Yes if you know it or think you have seen it before; click No if you have not. Know the common building blocks of English, because fake words often combine real parts in impossible ways. Real prefixes include un-, re-, dis-, pre- and mis-; real suffixes include -tion, -ment, -ness, -able, -ous and -ive. A word like "ostentible" mixes the start of "ostentatious" with the ending of "ostensible", so it feels almost right but is not a word. Fake words also often change one letter of a common word ("parvest" for "harvest"). In Fill in the Blanks you see a sentence with an unfinished word (the second half is missing) and type the ending in 20 seconds. You are marked right or wrong, and you must spell the word correctly. There are 6 to 9 of these, and the missing words are adjectives, adverbs, nouns and verbs. Strategy: decide the word class first, then the word. In "Her argument was persu___ enough to change the decision", the gap follows "was" and comes before "enough", so it needs an adjective: "persuasive". "Persuade" is a verb and "persuasion" is a noun. In "struggling to aff___ basic goods", the infinitive "to" plus an object means you need a verb that fits the meaning: "afford". Spelling patterns that cost points: adverbs from -ial adjectives keep the double l ("especially"), -ful adjectives have one l ("careful"), and "-ence/-ance" endings must be memorised in pairs (evidence, importance). Build a personal list of words you misspell and review it daily. A simple daily routine: 10 minutes reading a short news article, noting five useful words and their forms (persuade, persuasive, persuasion, persuasively); then quiz yourself by covering the endings and writing them from memory.

lessons.title: Speaking Sample, pacing and how the score works
lessons.body: The last part of the test includes the Writing Sample and the Speaking Sample. The Speaking Sample gives you a written question about your experience or opinion, 30 seconds to prepare, and up to 3 minutes to speak. The question stays on screen, and a video of your answer is sent to the schools you share your results with. Schools see only the samples from the test you send them. Treat the Speaking Sample as a short, friendly interview with an admissions officer. Plan three parts in the 30 seconds: a direct answer, two developed points, and a short closing sentence. For "Describe a challenge you overcame", you might say what the challenge was, what you did step by step, and what you learned. Speak as long as you have relevant things to say; the guidance is to use the question to help you keep going. A natural, organised 2-minute answer is far better than 3 minutes of repetition. Pacing across the test. The main test takes about 45 minutes and is adaptive: many question types become harder or easier depending on your answers, so do not panic if items feel difficult; that can be a sign that you are doing well. Time limits are strict and per question, so you cannot save time from one item for another. A few practical rules: - In Interactive Reading, the 7 or 8 minutes is shared across six questions on one passage. Watch the timer so you reach Title the Passage. - In Interactive Listening, the 6 minutes 30 seconds is shared between Listen and Complete and Listen and Respond, so do not replay the scenario endlessly. - In timed writing tasks, stop adding new ideas with about 30 seconds left and proofread. How the score works. You receive an overall score from 10 to 160 and four subscores (Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing), each from 10 to 160. The overall score is the average of the four subscores; if the average falls between two reportable scores, it is rounded up to the next score ending in 0 or 5. Because the test is adaptive, your score is not simply the number of right answers. Before test day, take the official free practice test to experience the timing, check your microphone and camera, and prepare a quiet room. Technical or rule problems can cause a result to be withheld, which wastes far more time than any single difficult question.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "Please turn off the lights when you lea___ the room."
practice.explanation: You leave a room. The other words do not fit the meaning.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "She was too exha___ to finish the race."
practice.explanation: After "too" we need an adjective describing how she felt: "exhausted". "Exhausting" describes the race, not the person.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "The new bridge will signif___ reduce travel time."
practice.explanation: An adverb is needed to modify the verb "reduce": "significantly".

practice.explanation: "Yesterday" requires the past tense verb: "apologized" (also spelled "apologised").

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "The museum has a large colle___ of ancient coins."
practice.explanation: After "a large" and before "of", a noun meaning a group of items is needed: "collection".

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "Their reasons for leaving were not entirely cle___."
practice.explanation: Reasons can be clear (easy to understand). "Clean" and "clever" do not fit reasons; "clerk" is a noun.

practice.passage: Many people start the day with a cup of coffee. For some, it is a hab___ they have kept for years. Coffee contains caffeine, which can make people feel more al___. However, drinking too much can make it diff___ to sleep. Doctors often sug___ limiting coffee in the afternoon.
practice.prompt: Which word completes "hab___"?
practice.explanation: "It is a ___ they have kept for years" needs a singular noun after "a": "habit".

practice.passage: Many people start the day with a cup of coffee. For some, it is a hab___ they have kept for years. Coffee contains caffeine, which can make people feel more al___. However, drinking too much can make it diff___ to sleep. Doctors often sug___ limiting coffee in the afternoon.
practice.prompt: Which word completes "al___"?
practice.explanation: "Feel more ___" needs an adjective related to caffeine's effect: "alert".

practice.passage: Many people start the day with a cup of coffee. For some, it is a hab___ they have kept for years. Coffee contains caffeine, which can make people feel more al___. However, drinking too much can make it diff___ to sleep. Doctors often sug___ limiting coffee in the afternoon.
practice.prompt: Which word completes "diff___"?
practice.explanation: "Make it ___ to sleep" needs an adjective meaning hard: "difficult".

practice.passage: Many people start the day with a cup of coffee. For some, it is a hab___ they have kept for years. Coffee contains caffeine, which can make people feel more al___. However, drinking too much can make it diff___ to sleep. Doctors often sug___ limiting coffee in the afternoon.
practice.prompt: Which word completes "sug___"?
practice.explanation: After "Doctors often", a plural-subject present verb is needed: "suggest". "Suggests" would need a singular subject.

practice.prompt: After months of training, the team was finally ready to ______ the mountain.
practice.explanation: Training to reach the top of a mountain: "climb".

practice.prompt: The instructions were so ______ that nobody knew what to do.
practice.explanation: Instructions that leave people confused are unclear: "vague".

practice.prompt: Because our flight was ______, we waited at the airport for three extra hours.
practice.explanation: Waiting extra hours means the flight left late: "delayed".

practice.prompt: She has a ______ memory; she can recall phone numbers she has seen only once.
practice.explanation: Remembering numbers seen once shows an unusually good memory: "remarkable".

practice.prompt: The organizers decided to ______ the outdoor concert until the weather improved.
practice.explanation: Moving an event to a later time is to "postpone" it.

practice.prompt: His explanation was ______: short, yet it covered every important point.
practice.explanation: Brief but complete describes "concise". "Verbose" and "redundant" mean too many words.

practice.passage: Three years ago, the empty lot on Carver Street was full of weeds and broken glass. Today it is a community garden with forty raised beds. Neighbors take turns watering and weeding, and a local school uses one corner for science lessons. Much of what the garden grows, especially tomatoes and beans, is donated each week to a nearby food bank, which says fresh vegetables are among the items it receives least often.
practice.prompt: Which is the best title for the passage?
options: A Shared Garden That Feeds a Neighborhood
practice.explanation: The passage covers transforming the lot, shared work, and donations to a food bank. The other titles focus on single details or things not discussed.

practice.passage: Three years ago, the empty lot on Carver Street was full of weeds and broken glass. Today it is a community garden with forty raised beds. practice.prompt: Which of these is a real English word?
practice.explanation: "Harvest" (to gather crops) is a real word. The others change one or two letters of real-looking patterns but are not English words.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a real English word?
practice.explanation: "Frugal" means careful with money. The fakes swap a single consonant, which is a common way fake words are built in this task.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a real English word?
practice.explanation: "Linger" means to stay longer than necessary. The other forms follow English spelling patterns but are not real words.

practice.prompt: Which of these is a real English word?
practice.explanation: "Ostensible" means apparent or stated but perhaps not true. "Ostentible" blends it with "ostentatious", a typical trap that looks almost right.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "The library is open every day exc___ Sunday."
practice.explanation: "Except Sunday" means all days but Sunday. "Exceed", "excite" and "excuse" are real words with the same beginning, but none makes sense before a day of the week.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "Please write your answers clea___ so the teacher can read them."
practice.explanation: The gap describes how you write, so it needs the adverb "clearly". "Clearness" is a noun, and "clearing" and "cleared" are verb forms.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "The scientist made an important disc___ about how cells repair themselves."
practice.explanation: "Made an important discovery about" is a natural noun phrase. "Discuss" is a verb, and "discount" and "discipline" do not fit "about how cells repair themselves".

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "Prices have risen sharply, so many families are struggling to aff___ basic goods."
practice.explanation: After "struggling to" you need a verb, and the meaning (having enough money) requires "afford". "Affirm" is a verb but means to state firmly, which does not fit the context.

practice.prompt: Complete the word: "Her argument was persu___ enough to change the committee's decision."
practice.explanation: After "was" and before "enough", the gap needs an adjective: "persuasive". "Persuade" is a verb, "persuasion" a noun and "persuasively" an adverb, so each is the wrong word class.

practice.passage:
When Amira took over her grandfather's small bakery, she expected the hardest part to be the early mornings. Instead, it was the regular customers. When Amira took over her grandfather's small bakery, she expected the hardest part to be the early mornings. Instead, it was the regular customers. Every day they compared her bread with his, and every day they found something to (1) ___ about: too salty, too pale, not crusty enough. After a month, Amira was ready to (2) ___ the bakery.
[missing sentence]
In it, her grandfather had written the recipe in careful pencil, with notes in the margins: "Wet morning? Less water." "Old oven - turn the trays halfway." Amira realised that the recipe had never been fixed; he had adjusted it every day to the weather and the oven. She began keeping her own notes. Within a few weeks, an elderly customer paused at the counter, tasted a slice, and said quietly, "There it is."
practice.prompt: Highlight the part of the text that answers: What had Amira's grandfather done that she had not understood?
options: adjusted it every day to the weather and the oven
written the recipe in careful pencil
practice.explanation: Amira realises that "the recipe had never been fixed" because he "adjusted it every day to the weather and the oven". Writing in pencil is a detail, not the insight, and the customers, not the grandfather, compared the bread.

practice.passage:
Cutting an onion is one of the few kitchen tasks that can bring tears to almost anyone's eyes. The reason lies in the onion's (1) ___ defences. When an onion's cells are intact, certain substances are stored separately. Cutting breaks the cells open and allows these substances to mix.
[missing sentence]
When the gas reaches the eyes, it stimulates nerves that signal the tear glands, and tears are produced to wash the irritant away. Several simple methods can reduce the effect. Chilling the onion before cutting slows the chemical reaction, and a sharp knife crushes fewer cells than a blunt one, so less gas is released. Some cooks also work near an open window or under a fan, which carries the gas away before it reaches their eyes.
practice.prompt: Choose the best word for blank (1).
practice.explanation: The passage goes on to describe substances mixing and a chemical reaction, so "chemical defences" fits. The tears are not caused by emotion, which makes "emotional" a tempting but wrong choice.

practice.passage: Photo description: An older man and a young girl are kneeling in a vegetable garden. The girl is holding a green watering can, and the man is pointing at a row of small plants. Behind them is a wooden fence, and the sky is cloudy.
practice.prompt: Which is the best first sentence for your description?
options: This picture shows a situation that might be happening in everyday life, and I think it could be about many things.
An older man and a young girl are kneeling in a vegetable garden.
I think gardening is a good hobby for everybody.
practice.explanation: The best opening describes the main scene immediately in a full sentence. The official guidance warns against long, empty introductions, fragments are not full sentences, and a general opinion does not describe the photo.

The girl are holding a watering can and the man pointing at the plants.
practice.explanation: The correct sentence has proper subject-verb agreement and plural forms. The other options drop third-person "-s", mix singular and plural nouns, or use "are" with a singular subject.

options: It looks as if he is teaching her which plants need water, and the cloudy sky suggests it might rain soon.
The man is old and the girl is young and the fence is wooden and the sky is grey.

practice.prompt: Interactive Writing gives you 30 seconds before Part 1. What is the best use of this time?
options: Start typing immediately without reading the question carefully.
Decide your main point and one example to support it.
Write a list of difficult words to include.
Wait for Part 2, since the parts are scored separately.
practice.explanation: The guidance recommends using the 30 seconds to plan. Both parts are scored together, and planning a point with an example produces a more coherent answer than forcing in difficult words.

practice.prompt: In Part 1 you argued that part-time jobs teach students responsibility. Part 2 asks: "What might be the disadvantages of working while studying?" Which opening is best?
options: I worked at a café last summer and I enjoyed it very much.
As I said, part-time jobs teach students responsibility, which is very important.
There are no real disadvantages to working while studying.
On the other hand, a job can leave students too tired to study, especially if their shifts end late at night.
practice.explanation: Part 2 asks for an idea you did not cover before, so the best opening signals a new angle and starts developing it. Repeating Part 1 or denying any disadvantages does not answer the second question.

practice.prompt: Which revision best combines these sentences? "I worked in a café. I learned to manage my time. My grades improved."
options: I worked in a café and I learned to manage my time and my grades improved and.
Because working in a café. I learned to manage my time.
Working in a café taught me to manage my time, and as a result, my grades improved.
I worked in a café, I learned to manage my time, my grades improved.
practice.explanation: The revision links the ideas with a clear cause-and-effect connector and avoids repetition, which improves discourse coherence. The second option is a comma splice, and the others contain fragments or a dangling "and".

practice.prompt: Which sentence uses the strongest, most precise verb?
options: The new timetable had an effect of making waiting times go down by half.
The new timetable did a change to waiting times, making them half.
The new timetable cut waiting times by half.
The new timetable made waiting times become less by half.
practice.explanation: "Cut" expresses the idea directly in one precise verb. The other versions use weak verbs (make, do, have) with extra words, which makes the writing wordier and less clear.

practice.prompt: Which sentence is correctly punctuated and avoids a run-on?
options: Online classes are flexible; however, many students miss talking to classmates in person.
Online classes are flexible however, many students miss talking to classmates in person.
Online classes are flexible, many students miss talking to classmates in person.
Online classes are flexible, however many students miss talking to classmates in person.
practice.explanation: "However" joining two independent clauses needs a semicolon (or full stop) before it and a comma after it. Using only commas, or no punctuation before "however", creates a run-on sentence.

options: Schools can see Writing Samples from all of your past tests
Anyone who searches for your name online
The schools you send your test results to
practice.explanation: The Writing Sample is sent to the schools you share results with, and they see only the sample from the test you send. It is not public.

practice.prompt: Question: "Describe a teacher who influenced you and explain how." Which plan is best for a 5-minute response?
options: Write about why education is important for society in general.
Name the teacher, describe one specific moment, and explain how it changed your behaviour or thinking.
List every teacher you have had since primary school.
Describe the school building and your classroom in detail.
practice.explanation: A focused plan that answers both parts (who and how) with a specific example produces clear, developed content. A list or a general essay on education does not answer the question asked.

practice.passage: Photo description: A crowded train platform at night. On the left, a woman is checking her phone. In the background, a man is running toward a train with a suitcase. Above the platform is a large screen showing train times.
practice.prompt: Which sentence best uses position language to describe the photo?
options: Trains are a popular way to travel in many countries.
On the left, a woman is checking her phone, while in the background a man is running toward the train with a suitcase.
I took a train last year to visit my cousin.
There is a woman and a man and a train.
practice.explanation: Position phrases such as "on the left" and "in the background" help a listener picture the scene. The other options are too basic, too general or about your own life instead of the photo.

practice.passage: Photo description: A crowded train platform at night. On the left, a woman is checking her phone. In the background, a man is running toward a train with a suitcase. Above the platform is a large screen showing train times.
practice.prompt: You do not know the English word for the screen showing train times. What should you do?
options: Say the word in your first language.
Stop speaking and wait for the time to run out.

Skip it and say nothing about it.
practice.explanation: The guidance is not to skip important things but to explain them with easy words. Paraphrasing keeps communication going and shows flexible vocabulary.

practice.prompt: Question: "Talk about a place you go to relax. Say where it is, what you do there, and why it helps you relax." How should you use the 20 seconds of preparation?
options: Note one idea for each of the three points so you can follow them in order.
Think of as many advanced words as possible.
Choose only the most interesting point and ignore the others.
Write out your full answer word for word.
practice.explanation: The bullet points give you a ready-made structure, and a quick idea for each keeps your answer complete and organised. Writing a full script is impossible in 20 seconds and leads to unnatural reading.

practice.prompt: Which answer to the question about a relaxing place covers all three points best?
options: I like relaxing. Relaxing is very important for everyone, especially students, because life is busy.
I go to the river because it's quiet. I think everyone should have a quiet place.
There is a river near my flat. It is quite long and it goes through the whole city.
I often go to a path along the river near my flat. I walk there for about an hour and listen to podcasts. It helps me relax because it's quiet and I leave my laptop at home, so I can't check emails.
practice.explanation: The best answer says where, what and why, with specific detail for each. The others are general, describe only the place, or skip what the speaker does there.

practice.prompt: The character asks: "What do you usually do on weekends?" Which answer makes the best use of 35 seconds?
options: I usually do usual things on weekends, usual things.

On Saturdays I usually play football with friends in the park near my home. It's the only time in the week I'm outdoors for hours, and it helps me forget about studying. Last weekend we played for three hours.
Weekends are Saturday and Sunday, and everyone has weekends.
practice.explanation: The best answer responds directly, gives a reason and adds a specific example in varied tenses. The others are too short, too general or repetitive.

practice.prompt: You did not fully understand the character's question, and you cannot replay it. What is the best strategy?
options: Say something relevant about the topic you did hear.
Stay silent until the timer ends.
practice.explanation: Each question plays once, and the guidance advises trying to say something about the topic. A partly relevant answer still shows fluency, grammar and vocabulary, while silence shows nothing.

practice.prompt: What happens to your Speaking Sample?
options: It is shared publicly on social media.
It is used only for practice and not seen by anyone.
A video of your answer is sent to the schools you share your results with.
practice.explanation: The Speaking Sample is shared as a video with the schools that receive your results, so treat it like a short interview.

practice.prompt: You have up to 3 minutes for the Speaking Sample. Which approach is best?
options: Keep speaking while you have relevant ideas, using the question on screen to guide a clear beginning, middle and end.
Recite a memorised speech about a different topic.
Speak for about 30 seconds, then stop to avoid mistakes.
Talk for the full 3 minutes, even if you start repeating the same point.
practice.explanation: The guidance is to speak as long as you can say something relevant, using the question to help. Stopping very early limits evidence, while repetition or an off-topic memorised speech lowers content and coherence.

exams.name: PTE Academic
exams.best_for: Non-native English speakers applying to universities or for visas, especially in Australia, New Zealand, the UK and Canada, who want a fully computer-scored test with fast results.

sections.name: Speaking & Writing

sections.name: Reading

format.score_scale: 10-90 overall and per skill (Global Scale of English)

lessons.title: PTE Academic: format, scoring and integrated skills
lessons.body: PTE Academic is a computer-based test of about two hours taken at a Pearson test center, scored on a 10-90 scale. It has three parts: Speaking and Writing together, then Reading, then Listening. Many tasks are integrated, meaning one task contributes to two skills. For example, Repeat Sentence and Write From Dictation feed both listening and another skill, so a single strong habit can lift two scores. Since August 2025, the speaking part also includes Respond to a Situation and Summarize Group Discussion. Scoring is done by AI against fixed criteria such as content, form, fluency, pronunciation, grammar, vocabulary and spelling. That has practical consequences: stay within word limits exactly, because breaking the form can zero a response; speak smoothly without long pauses, because a silence of a few seconds can end the recording; and spell carefully. Scores usually arrive within a few days and are valid for two years. Mini-example: Summarize Written Text requires one sentence of 5-75 words; two sentences break the form, even if the content is perfect.

lessons.title: Speaking tasks: fluency first
lessons.body: In Read Aloud and Repeat Sentence, fluency and pronunciation carry great weight. Speak at a steady, natural pace in meaning chunks; do not restart after a mistake, just keep going. For Repeat Sentence, focus on reproducing the rhythm and as many words as possible; a confident partial repetition usually beats a hesitant, broken one. For Describe Image (40 seconds), use a fixed frame: what the image shows, the highest and lowest values or main stages, one comparison, and a one-sentence conclusion. For Retell Lecture, note keywords while listening and connect them in complete sentences. Respond to a Situation gives you a short scenario, for example asking a neighbor to lower music, and 40 seconds to speak; address the listener directly, state the problem, propose a solution, and stay polite. Summarize Group Discussion asks you to summarize the different views of several speakers in two minutes, so note each speaker's position and any agreement. Mini-example for a chart: "This bar chart compares rainfall in four cities. City B is the wettest at about 900 millimeters, while City D is the driest..."

lessons.title: Writing and Reading: form, collocations and logic
lessons.body: Summarize Written Text gives you 10 minutes to write one sentence of 5-75 words capturing the main ideas of a passage. Join the main point and two key supporting points with connectors such as "while", "because" and "which". Write Essay gives 20 minutes for 200-300 words: introduction with your position, two body paragraphs with examples, and a conclusion. Count words and proofread spelling. In Reading, the fill-in-the-blank tasks are heavily about collocation and grammar: you "conduct research", "pose a threat", "draw a conclusion", and an adverb is needed before an adjective. Read the entire sentence before choosing, because the word after the gap often decides it. Re-order Paragraphs asks you to arrange sentences in a logical order. Find the opener: it introduces a topic without pronouns such as "this" or "they" that need an earlier reference. Then link pairs using pronouns, time words and contrast words. Mini-example: "However, the plan was later abandoned" cannot be first, because "However" responds to something earlier. Multiple-answer questions may deduct points for wrong choices, so select only options you are sure of.

lessons.title: Listening: dictation, summaries and error-spotting
lessons.body: Write From Dictation is one of the most valuable tasks because it contributes to both listening and writing. You hear a short sentence once and type it exactly. Start typing the first few words while the audio plays if you can, and use grammar to rebuild what you missed: a plural subject needs a plural verb, and articles are often dropped by learners. Highlight Incorrect Words shows a transcript while you listen; click words that differ from the audio. Follow the text with your cursor so you do not lose your place, and only click when you are sure, because wrong clicks lose points. For Summarize Spoken Text, take notes on the main idea and two supporting points and write a short summary within the word limit. For Highlight Correct Summary and Select Missing Word, focus on the speaker's overall argument rather than isolated details. Mini-example: if the audio says "Researchers have recently expanded the program", and the transcript says "Researchers have recently extended the program", click "extended". Practise daily dictation with short academic sentences and check spelling of common academic words.

lessons.title: Summarize Group Discussion and Respond to a Situation
lessons.body: Two Speaking tasks in PTE Academic test how you handle real communication rather than reading or repeating. Both give you only a short preparation time, so a ready-made approach matters. Summarize Group Discussion: you hear a discussion of up to about three minutes between three speakers, then have 10 seconds to prepare and 2 minutes to speak. You must summarise the discussion in your own words and make clear which speaker made which point. Take notes in three columns, one per speaker, using initials or descriptions ("woman 1", "man", "woman 2"). Write two or three keywords for each contribution, and mark agreement or disagreement with simple symbols (+, -, ?). A clear spoken structure: (1) topic: "The speakers discussed whether university lectures should be recorded." (2) each speaker's view with a reason: "The first speaker, Emma, argued that all lectures should be recorded so that ill or working students can catch up. Raj disagreed, pointing out that attendance tends to fall." (3) development or outcome: "Lucia suggested a compromise, releasing recordings after a week, and Emma agreed as long as students with good reasons got immediate access." Two minutes is long, so including the reasons and the final outcome lets you speak fluently for most of the time without padding. Respond to a Situation: you read and hear a short everyday situation (text up to about 60 words), have 10 seconds to prepare and about 40 seconds to respond. You are scored partly on whether your response is appropriate, including the level of formality. Decide quickly: who am I speaking to (friend, manager, lecturer, stranger) and what do I need to do (apologise, request, explain, suggest)? A reliable pattern: greeting suited to the listener, the main purpose, a reason or detail, and a polite close. For a classmate whose textbook you damaged: "Hi Sara, I'm really sorry, but I spilled coffee on your textbook last night. I've checked the bookshop and I can buy you a new copy this afternoon, or pay you back if you'd prefer. Again, I'm sorry about that." For a manager, raise formality: "Hello Mr Chen, I wanted to ask whether it might be possible to take next Friday off..." In both tasks, speak smoothly at a natural pace. Long pauses and restarts reduce your fluency score more than a small grammar slip does.

lessons.title: Describe Image and Retell Lecture: content, not templates
lessons.body: Describe Image gives you 25 seconds to study an image (a chart, table, map, process or photo) and 40 seconds to speak. Retell Lecture plays a recording of up to about 90 seconds, then gives you 10 seconds to prepare and 40 seconds to speak. Both are scored on content, oral fluency and pronunciation. A common mistake is relying on a memorised template that says almost nothing about the actual image ("This image gives information about different things, and there are many colours"). Templates can help fluency, but content matters too: the best responses identify the main idea, key details and a conclusion or implication. Describe Image in three moves: 1. Main idea (1 sentence): "This table shows average monthly rainfall in a city in four months of the year." 2. Key details (2-3 sentences): pick the highest, the lowest and a clear comparison. "Rainfall peaks in October at 95 millimetres, while July is by far the driest month, with only 10." Use the 25 seconds to find these numbers, not to read every label. 3. Conclusion or implication (1 sentence): "Overall, the city has a dry summer and a wet autumn, which suggests that water storage is important for the summer months." Accuracy matters: say "the lowest", "roughly twice as much", "fell sharply" only if the data supports it. If you run short of time, the conclusion is more valuable than an extra detail. Retell Lecture: note structure, not sentences. Before the audio starts, an image may give clues about the topic. While listening, write the topic, three or four keywords for the main points, and any contrast word you hear (however, but, importantly). Example notes for a lecture on city parks: "green space - lower stress - quality > quantity - unequal (richer areas) - plan new parks in poorer areas". Then retell: "The lecture was about green space in cities. The speaker explained that access to parks is linked with lower stress, but that quality matters more than quantity. She also noted that green space is unequally distributed, so planners are being encouraged to build new parks in poorer areas." Speak continuously. A pause of a few seconds may end the recording, so if you lose your place, use a simple bridge ("Another point was...") and continue with your next note.

lessons.title: Summarize Written Text and Write Essay
lessons.body: PTE has two main written production tasks in the Speaking & Writing part. Both are scored on several traits, including content and form, so following the format rules exactly is essential. Summarize Written Text: you read a passage of up to about 300 words and have 10 minutes to write a one-sentence summary of 5 to 75 words. The sentence must capture the main points. A response that is not a single sentence, or falls outside the word limits, risks losing marks for form. Aim for one well-built complex or compound sentence of roughly 25 to 50 words. Method: (1) identify the topic and the writer's main claim; (2) find the key supporting or contrasting point, which often follows "however" or "but"; (3) join them with a connector that shows the relationship. Frame: "Although [point A], [main point B], because [reason C]." Example for a passage on four-day working weeks: "Trials of a four-day working week have often maintained productivity and reduced stress, but critics argue the results may not apply to sectors that need fixed staffing, since most participating firms were self-selected office businesses." That sentence covers the trend, the evidence, the criticism and the reason. Avoid copying long chunks of the passage word for word; paraphrase key ideas where you can. Check that the sentence has one main verb structure and ends with a single full stop. Write Essay: you get a 2-3 sentence prompt and 20 minutes to write an argumentative essay of 200 to 300 words. Plan for 2-3 minutes: decide your position, choose two main reasons and one example for each. A clear structure is: introduction with position (2-3 sentences), two body paragraphs, a short conclusion. For "Governments should spend more on public transport than on roads. Do you agree?", a thesis might be: "I largely agree, because public transport moves more people with less pollution, although some road investment remains necessary in rural areas." Each body paragraph then develops one reason with an example. Keep within 200-300 words; going far over wastes time and increases errors. Spend the final 2-3 minutes checking spelling (the computer marks spelling errors as mistakes), agreement and punctuation. Use a consistent spelling convention, British or American, throughout.

lessons.title: Reading: fill in the blanks and reorder paragraphs
lessons.body: The Reading part includes two kinds of fill-in-the-blank tasks and Reorder Paragraph. All three give partial credit, so every correct blank or correct pair of adjacent boxes counts. Reading & Writing Fill in the Blanks (dropdown): a passage of up to about 200 words has several gaps, each with a dropdown list. The options test grammar (word form, tense, agreement), collocation and meaning. Work in two passes. First, check grammar: in "Urban farming has ___ rapidly", only a past participle fits ("grown"). Second, check collocation and meaning: in "enough food to ___ a significant difference", the fixed phrase is "make a difference". For logic, read the sentence before and after: "Supporters ___ that their main value lies elsewhere" needs a verb like "argue", because the sentence contrasts with the critics' view. "Deny" would reverse the meaning. Fill in the Blanks (drag and drop): a shorter passage (up to about 80 words) and a word bank that contains more words than gaps. Start with the gaps you are sure of to reduce the options. Watch for near pairs placed in the bank on purpose: affect (verb) and effect (noun), lose and loose, economic and economical. Grammar usually decides: "the ___ depends on" needs a noun, so "effect". Reorder Paragraph: up to about 110 words in several text boxes, which you arrange into the original order. Find the opening sentence first: it introduces the topic and does not depend on anything before it. Sentences that begin with "However", "This", "As a result", "Such" or a pronoun cannot usually start the text. Then build pairs: "This sharp rise in the number of books" must follow a sentence that mentions a large number of books. Time order and general-to-specific movement also help: background (books were copied by hand), event (Gutenberg's press), result (millions of books printed), wider consequence (spread of ideas). Because scoring rewards correct adjacent pairs, even if you are unsure of the whole order, secure the pairs you are confident about. A strong link such as "approach often failed ... a well-known example of such a failure" should always stay together. Pace yourself. The Reading part lasts about half an hour, so do not spend five minutes on one dropdown. Make your best choice and move on.

lessons.title: Negative marking: when to select fewer answers
lessons.body: Most PTE tasks give partial credit or score answers as simply right or wrong, but three task types can cost you points for wrong selections: Reading: Multiple Choice, Multiple Answers; Listening: Multiple Choice, Multiple Answers; and Listening: Highlight Incorrect Words. Knowing how they are scored changes your strategy. Multiple Choice, Multiple Answers (Reading and Listening): more than one option is correct. You gain credit for correct options, but incorrect selections reduce your score, so selecting every option does not work. The practical rule: choose only the options you can support with evidence from the passage or recording. If you are confident about one option and unsure about a second, selecting only the confident one is usually the safer choice. Treat each option like a True/False/Not Given statement: true only if the text clearly supports it. Words like "always", "never" and "all" are often signs of an overgeneralised option. In a passage that says bilingual children "may know fewer words in each individual language" but have a similar total vocabulary, an option claiming they "always have larger vocabularies" goes beyond the evidence. Highlight Incorrect Words: you read a transcript while listening, and some words on screen differ from what the speaker says. Each correct click earns a point, and each incorrect click loses one. Keep your eyes moving with the audio, and keep the cursor just ahead of the speaker. Click only when you clearly hear a different word. Typical changes are numbers (twelve/twenty), similar verbs (expand/extend) and connectors that change logic (although/because). If you are not sure, do not click. By contrast, Multiple Choice, Single Answer and Highlight Correct Summary are scored as right or wrong with no penalty beyond losing that item, so you should always choose an answer. Practice idea: after completing a multiple-answer item, write next to each option the line of evidence that supports or rules it out. If you cannot write a supporting line, you should not have selected it. This habit trains you to select based on evidence rather than on familiar words.

lessons.title: Listening: Summarize Spoken Text, Select Missing Word and Write from Dictation
lessons.body: Three Listening tasks reward very specific habits. Summarize Spoken Text: you hear a recording of about 60-90 seconds and have 10 minutes to write a summary of 50 to 70 words. Scoring considers content, form, grammar, vocabulary and spelling. A response under 40 words or over 100 words scores zero for the task, as does one that misrepresents the topic, so count your words. While listening, note the topic, the main claim, two or three supporting points and any final recommendation. Then write three or four sentences: "The speaker explained that only a small share of plastic is actually recycled. This is because different plastic types are hard to process together, food waste contaminates batches, and recycled plastic often costs more than new plastic. Therefore, some researchers believe reducing single-use plastic, for example through refill systems, would be more effective than improving recycling." That is around 55 words, clear, and complete. Select Missing Word: the final word or phrase of a short recording is replaced by a beep, and you choose the option that completes it. Focus on the direction of the argument. If the speaker says the first prototype was cheap but broke down constantly, while the second cost twice as much but proved far more ___, the contrast tells you the answer is "reliable". Listen especially to the last two sentences, where the logic is set up. Each item is scored right or wrong, so always answer. Write from Dictation: you hear one short sentence and type it exactly. Every correct word counts, so spelling and small grammar words matter. Common errors are missing plural or past-tense endings, missing apostrophes ("the library's opening hours"), and confusing similar words such as "access" and "excess". Strategy: listen to the whole sentence for meaning, then type it at once while it is fresh. Read your sentence back and ask whether it is grammatical; if "have been extended" sounds wrong as "have be extended", fix it. Do not add words that were not spoken. For all three, regular dictation practice with short academic sentences, followed by a word-by-word comparison with the transcript, quickly reveals your personal patterns of error, such as dropped endings or article mistakes.

practice.passage: Electric scooters for rent have spread quickly through many cities. Supporters say they reduce short car trips and make it easier to reach public transport. Critics point to scooters left blocking footpaths and to injuries among inexperienced riders. Several cities have responded not by banning the scooters but by creating designated parking zones and lowering speed limits in busy areas.
practice.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Speed limits for cars have been lowered.
Electric scooters should be banned in all cities.
Rental scooters bring benefits and problems, and some cities are regulating them rather than banning them.
practice.explanation: The passage gives supporters' and critics' views and then describes regulation instead of bans.

practice.passage: Electric scooters for rent have spread quickly through many cities. Supporters say they reduce short car trips and make it easier to reach public transport. Critics point to scooters left blocking footpaths and to injuries among inexperienced riders. Several cities have responded not by banning the scooters but by creating designated parking zones and lowering speed limits in busy areas.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, how have several cities responded to complaints?
options: By requiring riders to take a test
By creating parking zones and lowering speed limits in busy areas
practice.explanation: The last sentence names designated parking zones and lower speed limits in busy areas.

practice.prompt: The team plans to ______ further research into the long-term effects of the drug.
practice.explanation: "Conduct research" is the standard academic collocation.

practice.prompt: Rising temperatures ______ a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide.
practice.explanation: The fixed expression is "pose a threat".

practice.prompt: Based on the limited data, it is too early to ______ any firm conclusions.
practice.explanation: We "draw conclusions" from evidence.

practice.prompt: The number of international students ______ steadily over the past decade.
practice.explanation: "The number of ..." takes a singular verb, and "over the past decade" calls for the present perfect: "has risen".

practice.prompt: Had the committee received the report earlier, it ______ a different decision.
practice.explanation: This is an inverted third conditional (If the committee had received...), so the result clause is "would have made".

practice.passage: (A) However, the plan was abandoned when costs doubled. (B) In 2019, the city proposed a tunnel beneath the river. (C) Instead, officials chose to expand the ferry service. (D) The tunnel was intended to ease traffic on the old bridge.
practice.prompt: Which sentence should come first?
practice.explanation: B introduces the topic (the tunnel proposal) with no reference to earlier text. A starts with "However", C with "Instead", and D with "The tunnel", all of which depend on earlier information.

practice.passage: (A) However, the plan was abandoned when costs doubled. (B) In 2019, the city proposed a tunnel beneath the river. (C) Instead, officials chose to expand the ferry service. (D) The tunnel was intended to ease traffic on the old bridge.
practice.prompt: What is the correct order of the four sentences?
practice.explanation: Proposal (B), its purpose (D), its abandonment (A), and the alternative chosen (C).

practice.passage: Electric scooters for rent have spread quickly through many cities. Supporters say they reduce short car trips and make it easier to reach public transport. Critics point to scooters left blocking footpaths and to injuries among inexperienced riders. Several cities have responded not by banning the scooters but by creating designated parking zones and lowering speed limits in busy areas.
practice.prompt: Which single sentence best summarizes the passage?
options: Critics say scooters cause injuries, so they should be banned everywhere.
Although rental scooters can cut short car trips, problems with parking and injuries have led several cities to regulate rather than ban them.
practice.explanation: It captures the benefit, the problems, and the regulatory response in one grammatical sentence within 5-75 words. The others omit main points or add claims not in the text.

practice.prompt: Which spelling is correct?
practice.explanation: "Environment" contains the letters n-m-e-n-t after "enviro". Spelling errors cost points in Write From Dictation.

practice.prompt: The study's findings were ______ by a second, larger experiment, which produced the same results.
practice.explanation: A second experiment with the same results confirms the findings: "corroborated".

practice.passage: Although the museum was founded over a century ago, its collection has grown significantly in recent decades, thanks largely to private donations from local families.
practice.prompt: Where are the most natural places to pause briefly when reading this text aloud?
options: After every word, to make each one clear
After "ago" and after "decades", where the commas are
Only at the very end, without any pauses
practice.explanation: Pausing at punctuation and between meaningful word groups sounds natural and helps fluency. Pausing after "its" breaks a phrase apart, and pausing after every word sounds robotic.

practice.passage: Although the museum was founded over a century ago, its collection has grown significantly in recent decades, thanks largely to private donations from local families.
practice.prompt: While reading aloud, you mispronounce "significantly". What is the best thing to do?
options: Pause silently until you remember the correct pronunciation.
Stop and restart the whole text from the beginning.
Continue smoothly with the rest of the text without going back.
Repeat the word several times until it sounds right.
practice.explanation: Restarts, repetitions and long pauses reduce your oral fluency score, and a long silence can stop the recording. Keeping a steady rhythm protects fluency even if one word is imperfect.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: The assignment must be submitted through the online portal by Friday.
practice.prompt: Which response would receive the most credit?
options: You must submit the assignment by Friday.
The assignment must be submitted by Friday through the portal online.
The assignment should be submitted on the online portal by Friday.
The assignment must be submitted through the online portal by Friday.
practice.explanation: Repeat Sentence rewards repeating the sentence exactly. Changing words, paraphrasing or reordering phrases reduces the content score even when the meaning is similar.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: Students who wish to change their course should speak to an adviser before the end of the second week.
practice.prompt: You cannot remember the whole sentence. Which response is likely to score best?
options: Students who wish to change their course should speak to an adviser ... before the end of the second week.
Students can talk to someone if they want a different course.
Speak to an adviser students before change their course the second week.
practice.explanation: Partial credit is given for correct word sequences, so reproducing long accurate chunks in the right order scores well even with a small gap. Keywords alone, scrambled order or a paraphrase lose most of the sequences.

table.caption: Average monthly rainfall in a coastal city (millimetres)

practice.prompt: Which is the best opening sentence for describing this image?
options: This table shows average monthly rainfall in a coastal city in four months of the year.
This image gives information about different things and has many numbers.
I think this city has very bad weather.
July, ten. October, ninety-five. January, eighty.
practice.explanation: A strong opening states what the image shows, including its topic and scope. A vague template sentence gives no content, an opinion is not a description, and reading numbers without structure is not an introduction.

table.caption: Average monthly rainfall in a coastal city (millimetres)

practice.prompt: Which statement about the image is accurate?
options: Rainfall increases steadily from January to October.
October is the wettest of the four months, with almost ten times as much rain as July.
April and July have similar rainfall.
January has twice as much rain as October.
practice.explanation: October has 95 mm and July 10 mm, so October is wettest and has 9.5 times as much rain. January (80) does not have twice October's rainfall, rainfall falls before it rises, and April (45) is far wetter than July (10).

table.caption: Average monthly rainfall in a coastal city (millimetres)

practice.prompt: Which concluding sentence best adds a reasonable implication?
options: Overall, the city has the same amount of rain all year.
Overall, the city will probably suffer from floods every July.
Overall, tourists should only visit the city in October.
Overall, the city has a very dry summer and a wet autumn, so storing water for the summer months is likely to be important.
practice.explanation: A good conclusion summarises the pattern accurately and adds a cautious, logical implication. The first misreads the data, the second contradicts it (July is driest), and the third is an opinion not supported by rainfall alone.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Lecturer: Today's topic is green space in cities. Studies in several countries have linked access to parks with lower stress levels and better mental health. Importantly, the benefit seems to depend on quality, not just quantity: well-maintained parks with trees and seating are used far more than empty patches of grass. However, green space is often unequally distributed, with wealthier neighbourhoods having much more of it. So city planners are now being encouraged to prioritise new parks in poorer areas.
practice.prompt: Which retelling covers the lecture's main points best?
options: The lecturer talked about stress. Stress is a big problem in modern life, and many people feel stressed at work.
The lecture said that all cities have enough parks and that wealthy areas need more green space.

The lecture was about urban green space. Parks are linked to lower stress, but their quality matters more than their size. Green space is unevenly distributed, favouring wealthier areas, so planners are being urged to build new parks in poorer neighbourhoods.
The lecture was about parks. Parks have trees and seating. People like grass.
practice.explanation: The best retelling includes the topic, the main finding, the key contrast (quality over quantity), the problem of unequal distribution and the recommendation. The second reverses the lecture's point, and the others miss most of the content.

practice.prompt: What is the most effective way to take notes during Retell Lecture?
options: Write only the numbers and names you hear.
Write the topic and a few keywords for each main point, including contrast words such as "however".
Try to write down every sentence the lecturer says.
Do not take notes; just listen and remember.
practice.explanation: Keywords that follow the lecture's structure give you a route for a fluent 40-second retelling. Writing full sentences makes you miss later points, and names or numbers alone do not show the main ideas.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: What do we call a period of ten years?
practice.prompt: What is the best answer?
practice.explanation: A decade is ten years. A century is one hundred years and a millennium one thousand, which are common confusions.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: Which organ pumps blood around the human body?
practice.prompt: What is the best answer?
practice.explanation: The heart pumps blood through the body. The lungs are involved in breathing, a related but different function.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: If a meeting starts at a quarter past two and lasts forty-five minutes, what time does it finish?
practice.prompt: What is the best answer?
practice.explanation: 2:15 plus 45 minutes is 3:00. "A quarter past three" adds an hour, and "a quarter to three" adds only 30 minutes.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Emma: I think all lectures should be recorded. Students who are ill or have jobs can catch up, and everyone can review difficult parts before exams.
Raj: I see the benefit, but attendance tends to drop when recordings are available, and students lose the chance to ask questions in real time.
Lucia: Maybe there's a middle way. We could record lectures but release them only after a week, or make attendance count toward the grade, so people still come.
Emma: That could work, as long as students with a genuine reason can get access straight away.
practice.prompt: Which summary best reports the discussion?
options: Emma wants recordings. Raj also wants recordings. Lucia thinks attendance should be graded.

The speakers discussed recording lectures. Emma supported recording everything so that ill or working students could catch up and review. Raj worried that attendance and live questions would suffer. Lucia proposed a compromise of delayed release or graded attendance, which Emma accepted provided students with genuine reasons got immediate access.
The speakers agreed that all lectures should be recorded and released immediately to everyone.
Recording lectures is a modern technology. Many universities use it, and it is useful for exams.
practice.explanation: The best summary states the topic, attributes each view and reason to the right speaker and reports the outcome. The first misstates the outcome, the second misattributes Raj's view, and the last ignores the speakers altogether.

practice.prompt: What is the most important thing to record in your notes while listening to a group discussion?

The exact words of the first speaker only
Each speaker's main point and whether they agree or disagree with the others
practice.explanation: This task asks you to summarise the discussion and make clear who said what. Notes organised by speaker, with agreement and disagreement marked, make that possible within the 2-minute response.

practice.passage: Situation: You borrowed a classmate's textbook and accidentally spilled coffee on it. Your classmate now asks for it back. What do you say?
practice.prompt: Which response is most appropriate?
options: I'm really sorry, but I spilled coffee on your textbook last night. I can buy you a new copy today, or pay you back if you'd prefer.
Here's your book. It's a bit wet, but it's fine.
Dear Sir or Madam, I regret to inform you of an incident involving your property.
You shouldn't lend books if you're worried about them.
practice.explanation: The best response apologises, explains honestly and offers a solution, in a friendly tone that suits a classmate. The second option avoids responsibility, the third is rude, and the last is far too formal for a classmate.

practice.passage: Situation: You work part-time in a shop. You need to ask your manager for next Friday off to attend a family wedding.
practice.prompt: Which response uses the most appropriate level of formality?
options: I demand a day off next Friday for a wedding.
Hey! I'm not coming in Friday, got a wedding.
Hello, Mr Chen. I wanted to ask whether it might be possible to take next Friday off, as I've been invited to a family wedding. I'm happy to swap shifts with a colleague if that helps.
practice.explanation: A polite, semi-formal request with a reason and an offer to help suits speaking to a manager. The first is too casual and presents a decision rather than a request, the second sounds demanding, and the last is not proper sentences.

practice.passage: A growing number of companies have experimented with a four-day working week, in which employees work fewer hours for the same pay. In several trials, companies reported that productivity stayed the same or improved, while staff reported lower stress and fewer sick days. Supporters argue that shorter weeks force teams to cut unnecessary meetings and focus on essential work. Critics, however, note that the trials mostly involved office-based firms that volunteered to take part, which may have been especially well suited to the change. They warn that sectors such as healthcare or retail, where staff must be present for fixed hours, could find the model far harder to apply without hiring more workers.
practice.prompt: Which response is the best summary?
options: Trials of a four-day working week have often maintained productivity and reduced stress, but critics argue the results may not apply to sectors that need fixed staffing, since most participating firms were self-selected office businesses.
A four-day week reduces stress and sick days, so every company should introduce it immediately.
Many people work in healthcare and retail, where staff must be present for fixed hours.
Companies have experimented with a four-day working week. Productivity stayed the same.
practice.explanation: The best response is one sentence that captures the main trend, the evidence and the key criticism with its reason. The first is two sentences and incomplete, the second ignores the criticism and adds an opinion, and the third covers only a detail.

practice.prompt: Which response meets the form requirement for Summarize Written Text?
options: A bullet-point list of the main ideas
Two or three sentences of about 50 words in total
One complete sentence of between 5 and 75 words
practice.explanation: Summarize Written Text requires a single sentence of 5 to 75 words. Multiple sentences, bullet points or longer paragraphs do not meet the form requirement.

practice.prompt: What are the word range and time limit for Write Essay?
practice.explanation: Write Essay asks for 200 to 300 words in 20 minutes. 50-70 words in 10 minutes is the rule for Summarize Spoken Text in the Listening part.

practice.prompt: Prompt: "Some argue that governments should spend more on public transport than on roads. To what extent do you agree?" Which thesis is strongest?

Transport is an important topic in today's world.
practice.explanation: A strong thesis states a clear position, previews the main reason and shows awareness of limits. The other options announce the topic without taking a position.

practice.passage: Bilingual children are sometimes thought to fall behind their peers in language development. Research suggests a more complicated picture. Bilingual children may know fewer words in each individual language than monolingual children of the same age, but when the words they know in both languages are counted together, their total vocabulary is often similar or larger. practice.explanation: Statement 1 matches "may know fewer words in each individual language", and statement 3 matches the note that other researchers could not reproduce the results consistently. Statement 2 overstates "often similar or larger" as "always", and statement 4 contradicts the passage.

Employers are responding in different ways to changes in where people work.
Working from home has ended in most countries.

practice.passage: Honey found in ancient tombs has been reported to remain edible after thousands of years. Its durability comes from its chemistry: honey contains very little water, and its high sugar concentration draws moisture out of microorganisms, preventing them from growing. It is also mildly acidic. However, if honey absorbs water from the air, it can ferment, which is why it should be stored in a sealed container.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, why should honey be stored in a sealed container?
options: Microorganisms are attracted by its smell.
Its sugar content rises when exposed to air.
It becomes too acidic if left open.
It can absorb moisture from the air and ferment.
practice.explanation: The final sentence explains that honey can absorb water from the air and ferment. The passage never says sugar rises, acidity increases or smell attracts microorganisms.
