practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: Most people assume that when they put plastic in a recycling bin, it becomes new plastic. In reality, only a small share of plastic is recycled. Part of the problem is that there are many different types of plastic, and they cannot easily be processed together. Food waste left on containers also contaminates whole batches. And recycled plastic often costs more to produce than new plastic made from oil, so manufacturers have little financial reason to use it. Some researchers argue that the most effective solution is not better recycling, but reducing the amount of single-use plastic produced in the first place, for example through refill systems and standard reusable packaging.
practice.prompt: Which response is the best summary (50-70 words)?
options: Recycling plastic is cheap and easy, but people do not use recycling bins enough, so governments should fine people who throw plastic away.
The speaker talked about plastic and recycling and food and oil and packaging.

The speaker explained that, contrary to popular belief, only a small share of plastic is recycled. Mixed plastic types are hard to process together, food waste contaminates batches, and recycled plastic often costs more than new plastic. Therefore, some researchers believe that reducing single-use plastic, for example through refill systems and reusable packaging, would be more effective than improving recycling.
Plastic is recycled. People put it in bins and it becomes new plastic, which is good for the environment and reduces waste in all countries around the world today.
practice.explanation: The best summary is about 60 words and covers the main claim, the three reasons and the proposed solution. The first misrepresents the topic, the second is far under 40 words, and the third contradicts the speaker on cost.

It scores zero, because responses under 40 words receive no credit.
It is scored only for spelling and grammar.
It loses one point for each missing word.
practice.explanation: The required range is 50-70 words, and a response of fewer than 40 or more than 100 words scores zero. Counting words before moving on is therefore essential.

practice.prompt: On-screen text: "The results were broadly consistent with earlier studies, because the effect was smaller." Which word on screen differs from the recording?
practice.explanation: The speaker says "although", which signals contrast; the screen shows "because", which changes the logic. Changed connectors are easy to miss because the rest of the sentence is identical.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: Students must submit their assignments before the deadline.
practice.prompt: Which typed sentence matches the recording exactly?
options: Students must submitted their assignments before the deadline.
Students must submit their assignments before the deadline.
Student must submit their assignments before the deadline.
Students must submit their assignment before the deadline.
practice.explanation: Every word must be included and spelled correctly. The distractors drop a plural ending or use the wrong verb form after "must".

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: The library's opening hours have been extended during exams.
practice.prompt: Which typed sentence matches the recording exactly?
options: The library's opening hours have be extended during exams.
The library's opening hours has been extended during exams.
The library's opening hours have been extended during exams.
The library opening hours have been extended during exams.
practice.explanation: The correct version keeps the possessive "library's", plural agreement "hours have" and the passive "have been extended". Each distractor changes one small grammatical element.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: Access to reliable data is essential for accurate forecasts.
practice.prompt: Which typed sentence matches the recording exactly?
options: Access to a reliable data is essential for accurate forecasts.
Access to reliable data is essential for accurate forecast.
Excess to reliable data is essential for accurate forecasts.
Access to reliable data is essential for accurate forecasts.
practice.explanation: "Access" (the ability to use) sounds like "excess" (too much), but only "access" makes sense. "Data" here takes no article, and "forecasts" is plural in the recording.

lessons.title: C1 Advanced: papers, scale and what a pass means
lessons.body: C1 Advanced has four papers: Reading and Use of English (1 hour 30 minutes, 8 parts, 56 questions), Writing (1 hour 30 minutes, 2 tasks), Listening (about 40 minutes, 4 parts, 30 questions) and Speaking (15 minutes, usually in pairs with two examiners). Each skill, plus Use of English, receives a score on the Cambridge English Scale, and these are averaged into your overall result. A score of 180-199 earns the C1 Advanced certificate at level C1 (grades B and C); 200-210 is grade A, certified at C2; and 160-179 earns a certificate at B2. The certificate does not expire, although universities and employers may set their own time limits. You can take the exam on paper or digitally at an authorised centre, and both are the same qualification. Mini-example: Reading 185, Use of English 175, Writing 182, Listening 190 and Speaking 188 average 184, a C1 pass, even though Use of English alone was below 180. Use the free sample tests on Cambridge's preparation page to find your weakest paper.

lessons.title: Use of English Parts 1-4: collocations, grammar and transformations
lessons.body: Part 1 (multiple-choice cloze) tests collocations and fixed phrases: all four options often have similar meanings, but only one fits the words around it. Learn phrases, not single words: "hold water", "glowing reviews", "reach a record". Part 2 (open cloze) needs one word per gap, mostly grammar words: prepositions, articles, linkers and auxiliaries. Read the whole text first, then look at the words immediately before and after each gap. Part 3 (word formation) gives a stem in capitals; decide the part of speech, then whether it needs a prefix (un-, ir-, mis-) or a plural. Part 4 (key word transformation) asks you to rewrite a sentence in three to six words using a given word that must not change. Marks are split, so a partly correct answer can still earn one of two marks. Mini-example: "I regret not studying harder. WISH" becomes "I wish I had studied harder." Count your words: contractions count as two. Common tested structures include wishes, passives, reported speech, inversion ("No sooner had... than") and modal perfects ("may have missed").

lessons.title: Reading Parts 5-8: attitude, structure and matching
lessons.body: Part 5 contains a long text with six multiple-choice questions, often about the writer's attitude, purpose or the meaning of a phrase. Find the exact lines, then check that the option matches the whole sentence, not just a few words. Part 6 gives four short texts by different writers on one topic; questions ask which writer shares or contradicts another's view, so summarize each writer's opinion on each sub-topic in a few words in the margin. Part 7 is a gapped text: choose which paragraph fits each gap. Look for reference words, such as "this approach", "the latter" and "such criticism", which must point back to something in the text before the gap, and check the paragraph after the gap too. Part 8 is multiple matching: read the questions first, then scan the sections. Mini-example for Part 7: a missing paragraph beginning "This setback, however, proved temporary" must follow a paragraph that describes a setback. Time plan for the whole paper: about 30 minutes for Parts 1-4 and about 60 minutes for Parts 5-8.

lessons.title: Writing and Speaking: register, range and interaction
lessons.body: Writing Part 1 is a compulsory essay (220-260 words) based on notes; you must discuss two of the three points given and say which is more important, with reasons. Part 2 offers a choice of formats such as an email or letter, proposal, report or review. Examiners assess Content, Communicative Achievement (the right register and conventions for the format and reader), Organisation and Language. A proposal or report needs clear headings and recommendations; a review should engage the reader and give a recommendation. Use a range of structures, such as cleft sentences ("What surprised me most was..."), but accuracy still matters. In Speaking, Part 1 is a short interview, Part 2 is a one-minute long turn comparing pictures, Part 3 is a collaborative discussion with your partner, and Part 4 extends that discussion. In Part 3, interaction is assessed: invite your partner's opinion, build on it, and work toward a decision. Mini-example: "That's a fair point about cost, but wouldn't the training option have a longer-lasting effect? What do you think?"

lessons.title: Use of English Part 4: key word transformations in depth
lessons.body: Part 4 has six key word transformations, and each is worth up to 2 marks, so it carries far more weight than its size suggests. You get a sentence, a key word and a second sentence with a gap. You must complete the second sentence so that it means the same as the first, using between three and six words including the key word, and you must not change the key word in any way. Each item usually tests two things at once, which is why marks are split. In "It was wrong of you to leave without telling anyone. SHOULD - You ____ without telling anyone," the answer "should not have left" tests both the modal structure (should have + past participle) and the negative. A partly correct answer can still earn 1 mark. Common target structures: - Third conditionals: "I didn't know, so I went to the wrong building" becomes "If I had known about..., I wouldn't have gone..." - Reporting passives: "People say the castle was built..." becomes "The castle is said to have been built..." Note the perfect infinitive for a past event. - Noun phrases replacing clauses: "She is unlikely to accept" becomes "The chances of her accepting the offer are slim." - Fixed phrases and phrasal verbs: "take into account", "come up with", "on the verge of", "in spite of". - Comparatives and inversion: "As soon as we arrived, it started to rain" becomes "No sooner had we arrived than it started to rain." Method: first identify what the key word demands grammatically. "SAID" with a subject like "The castle" signals a passive reporting structure; "CHANCES" signals a noun phrase plus "of" + -ing. Then check what else in the original sentence must be kept: tense, negatives, and who did what. Finally, count the words. Contractions count as two words (wouldn't = would not), so be careful near the six-word limit. The most frequent errors are changing the key word ("chance" instead of "chances"), losing part of the meaning (dropping "not" or "about"), and adding words outside the gap. Write your answer, then read the whole new sentence aloud in your head and compare it with the original: same meaning, same time reference, same people. Practise by keeping a notebook of transformations you get wrong, grouped by structure, and reviewing it weekly.

lessons.title: Use of English Parts 2 and 3: grammar words and word families
lessons.body: Part 2 (open cloze) and Part 3 (word formation) each have eight gaps in a text. In Part 2 you write one word in each gap with no options; in Part 3 you change a given stem word to fit the gap. Both reward knowing patterns rather than isolated words. Part 2: think about function words. The answers are mostly prepositions, articles, pronouns, auxiliaries, conjunctions, quantifiers and parts of fixed phrases. Read the whole sentence and ask what the grammar requires. - Relative clauses: "The new policy, ___ aim is to reduce waste" needs a possessive relative: "whose". - Cleft and emphatic structures: "It was not ___ she read the letter again that she understood" needs "until". - Concession: "___ hard she tried, she could not open the jar" needs "However" (however + adjective/adverb + subject + verb). - Inverted conditionals: "___ any further information be required" needs "Should". - Fixed phrases: "on the verge of", "in spite of", "by no means", "as far as I know". Contractions are not accepted as one word, and spelling must be correct. Part 3: build the word in steps. Decide the word class from the position (after an article usually a noun, before a noun usually an adjective, modifying a verb usually an adverb), then decide whether the meaning needs a negative prefix, a plural or a change of form. - "of enormous historical ___ (SIGNIFY)" needs a noun: "significance". - "His ___ to compromise cost him support (WILLING)" needs a noun with a negative meaning, because refusing to compromise costs support: "unwillingness". Many candidates write "willingness" and lose the mark. - "The instructions were so ___ that nobody could follow them (COMPREHEND)" needs a negative adjective: "incomprehensible". Many Part 3 answers need two or three changes at once (prefix + suffix + spelling). Learn negative prefixes by family: un- (unknown, unwilling), in- (incomprehensible, insufficient), im- (impractical), ir- (irrelevant), il- (illogical), dis- (disapproval), mis- (misleading). Learn spelling changes too: "argue" becomes "argument" (the e disappears), "maintain" becomes "maintenance". For practice, take any article and highlight ten words; write the other members of each word family. This builds the flexible knowledge that Part 3 tests.

lessons.title: Reading Parts 6 and 7: comparing opinions and following structure
lessons.body: Parts 6 and 7 test different reading skills from the detail-focused Parts 5 and 8. Part 6 (cross-text multiple matching) presents four short texts by different writers on the same topic, for example four reviews of a book about cities. The four questions ask you to compare opinions across texts: "Which reviewer has a different view from the others about the quality of the evidence?" or "Which reviewer shares reviewer A's opinion of the proposals?" The most effective method is a quick opinion grid. Identify the aspects that the writers all comment on, usually three or four (evidence, proposals, writing style, intended audience). Then, for each text, note the writer's position on each aspect as +, - or a short phrase. With the grid complete, each question becomes a matter of reading across a row. For example, if A, C and D all praise the evidence and B calls it selective, B is the "different view". Be careful with concessive language: "Although the proposals are hard to fault for major cities, they would be unworkable in a small market town" is a negative view about small towns despite the positive opening. Part 7 (gapped text) removes six paragraphs from a long text; you choose from seven, so one paragraph is extra. This is a test of cohesion and coherence. Read the main text first to understand the overall line, then look at what comes immediately before and after each gap. Typical links include: - Reference words: "That patience was tested..." requires the previous paragraph to mention patience or a warning about hurrying. - Time and sequence: "It took the team eleven months to reassemble it" needs a previous paragraph explaining why reassembly was needed. - Topic shifts: a paragraph that reports a reaction ("People were crying") must follow the event that caused it. The extra paragraph usually fits the topic well but breaks a specific link. In the clockmaker article, a paragraph about the pay in banking is on-topic but gives "That patience" nothing to refer to. Always check both sides of a gap: a paragraph can fit the text before it and still contradict the text after it. Give Part 7 enough time; it is worth 2 marks per question, as is Part 6. Part 8 (multiple matching, 1 mark each) can be done more quickly by scanning.

lessons.title: Listening Parts 1 to 4: what each part rewards
lessons.body: The Listening paper has four parts and 30 questions, and you hear each recording twice. Each part rewards a different listening skill. Part 1 has three short extracts, each a conversation with two multiple-choice questions. Questions often focus on opinion, agreement or attitude: "What do the speakers agree about?" or "What does the man criticise?" Listen for agreement markers ("Absolutely", "I'd go along with that") and disagreement markers ("Funny, I'd have...", "I didn't mind him"). If one speaker praises something and the other disagrees, it cannot be the point they agree about. Part 2 is a monologue of about three minutes with eight sentence-completion gaps. The words you need are usually spoken in the recording, so write exactly what you hear, but the sentence around the gap is paraphrased. Predict the type of word before you listen: "Volunteers must bring their own ____" needs a noun, probably clothing or equipment. Watch for distractors: the speaker may mention boots and then say they can be lent, before naming the jacket that volunteers must bring. Part 3 is a conversation of about four minutes, often an interview, with six four-option multiple-choice questions. The questions follow the order of the recording and focus on attitudes and reasons. The wrong options often repeat words the speaker uses, while the right option paraphrases the idea. If a novelist says she "kept imagining reviewers reading over my shoulder" and "found myself playing safe", the answer is about pressure making her cautious, even if no option uses those exact words. Part 4 has five short monologues on a shared theme and two tasks: for each speaker you choose from one list (for example, their reason for doing something) and from a second list (for example, what surprised them). Use the first listening for Task One and the second for Task Two, or attempt both each time if you can. Speakers often mention more than one option, so focus on what they actually conclude or emphasise. Phrases like "what really struck me" or "the reason I stayed" point to the answer. On paper, transfer answers carefully at the end; on computer, answer directly. Spelling must be correct in Part 2.

lessons.title: Writing: the Part 1 essay and choosing a Part 2 genre
lessons.body: The Writing paper has two parts, each of 220-260 words. Part 1 is a compulsory essay. In Part 2 you choose one task from three, which can include a letter or email, a proposal, a report or a review. Part 1 essay. You receive notes from a seminar or discussion with three points, for example three ways governments could encourage healthier lifestyles: taxes on unhealthy food, public sports facilities and education campaigns. You must write about two of the three, explain which is more effective (or more important), and give reasons. The notes may include opinions expressed in the discussion; you may use them but should express them in your own words. A clear structure: an introduction that sets out the issue and your approach; one paragraph per method, each evaluating effectiveness with a reason and an example; and a conclusion that clearly states which method is more effective and why. A strong thesis might read: "While public sports facilities can help those already motivated to exercise, taxing unhealthy food is likely to be more effective because it changes the choices of the whole population." Keep a neutral to formal register: avoid contractions and conversational phrases. Part 2 genres. Choose the task whose genre you can control, not just the most interesting topic. - Report: written for a superior or committee; describes and evaluates a current or past situation, usually with headings, and ends with recommendations based on findings. - Proposal: also often uses headings, but its main purpose is to suggest a future plan and persuade the reader to adopt it. - Review: describes and evaluates something (a book, film, exhibition, venue) for readers of a magazine or website, and usually ends with a recommendation. A lively, engaging tone is appropriate. - Letter or email: register depends on the reader. A letter to a newspaper editor or a college principal needs a formal, polite tone. Language for range. Examiners look at content, communicative achievement, organisation and language. Show range accurately rather than forcing it: a cleft sentence ("What concerns many residents is the lack of lighting"), an inversion ("Not only is the venue spacious, but it is also easy to reach"), or a precise collocation ("pose a risk", "draw attention to"). One accurate complex structure per paragraph is better than several faulty ones. Plan for about five minutes per task, write, then keep five minutes to check word count, register and errors.

lessons.title: Speaking Parts 2 to 4: compare, interact and develop opinions
lessons.body: The Speaking test is taken in pairs with two examiners and lasts about 15 minutes for a pair. After a short interview in Part 1, the remaining parts test extended speaking and interaction. Part 2 long turn. You receive three pictures and two questions printed above them. You choose two pictures, compare them and answer the questions, speaking for about a minute. Then your partner does the same with a different set, and you are asked a short question about your partner's pictures, answering in about 30 seconds. The key is to compare and speculate, not describe. Instead of "In the first picture there is a man in a kitchen...", say: "Both pictures show people learning a skill, but the situations are very different. The man in the kitchen seems to be learning alone, perhaps from a video, whereas the students in the workshop have a teacher to guide them. I imagine the students might feel more confident, although the man probably enjoys the freedom." Speculative language (might, could, I imagine, it looks as if) and contrast language (whereas, while, on the other hand) are exactly what this part rewards. Answer both printed questions. When your partner speaks, listen. Your 30-second question will refer to their pictures, so a short, direct answer with a reason is ideal. Part 3 collaborative task. You and your partner discuss a question with five prompts for about two minutes, then have one minute to reach a decision. Interaction is assessed: respond to what your partner says, build on it, invite their opinion and politely disagree. "That's a good point about cost. I'd add that it could also bring people together. What do you think about the second option?" In the decision minute you do not have to agree, but you should negotiate: "So shall we go for... ? Or would you rather...?" Part 4 discussion. The examiner asks broader questions related to Part 3. Develop your answers with reasons, examples and nuance: "To some extent, yes. Technology clearly makes information more accessible, but I'm not convinced it makes people better informed, because..." If your partner dominates, bring yourself in politely: "Could I just add something there?" If you have little to say, react to your partner's view and extend it. Throughout, aim for natural interaction rather than a sequence of mini-speeches.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: multiple-choice cloze
practice.prompt: The play received ______ reviews from critics, who praised its originality.
practice.explanation: "Glowing reviews" is a fixed collocation meaning very positive reviews.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: multiple-choice cloze
practice.prompt: On closer inspection, her argument simply doesn't ______ water.
practice.explanation: The idiom is "hold water", meaning to be logically sound.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: multiple-choice cloze
practice.prompt: Online sales ______ a record high in the final quarter of the year.
practice.explanation: We "reach a record high"; "arrived" and "came" would need "at", and "got" is too informal and not the fixed phrase.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 2: open cloze
practice.prompt: ______ having very little experience, she was offered the position.
practice.explanation: "Despite" is followed by a noun or -ing form ("having"). "Although" needs a full clause ("Although she had...").

practice.skill: Use of English Part 2: open cloze
practice.prompt: No sooner had we sat down ______ the fire alarm went off.
practice.explanation: The fixed inverted structure is "No sooner had ... than ...". "When" pairs with "Hardly/Scarcely had ...".

practice.skill: Use of English Part 3: word formation
practice.prompt: The ______ of the new ring road took two years longer than planned. (CONSTRUCT)
practice.explanation: After "The" and before "of" a noun naming the process is needed: "construction".

practice.skill: Use of English Part 3: word formation
practice.prompt: Most of his comments were completely ______ to the discussion and wasted everyone's time. (RELEVANT)
practice.explanation: The meaning is negative ("wasted everyone's time") and an adjective is needed after "were completely": "irrelevant".

practice.skill: Use of English Part 4: key word transformation
practice.prompt: "I regret not studying harder at school." Using WISH: I ______ harder at school.
practice.explanation: Regret about the past uses wish + past perfect: "I wish I had studied harder" (four words, within the 3-6 limit).

practice.skill: Use of English Part 4: key word transformation
practice.prompt: "It's possible that he missed the train." Using MAY: He ______ the train.
practice.explanation: Possibility about the past uses may + have + past participle.

practice.passage: When the city museum announced that it would put its entire archive online, I expected to be delighted. As a historian, I have spent countless hours in reading rooms requesting boxes that turned out to contain nothing of use. Yet my first week with the digital archive left me oddly unsettled. The search function is superb, but it returns exactly what I ask for and nothing else. In the reading room, the irrelevant letter that happened to sit beside the one I wanted occasionally proved more interesting than my original question. I am not arguing that digitisation is a mistake; it has opened collections to people who could never travel to see them. I simply suspect that researchers will need to cultivate deliberate habits of wandering, because the technology will no longer wander for them.
practice.prompt: How does the writer feel about the digital archive after the first week?
options: Convinced that it should be withdrawn
Indifferent, because she rarely uses archives
Entirely disappointed with its search function
Impressed by it, yet uneasy about what it might cause researchers to miss
practice.explanation: She calls the search "superb" but feels "oddly unsettled" because it returns only what she asks for. She explicitly says digitisation is not a mistake.

practice.passage: When the city museum announced that it would put its entire archive online, I expected to be delighted. As a historian, I have spent countless hours in reading rooms requesting boxes that turned out to contain nothing of use. Yet my first week with the digital archive left me oddly unsettled. The search function is superb, but it returns exactly what I ask for and nothing else. In the reading room, the irrelevant letter that happened to sit beside the one I wanted occasionally proved more interesting than my original question. I am not arguing that digitisation is a mistake; it has opened collections to people who could never travel to see them. I simply suspect that researchers will need to cultivate deliberate habits of wandering, because the technology will no longer wander for them.
practice.prompt: What point does the writer make with the example of "the irrelevant letter"?
options: Letters are more interesting than other documents.
Unplanned discoveries can be valuable to research.
practice.explanation: The neighboring letter sometimes "proved more interesting than my original question": chance finds can be valuable.

practice.passage: When the city museum announced that it would put its entire archive online, I expected to be delighted. As a historian, I have spent countless hours in reading rooms requesting boxes that turned out to contain nothing of use. Yet my first week with the digital archive left me oddly unsettled. The search function is superb, but it returns exactly what I ask for and nothing else. In the reading room, the irrelevant letter that happened to sit beside the one I wanted occasionally proved more interesting than my original question. I am not arguing that digitisation is a mistake; it has opened collections to people who could never travel to see them. I simply suspect that researchers will need to cultivate deliberate habits of wandering, because the technology will no longer wander for them.
practice.prompt: What does the writer recommend in the final sentence?
options: Researchers should return to using only reading rooms.
Search tools should return fewer results.
Researchers should consciously build habits of browsing beyond their exact query.
practice.explanation: She suggests researchers "cultivate deliberate habits of wandering" because the technology will not do it for them.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: Multiple-choice cloze
practice.passage:
The rise of the remote village
For most of the twentieth century, small villages (1) ___ population steadily as young people moved to cities in search of work. In recent years, however, the trend has begun to (2) ___ in some regions. Fast internet connections have made it possible for many professionals to work from home, and rising city rents have (3) ___ them to look elsewhere. Some local councils are now (4) ___ advantage of this shift, offering grants to people who renovate empty houses.
practice.prompt: Choose the word that best fits gap (1).
practice.explanation: "Lose population" is the natural collocation for places becoming emptier. "Drop" can describe a falling number but does not take "population" as an object in this way.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: Multiple-choice cloze
practice.passage:
The rise of the remote village
For most of the twentieth century, small villages (1) ___ population steadily as young people moved to cities in search of work. In recent years, however, the trend has begun to (2) ___ in some regions. Fast internet connections have made it possible for many professionals to work from home, and rising city rents have (3) ___ them to look elsewhere. Some local councils are now (4) ___ advantage of this shift, offering grants to people who renovate empty houses.
practice.prompt: Choose the word that best fits gap (2).
practice.explanation: "The trend has begun to reverse" uses "reverse" intransitively, meaning to go in the opposite direction. "Revert" and "return" need "to" plus a previous state, and "restore" needs an object.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: Multiple-choice cloze
practice.passage:
The rise of the remote village
For most of the twentieth century, small villages (1) ___ population steadily as young people moved to cities in search of work. In recent years, however, the trend has begun to (2) ___ in some regions. Fast internet connections have made it possible for many professionals to work from home, and rising city rents have (3) ___ them to look elsewhere. Some local councils are now (4) ___ advantage of this shift, offering grants to people who renovate empty houses.
practice.prompt: Choose the word that best fits gap (3).
practice.explanation: Only "prompt" fits the pattern verb + object + to-infinitive: "prompted them to look". "Made" and "let" take a bare infinitive (made them look), and "result" needs "in".

practice.skill: Use of English Part 1: Multiple-choice cloze
practice.passage:
The rise of the remote village
For most of the twentieth century, small villages (1) ___ population steadily as young people moved to cities in search of work. In recent years, however, the trend has begun to (2) ___ in some regions. Fast internet connections have made it possible for many professionals to work from home, and rising city rents have (3) ___ them to look elsewhere. Some local councils are now (4) ___ advantage of this shift, offering grants to people who renovate empty houses.
practice.prompt: Choose the word that best fits gap (4).
practice.explanation: "Take advantage of" is a fixed phrase. "Have an advantage" exists but does not combine with "of this shift" in the meaning of exploiting an opportunity.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 2: Open cloze
practice.prompt: Which word fills the gap? "______ any further information be required, please contact the main office."
practice.explanation: This is an inverted conditional: "Should any further information be required" means "If any further information is required". "If" would need "is required", not "be required".

practice.skill: Use of English Part 2: Open cloze
practice.prompt: Which word fills the gap? "It was not ______ she read the letter a second time that she understood what had happened."
practice.explanation: "It was not until ... that" is a fixed emphatic structure meaning that something happened only after a particular moment. "When" and "before" do not form this pattern.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 2: Open cloze
practice.prompt: Which word fills the gap? "The new policy, ______ aim is to reduce waste, has been widely criticised."
practice.explanation: A possessive relative pronoun is needed before "aim": the aim of the policy. "Which aim" is ungrammatical here, and "that" cannot introduce a non-defining clause after a comma.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 2: Open cloze
practice.prompt: Which word fills the gap? "______ hard she tried, she could not get the old window to open."
practice.explanation: "However + adjective/adverb + subject + verb" expresses concession: no matter how hard she tried. "Although" cannot be followed directly by "hard", and "Whatever" needs a noun.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 3: Word formation
practice.prompt: Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits the gap: "The museum's collection is of enormous historical ______." (SIGNIFY)
practice.explanation: After the adjective "historical", a noun is needed, and the standard noun meaning importance is "significance". "Significant" is an adjective.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 3: Word formation
practice.prompt: Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits the gap: "His ______ to compromise eventually cost him the support of his colleagues." (WILLING)
practice.explanation: A noun is needed after "His", and the meaning must be negative, because refusing to compromise is what cost him support. "Willingness" is grammatically possible but gives the opposite meaning.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 3: Word formation
practice.prompt: Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits the gap: "The instructions were so ______ that nobody could follow them." (COMPREHEND)
practice.explanation: The gap needs a negative adjective after "so". The correct prefix is in-, giving "incomprehensible". "Comprehensive" means complete, and "incomprehension" is a noun.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 3: Word formation
practice.prompt: Use the word in capitals to form a word that fits the gap: "Despite years of research, the cause of the disease remains largely ______." (KNOW)
practice.explanation: "Despite years of research" signals that the cause is still not understood, so the negative adjective "unknown" is needed. "Known" reverses the meaning.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 4: Key word transformation
practice.prompt: "I didn't know about the change of venue, so I went to the wrong building." HAD: If I ______ the change of venue, I wouldn't have gone to the wrong building.
practice.explanation: A third conditional needs "if + past perfect": "had known about". It also keeps "about" from the original. "Knew about" omits the key word, and "would have known" cannot follow "if" here.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 4: Key word transformation
practice.prompt: "People say that the castle was built in the twelfth century." SAID: The castle ______ in the twelfth century.
options: is said to have been built
practice.explanation: The reporting passive needs "is said" (people say it now) plus a perfect passive infinitive for a past event: "to have been built". "To be built" loses the past time reference, and the last option has no main verb.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 4: Key word transformation
practice.prompt: "It was wrong of you to leave without telling anyone." SHOULD: You ______ without telling anyone.
practice.explanation: Criticism of a past action uses "should not have + past participle". "Should not leave" refers to the present or future, and the other options have incorrect word order or verb form.

practice.skill: Use of English Part 4: Key word transformation
practice.prompt: "She is unlikely to accept the offer." CHANCES: The ______ the offer are slim.
practice.explanation: The key word must stay exactly as given (CHANCES), followed by "of" + object pronoun + -ing. Changing it to "chance" breaks the rules of the task, and the other options are ungrammatical.

practice.passage:
For years I resisted the advice, repeated in every productivity guide I skimmed and abandoned, to keep a notebook by the bed. It struck me as faintly precious, the sort of habit that belongs to people who photograph their breakfast. My ideas, I assumed, would either survive until morning on their own merits or deserve to perish.
What changed my mind was not a book but a power cut. Unable to read or scroll, I lay awake composing, of all things, the opening of an essay I had been failing to start for months. By the time the lights flickered back I had a paragraph I was rather pleased with, and by breakfast I had lost all but its first clause. The sentence that survived was the weakest of the lot.
So I bought the notebook. I would like to report that it transformed my working life; it did not, quite. Most of what I scrawl at two in the morning is illegible, and what can be deciphered is often banal: "ring the dentist", "the problem is the middle". Yet every few weeks there is a line that earns the whole enterprise, a phrase that reorganises a stalled piece of work in a way no amount of daytime staring achieved.
I have come to think the value lies less in capturing brilliance than in permission. Knowing that a thought can be put down, rather than held, seems to let the mind stop rehearsing it and move on to the next. The notebook is not an archive so much as a place to set things down, the mental equivalent of emptying one's pockets at the door.
practice.prompt: What was the writer's original attitude to keeping a notebook by the bed?
options: He thought it was useful but too difficult to maintain.
He believed it would disturb his sleep.
He had tried it and found it made no difference.
He considered it a slightly pretentious habit.
practice.explanation: He calls it "faintly precious", linking it to people who photograph their breakfast, which shows he saw it as affected or pretentious. He says he resisted the advice, so he had not tried it.

practice.passage:
Four reviewers comment on a book called The Walkable City, which argues that city centres should be largely closed to private cars.
A: The author marshals an impressive range of studies linking car-free streets with better health and cleaner air, and the evidence is hard to dispute. Where the book falters is in its proposals, which assume dense populations and frequent public transport; in a small market town they would simply be unworkable. Still, the prose is lively and often witty.
B: For all its confidence, the book's evidence is curiously selective: the effect on small shopkeepers, many of whom depend on passing motorists, is barely mentioned. The proposals themselves are sensible enough, and several have been tried successfully. Readers should be warned, however, that the writing is dense and rather dry.
C: This is a thorough piece of work, drawing on research from a dozen countries. Better still, the author shows convincingly that the proposals can be scaled down, so that even a modest town could adopt them with little expense. Add an engaging, conversational style, and the result is a book that deserves a wide readership.
D: The research here is meticulous, and the author is scrupulous about its limits. I am less persuaded by the plans, which seem designed for capital cities and would struggle anywhere smaller. The book also repeats its central argument so often that the final chapters become a chore.
practice.prompt: Which reviewer has a different view from the others about the quality of the evidence presented in the book?
practice.explanation: A, C and D all praise the evidence ("hard to dispute", "thorough", "meticulous"), while B calls it "curiously selective" because it ignores the effect on small shopkeepers.

practice.passage:
Main text:
When Hannah Price answered an advertisement for an apprentice at a small clock-repair workshop, she had never so much as changed a watch battery. "I'd just left a job in banking," she says. "I wanted to make something with my hands, and I liked the idea of fixing things rather than replacing them."
[Gap 1]
That patience was tested in her first winter, when the workshop took on the restoration of a nineteenth-century tower clock from a nearby village church. The mechanism had not run for forty years.
[Gap 2]
It took the team eleven months to reassemble it. On the day the clock was reinstalled, much of the village turned out to hear it strike.
[Gap 3]
Today Hannah runs the workshop herself and trains apprentices of her own. "I tell them what I was told," she says. "The clock will wait for you. Don't rush it."

Removed paragraphs:
A. Her employer, a clockmaker in his seventies, warned her that the trade would not suit anyone in a hurry. For the first three months she was allowed to do little more than clean parts and watch.
B. Many of its parts were so badly rusted that they had to be made from scratch, using the surviving pieces as models. Each new wheel had to be cut by hand.
C. "People were crying," Hannah remembers. "Some of them had grown up hearing that bell and thought they would never hear it again."
D. Banking, she admits, had paid considerably better, and several friends told her she was making a mistake.
practice.prompt: Which paragraph fits Gap 1?
practice.explanation: The text after the gap begins "That patience was tested", so Gap 1 must mention patience; A's warning that the trade does not suit anyone in a hurry, and months of watching, provide it. D fits the topic of leaving banking but gives "That patience" nothing to refer to, so it is the extra paragraph.

practice.passage:
Four adults describe learning a musical instrument.
A - Tomasz: I took up the cello at forty-five. Honestly, my biggest fear at the start was looking foolish in front of my teacher, who was half my age. That faded quickly. I practise for twenty minutes before work every day, and last year I joined an amateur orchestra. Playing as part of a group is the most rewarding thing I've done in years.
B - Leila: I began the piano with an app, and for a few months it was brilliant: quick rewards, little songs, a sense of progress. Then I seemed to stop improving, however much I practised. Switching to a teacher was a revelation, mainly because she corrected my posture and hand position, which the app never could.
C - Martin: I had guitar lessons as a boy and gave up at twelve. Coming back thirty years later, I was amazed how much my fingers remembered; chord shapes I hadn't thought about for decades came back within weeks. I only play for myself, though. Performing has never appealed to me.
D - Ruth: Six months into learning the violin I almost gave up. The progress felt invisible. My teacher suggested recording myself on the first day of every month, and listening back to those recordings changed everything. I could finally hear how far I'd come.
practice.prompt: Which person mentions that an earlier experience with the instrument helped them?
practice.explanation: Martin had lessons as a boy and found that his fingers remembered chord shapes when he returned. None of the others mentions previous experience of their instrument.

Transcript:
Extract One. You hear two friends talking about a television documentary.
Woman: Did you watch that documentary about the deep sea last night?
Man: I did. Visually it was stunning, wasn't it? Some of those creatures looked like they'd come from another planet.
Woman: Absolutely. Though I thought they rushed the section on how the footage was actually filmed. That's what I was most curious about.
Man: Funny, I'd have cut that part altogether. What grated on me was the narration. Every two minutes he'd tell us how mysterious everything was, as if we couldn't work that out for ourselves.
Woman: Oh, I didn't mind him. He's got a lovely voice.
practice.prompt: What do the two friends agree about?
options: The section on filming techniques was too short.
The images in the documentary were impressive.
practice.explanation: The man calls it "visually stunning" and the woman replies "Absolutely". They disagree about the filming section, and only the woman likes the narrator's voice.

practice.prompt: Why did the woman leave architecture?

She had too little opportunity to do creative design work.
She wanted to start her own furniture business.
A friend persuaded her to become a full-time teacher.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
Speaker: Hi, I'm Dana, and I coordinate the seabird monitoring project on Rook Island. Every summer we take about twelve volunteers. People often imagine they'll spend their days watching puffins through binoculars, and there is some of that, but the main task is actually counting nests on the cliff tops, which means a lot of careful walking in strong winds. We start at six in the morning, because that's when the birds are most active around the colony. Accommodation is in an old lighthouse keeper's cottage. It's basic, and there's no mobile signal at all, but there is a radio for emergencies. The one thing every volunteer must bring is a good waterproof jacket. We can lend boots, but jackets never seem to come back in one piece. Last year we recorded a fall in the number of puffin chicks, which we think is linked to a shortage of sand eels, the small fish the adults feed them.
practice.prompt: Complete the sentence: The volunteers' main task is counting ______ on the cliff tops.
practice.explanation: Dana says the main task is "counting nests on the cliff tops". Watching puffins is what people imagine, which she contrasts with the real main task.

Transcript:
Interviewer: Your first novel was a huge success. Did that make the second one easier?
Author: Quite the opposite, I'm afraid. With the first book, nobody was waiting for it, so I could take risks. With the second, I kept imagining reviewers reading over my shoulder, and I found myself playing safe. I threw away nearly a year's work because it read like an imitation of the first book.
Interviewer: What got you going again?
Author: Oddly enough, a change of routine. I'd always written in the mornings, but I started writing late at night instead, when I was too tired to censor myself. The first drafts were messy, but they had energy.
Interviewer: The new novel is set in a fishing town. Did you research that much?
Author: Less than people assume. I spent a week there, mostly listening to how people talked rather than taking notes on the place itself. I find that if I research too much, I'm tempted to put everything in, and the story gets buried.
Interviewer: And what's next?
Author: I'm deliberately not planning anything in public. I've learned that announcing a project too early makes it feel like an obligation.
practice.prompt: Why did the author find her second novel difficult to write?
options: She had run out of ideas after her first book.
Reviewers had criticised her first novel.
Awareness of people's expectations made her too cautious.
She had less time because of her success.
practice.explanation: She imagined reviewers "reading over my shoulder" and found herself "playing safe". The first novel was a success, so reviewers had not criticised it.

practice.passage:
Transcript:
You will hear five short extracts in which people talk about volunteering.
Speaker 1: I'll be honest, I first signed up at the animal shelter because I thought it would look good on my CV. But within a month that had gone out of the window. I'd go in on my days off just to see how the dogs were getting on. What nobody tells you is how exhausting it is; I'd come home aching all over.
Speaker 2: A friend had been helping at the food bank for years and kept asking me to come along, so eventually I did. What really shocked me was how many of the people we helped had jobs. I'd assumed it was mainly people out of work.
Speaker 3: When I retired, I found the days had no shape. I'd always liked history, so I started guiding visitors at the local museum two mornings a week. The children's groups are my favourite. Some of them know more about the Romans than I do.
Speaker 4: My son's football team lost its coach, and somebody had to step in. I thought it would just be a matter of running training on Saturdays. In fact, half my time goes on forms, emails, booking pitches and sorting out transport. The coaching is the easy bit.
Speaker 5: I'd always wanted to try broadcasting, so I volunteered at the hospital radio station. I present a request show on Thursday evenings. I'm still surprised by how few people actually tune in, but the ones who do really appreciate it.
practice.prompt: Which speaker began volunteering to give structure to their time after stopping work?
practice.explanation: Speaker 3 says that after retiring "the days had no shape" and started guiding at the museum. Speaker 2 mentions people with jobs, but that refers to the people they help.
