exams.name: GRE General Test
exams.best_for: Applicants to graduate programs (master's and PhD) and many business and law schools that accept the GRE.

sections.name: Analytical Writing
sections.notes: One 'Analyze an Issue' essay; always first.

sections.name: Verbal Reasoning
sections.notes: Two sections: 12 questions in 18 minutes and 15 questions in 23 minutes; section-level adaptive.

sections.name: Quantitative Reasoning
sections.notes: Two sections: 12 questions in 21 minutes and 15 questions in 26 minutes; on-screen calculator; section-level adaptive.

format.score_scale: Verbal 130-170 and Quant 130-170 (1-point steps); Analytical Writing 0-6 (half-point steps)
format.validity: 5 years (reportable for 5 years after the test date)
format.delivery: Computer-delivered at a test center or at home; an unscored section may appear.

free_resources.title: POWERPREP Online: two free full-length practice tests
GRE General Test prep hub
GRE test content and structure

lessons.title: The shorter GRE: structure and section adaptivity
lessons.body: The GRE General Test takes about 1 hour 58 minutes: one 30-minute Analyze an Issue essay first, then two Verbal and two Quantitative sections in any order. Verbal sections have 12 questions in 18 minutes and 15 in 23 minutes; Quant sections have 12 in 21 minutes and 15 in 26 minutes. Adaptivity happens between sections, not between questions: your performance on the first section of a measure sets the difficulty of the second. Within a section you can skip, mark, and return, so use that freedom. Answer every question because there is no penalty for wrong answers. Pacing: roughly 90 seconds per Verbal question and 1 minute 45 seconds per Quant question. Scores: Verbal and Quant run from 130 to 170, and Analytical Writing from 0 to 6. Scores are reportable for five years. Mini-example: if a quant question needs a long computation, use the on-screen calculator only for ugly arithmetic; estimation often eliminates three choices faster than exact work.

lessons.title: Text completion and sentence equivalence
lessons.body: These questions test vocabulary through logic. The method: cover the options, find the clue words in the sentence, and identify trigger words that tell you the direction: "although", "but" and "despite" signal contrast; "because", "thus" and a semicolon often signal support. Write your own word for the blank, then match. In Sentence Equivalence you must pick two options that produce sentences with the same meaning; the correct pair are usually near-synonyms, but not every synonym pair is correct, so check the pair against the context. Mini-example: "Although the critic was famous for his ___ reviews, his assessment of the debut novel was surprisingly generous." The contrast with "generous" means the blank must mean harsh: "scathing" or "caustic" fit, while "effusive" is the opposite. Build vocabulary in context: learn words in families (harsh: acerbic, caustic, trenchant; praise: laud, extol, eulogize) and review them with sentences you write yourself.

lessons.title: Quantitative comparison without heavy math
lessons.body: Quantitative comparison questions ask whether Quantity A or B is greater, whether they are equal, or whether the relationship cannot be determined. They are designed to be solved by reasoning. Strategy one: simplify both sides the same way, as with an inequality, by adding, subtracting, or dividing by positive numbers. Strategy two: when variables appear, test several kinds of numbers: a positive integer, a fraction between 0 and 1, zero, and a negative number if allowed. If different picks give different results, the answer is "cannot be determined". Mini-example: x > 0; Quantity A is x squared, Quantity B is x. With x = 2, A is greater; with x = 1/2, B is greater. So the answer is D. If a question has only numbers and no variables, D is impossible, because fixed numbers always have a definite relationship. Caution: never multiply or divide both sides by a quantity that could be negative, because that would flip the comparison.

lessons.title: Analytical Writing: a reliable Issue essay template
lessons.body: You have 30 minutes for one Issue task. Spend 5 minutes planning, 22 writing, and 3 proofreading. Readers reward a clear, qualified position, well-developed reasons with specific examples, logical organization, and controlled language; length helps only when it adds development. A dependable structure: an introduction that restates the issue and gives a nuanced thesis ("largely true, except when..."); two or three body paragraphs, each built on one reason and one concrete example from history, science, business or personal observation; a paragraph that acknowledges the strongest counterargument and answers it; and a short conclusion. Follow the task's specific instruction, for example to discuss when the claim might not hold, because ignoring it costs points. Mini-example: claim: "Governments should fund only research with immediate practical benefits." Thesis: "Practical returns matter, but limiting funding to them would sacrifice basic research, such as early studies of the immune system, that later produced unforeseen medical breakthroughs."

lessons.title: Building a GRE study plan from your target scores
lessons.body:
Start with the numbers you need, not with a book. Look up the median or typical Verbal and Quantitative scores for the programs on your list; many departments publish them, and some state minimums or say that the GRE is optional. Write down a target for each measure and for Analytical Writing.

Next, take one full official practice test (ETS offers free POWERPREP tests) under real conditions: the 30-minute Analyze an Issue essay first, then two Verbal sections (12 questions in 18 minutes and 15 in 23 minutes) and two Quantitative sections (12 in 21 minutes and 15 in 26 minutes). The whole test takes about 1 hour 58 minutes. Your baseline tells you how far each score is from its target.

Remember how the scoring works. Verbal and Quant are each scored from 130 to 170 in one-point steps, and Analytical Writing from 0 to 6 in half-point steps. The test is adaptive by section: how well you do on the first Verbal or Quant section decides whether the second section of that measure is easier or harder. A strong first section therefore unlocks access to higher scores, so do not treat it as a warm-up.

A ten-week plan for a working student, about eight hours a week:
Weeks 1 to 4: content. Two Quant sessions on the four content areas (arithmetic, algebra, geometry and data analysis) and two Verbal sessions on question types, plus 15 minutes of vocabulary in context each day.
Weeks 5 to 8: timed sets. Mix question types the way the test does and keep an error log with three columns: topic, what went wrong, and the rule that would have prevented it.
Weeks 9 and 10: two more full practice tests, one Issue essay a week, and review of the error log.

Scores are reportable for five years, and with ScoreSelect you choose which test dates to send, so a retake is low risk if your first attempt falls short.

Mini-example: if your baseline is Verbal 152 and Quant 158 and your target is 160 for both, Verbal needs the bigger gain, so give it three of your four weekly sessions until the gap narrows.

lessons.title: Text Completion: two- and three-blank strategy
lessons.body:
Text Completion passages are one to five sentences long with one to three blanks. A one-blank question has five choices; two- and three-blank questions have three choices per blank, and you get credit only if every blank is right. There is no partial credit, which is why method matters more than vocabulary alone.

Step 1: ignore the choices. Read the text and look for clues: words that define the blank (a colon, a phrase after a dash), and signal words. Contrast signals include although, but, yet, despite, far from and rather than. Continuation signals include and, because, indeed, in fact and the colon.

Step 2: predict a simple word for each blank in your own words, such as "harsh" or "not finished." Write it down if needed.

Step 3: start with the blank that has the strongest clue, which is not always the first. In a two-blank text, the second blank often depends on the first, so solving the easier blank first narrows the other.

Step 4: plug your full choice back into the text and read the whole thing. A choice can fit one clause and contradict another.

Traps to watch for. Opposite meanings: test writers put a word with the reverse charge next to the correct one. Related but wrong: a word in the same topic area but with the wrong meaning, such as "verbose" when the text needs "vague." Second meanings: common words used in less common senses, such as "qualify" meaning to limit a claim, not to pass a test.

Mini-example: "The scientist was careful to (i) ___ her findings, noting that the small sample made any broad conclusion (ii) ___." The clue "small sample" means conclusions would be too early, so (ii) is "premature." A careful scientist with a small sample would limit her claims, so (i) is "qualify," not "trumpet."

Build vocabulary through reading quality journalism and by learning words in groups of related meaning, such as words for praise (laud, extol) and for criticism (censure, disparage).

lessons.title: Sentence Equivalence: finding the matching pair
lessons.body:
Sentence Equivalence gives one sentence with one blank and six answer choices. You must select exactly two, and both must produce sentences that fit the meaning and are alike in meaning. There is no partial credit for getting one of the two. (In this app's practice format, the four options are already written as pairs, and exactly one pair is correct.)

Method. First, cover the choices and predict the meaning of the blank from the clues, just as in Text Completion. Second, look for choices that match your prediction. Third, confirm that the two choices you pick are close in meaning to each other and that each one, alone, makes a sensible sentence.

Why not just find synonyms? Because the answer choices usually include a pair of near-synonyms that do not fit the sentence. For example, if the sentence calls for a word meaning "brief," a choice list might include "verbose" and "prolix," which are synonyms of each other but the opposite of what the sentence needs. Always start from the sentence's meaning.

Also watch for a choice that fits the sentence but has no partner. If only one word matches your prediction and nothing else is close in meaning, re-read the clues: your prediction may be too narrow. For instance, if you predicted "careful" and see "meticulous" and "punctilious," both match, even if "punctilious" is less familiar.

Signal words. Despite, though and rather than reverse the direction; so, because and a colon continue it. A sentence like "Rather than ___ the critics, the director thanked them" needs a word that contrasts with thanking, such as "rebuff" or "dismiss."

Pacing. Sentence Equivalence questions are usually the fastest Verbal items, about 45 to 60 seconds each. Banking time here helps with longer Reading Comprehension passages.

Mini-example: "The professor's explanation was admirably ___, conveying in two sentences what the textbook took two pages to say." The clue points to brevity, and the positive word "admirably" rules out negative words, so "succinct" and "concise" form the pair.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: short passages and argument questions
lessons.body:
About half of GRE Verbal questions are Reading Comprehension. Passages range from one paragraph to several, on topics in the sciences, social sciences, humanities and everyday subjects. Some ask you to select one answer, some ask you to select all correct answers, and some ask you to select a sentence in the passage. You do not need outside knowledge; every answer is supported by the text.

Read for structure. For each paragraph, note its job in a few words: "old view," "new evidence," "objection," "author's conclusion." Most GRE passages contrast two positions, so pay special attention to words such as however, yet, recent and once assumed.

Common question types and how to approach them:
Primary purpose: choose the answer that covers the whole passage, with a verb that matches its tone (explain, challenge, describe). Answers that cover only one paragraph are too narrow.
Function of a detail: ask why the author mentions it, usually to support or illustrate a nearby claim.
Inference: the correct answer must be true based on the passage. Avoid choices that go further than the text, especially with words like "entirely" or "proved."

Argument passages. Some short passages present an argument and ask what would strengthen it, weaken it, explain a puzzle, or must be true. Identify the conclusion and the evidence, then find the gap between them. Typical gaps are an alternative cause, a non-representative sample, or the assumption that a past trend will continue. To weaken, choose a fact that widens the gap; to strengthen, choose one that closes it. For "must be true" questions, test each answer against the statements and reject any that could be false.

Mini-example: a city's streetlight energy costs fell 40 percent after switching to LEDs, and the energy director predicts similar savings for buildings. If lighting is only a small share of building electricity use, the prediction fails, so that fact weakens the argument.

Time: give about 1.5 to 2 minutes per question, including reading time, and move on if you are stuck; you can mark and return within the section.

lessons.title: Quant: Numeric Entry, Data Interpretation and the calculator
lessons.body:
The Quantitative Reasoning measure covers arithmetic, algebra, geometry and data analysis at roughly a high-school level, but the questions demand careful reasoning. Four formats appear: Quantitative Comparison, Multiple-choice with one answer, Multiple-choice with one or more answers, and Numeric Entry. Some questions come in Data Interpretation sets that share a table or graph.

Numeric Entry. You type the answer into a box, so there are no choices to check against. Read the question twice for the requested form: an integer, a decimal, a fraction (two boxes), or a value "to the nearest tenth." Equivalent forms of a correct answer are accepted, such as 2.5 and 2.50, but rounding to the wrong place is not. Always re-read the final line of the question before typing; many errors come from answering for x when the question asked for 2x.

Data Interpretation. Before you calculate, read the title, the units (thousands? percent?), and any notes. Many questions ask for a percent change, which is (new - old)/old, or a share of a total. Estimate first: if the choices are far apart, rounding is enough and saves time. If they are close, compute exactly.

The on-screen calculator. It handles basic operations and square roots and follows order of operations. Use it for ugly arithmetic, such as 760 x 0.95^4, but not for things that are faster by hand, such as 15 percent of 240. A useful habit: write down the setup first, then use the calculator only for the final arithmetic, so a typing slip does not hide a reasoning mistake. The "Transfer Display" button can move the result into a Numeric Entry box.

Pacing. You have 21 minutes for 12 questions in the first Quant section and 26 minutes for 15 in the second, about 1 minute 45 seconds each. Data Interpretation sets often take longer, so bank time on quick Quantitative Comparisons.

Mini-example: enrollment rose from 4,500 to 5,560. The percent increase is 1,060/4,500, about 23.6 percent. A common error divides by the new total instead, giving about 19 percent.

lessons.title: Quant traps: number properties, algebra and geometry
lessons.body:
The GRE likes questions that look easy but contain a trap. Learn the traps and they turn into free points.

Quantitative Comparison logic. If you can find one case where A is greater and another where B is greater, the answer is "cannot be determined." Test numbers from different categories: positive and negative, zero, fractions between 0 and 1, and large values. For example, if 0 < x < 1, then x^2 is less than the square root of x, but for x > 1 it is the other way round. If the problem fixes the values completely, the relationship can always be determined.

Squares and roots. If x^2 = 16, x could be 4 or -4. But the square root of 16 is only 4.

Integers and divisibility. Count divisors with prime factorization: 360 = 2^3 x 3^2 x 5, so it has (3 + 1)(2 + 1)(1 + 1) = 24 divisors. Units digits of powers repeat in cycles; 3 cycles 3, 9, 7, 1, so divide the exponent by 4 and use the remainder.

Algebra identities. (x + 1/x)^2 = x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2, so if x + 1/x = 5, then x^2 + 1/x^2 = 23. Also remember a^2 - b^2 = (a - b)(a + b). For roots of a quadratic x^2 + bx + c, the sum is -b and the product is c.

Exponents. Factor out the smallest power: 2^(x+3) - 2^x = 2^x(8 - 1) = 7 x 2^x.

Geometry. The figure is not necessarily drawn to scale unless stated, so do not judge lengths by eye. A rectangle inscribed in a circle has a diagonal equal to the diameter. A square with diagonal d has area d^2/2, the same as a right isosceles triangle with legs d.

Counting and probability. Use combinations when order does not matter (nCr) and permutations when it does. For "or" questions, add and subtract the overlap; for "exactly one" questions, subtract the overlap twice.

Mini-example: for integers x > y with xy = 12, x + y can be 13, 8, 7 or negative values such as -7. Compared with 7, the relationship cannot be determined.

practice.prompt: Although the critic was known for her ___ reviews, her assessment of the debut novel was surprisingly warm.
practice.explanation: "Although" signals contrast with "surprisingly warm", so the blank must mean harsh. "Scathing" fits; "effusive" means warmly enthusiastic, the opposite.

practice.prompt: The mayor's reputation for ___ was well earned: she routinely changed positions on major issues to suit whichever audience she was addressing.
practice.explanation: Changing positions to suit an audience is avoiding a clear commitment, which is equivocation. Candor and steadfastness are the opposite; austerity is unrelated.

practice.prompt: The scientist's early hypothesis, once dismissed as fanciful, has been ___ by a decade of careful experiments. Which word best completes the sentence?
practice.explanation: "Once dismissed" suggests a reversal: the hypothesis was later shown to be right, so "vindicated". Its natural partner in a two-answer version would be "confirmed".

practice.passage: For decades, historians treated the medieval guild primarily as a cartel that restricted competition and kept prices high. Recent scholarship complicates this view. By setting quality standards and training apprentices, guilds may have helped buyers trust goods they could not inspect closely, a function that benefited consumers as well as members. Critics of the newer view respond that such benefits were modest compared with the costs of exclusion.
practice.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that guilds were harmful cartels.
present a reassessment of guilds and note a response to it.
practice.explanation: The passage describes an older view, a newer view that complicates it, and critics' reply. It does not take a final side or prove anything about prices.

practice.passage: For decades, historians treated the medieval guild primarily as a cartel that restricted competition and kept prices high. Recent scholarship complicates this view. By setting quality standards and training apprentices, guilds may have helped buyers trust goods they could not inspect closely, a function that benefited consumers as well as members. Critics of the newer view respond that such benefits were modest compared with the costs of exclusion.
practice.prompt: It can be inferred that the newer scholarship assumes that
options: apprentices were paid more than other workers.
buyers sometimes could not easily judge the quality of goods themselves.
practice.explanation: The claim that quality standards built trust only matters if buyers could not inspect goods well themselves; the passage says exactly that. The other options are unsupported or contradicted.

practice.prompt: A city installed brighter streetlights on Elm Street, and reported nighttime thefts there fell by 30% the following year. Officials concluded the lights caused the drop. Which finding would most weaken this conclusion?
options: Reported nighttime thefts fell by about 30% citywide that year, including streets with no new lights.
The new lights use less electricity.
Residents said they felt safer on Elm Street.
practice.explanation: If thefts fell equally where no lights were installed, something other than the lights likely explains the drop.

practice.passage: Quantity A: (0.4)^2    Quantity B: 0.4
practice.prompt: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
practice.explanation: (0.4)^2 = 0.16, which is less than 0.4. Squaring a number between 0 and 1 makes it smaller.

practice.passage: x > 0.   Quantity A: x^2    Quantity B: x
practice.prompt: Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
practice.explanation: If x = 2, A = 4 > 2. If x = 1/2, A = 1/4 < 1/2. If x = 1, they are equal. The relationship depends on x.

practice.prompt: The average of five numbers is 18. When one number is removed, the average of the remaining four is 16. What number was removed?
practice.explanation: Sum of five = 5 x 18 = 90. Sum of four = 4 x 16 = 64. Removed number = 90 - 64 = 26.

practice.prompt: A price is increased by 25% and the new price is then decreased by 20%. What is the net change from the original price?
practice.explanation: 1.25 x 0.80 = 1.00, so the final price equals the original.

practice.prompt: Pipe A fills a tank in 6 hours and Pipe B fills it in 3 hours. Working together at these rates, how many hours do they take to fill the tank?
practice.explanation: Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2 tank per hour, so time = 2 hours. 4.5 is the trap from averaging the times.

practice.prompt: What is the remainder when 2^10 is divided by 7?
practice.explanation: Powers of 2 mod 7 cycle 2, 4, 1 with period 3. 10 = 3 x 3 + 1, so 2^10 has the same remainder as 2^1, which is 2. (2^10 = 1024 = 7 x 146 + 2.)

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

The new manager's style was refreshingly ___: she explained every decision openly and invited staff to question her reasoning.
practice.explanation: The colon introduces a definition: explaining decisions openly is transparency. "Opaque" means the opposite, and "autocratic" clashes with inviting questions.

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

Far from being ___, the documentary's narrator often paused to admit the limits of what historians actually know.
practice.explanation: "Far from" signals the opposite of admitting limits, so the blank means rigidly certain: dogmatic. "Hesitant" describes someone who admits limits, so it reverses the logic.

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

Because the bridge's original blueprints had been lost, engineers had to ___ its load limits from careful measurements of the existing structure.
practice.explanation: Without blueprints, the engineers worked out the limits from evidence, which is to infer them. The other verbs do not describe deriving information from measurements.

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

Her reputation for ___ meant that colleagues were surprised when she submitted the quarterly report a week late.
practice.explanation: Colleagues were surprised by lateness, so she must be known for being on time. "Tardiness" would make the lateness expected, not surprising.

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

The senator's speech was so ___ that even reporters accustomed to political spin struggled to determine what, if anything, she had actually proposed.
practice.explanation: Reporters could not tell what she proposed, so the speech was deliberately unclear: equivocal. "Laconic" means brief, and a brief speech is not necessarily unclear.

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

Although the composer's early works were dismissed as merely ___, critics now recognize in them the seeds of the formal innovations that defined his later career.
practice.explanation: "Although" contrasts the early dismissal with recognizing innovation, so the works were dismissed as unoriginal: derivative. "Groundbreaking" agrees with the later view instead of contrasting with it.

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

The archive's holdings are ___: letters, ledgers, maps, and photographs sit side by side with no apparent principle of organization.
practice.explanation: The colon explains the blank: no principle of organization means haphazard. "Homogeneous" (all alike) contradicts the varied list of items.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of entries (blank (i) / blank (ii)) that best completes the text.

The scientist was careful to (i) ___ her findings, noting that the small sample size made any broad conclusion (ii) ___.
practice.explanation: A small sample makes broad conclusions premature, and a careful scientist would therefore qualify (limit) her claims. "Trumpet" means to proclaim loudly, which clashes with being careful.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of entries (blank (i) / blank (ii)) that best completes the text.

Critics who expected the novelist's memoir to be (i) ___ were disarmed by its candor: rather than burnishing her own legend, she dwelt on her failures with almost (ii) ___ thoroughness.
practice.explanation: Critics expected the memoir to burnish her legend, which is self-serving. Dwelling on failures with candor suggests unsparing thoroughness; "perfunctory" means minimal, which contradicts "thoroughness."

practice.prompt:
Select the choice that best completes the text.

The committee's report, though ___ in its language, was devastating in its implications; its mild phrasing could not disguise how badly the agency had failed.
practice.explanation: The later phrase "mild phrasing" defines the blank, so the language was measured. "Florid" means ornate, not mild, and "inflammatory" is the opposite.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of entries (blank (i) / blank (ii)) that best completes the text.

Initially (i) ___ by the sheer volume of the data, the team soon found that most of it was (ii) ___, and the genuinely informative measurements could be reviewed in an afternoon.
practice.explanation: "Initially" and "soon found" set up a reversal: the team was first intimidated (daunted), then learned most data was repetitive (redundant), which is why the useful part was small. "Indispensable" would make the data hard to cut down.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of entries (blank (i) / blank (ii)) that best completes the text.

The historian argues that the treaty, often (i) ___ as a triumph of diplomacy, was in fact a (ii) ___ compromise that left every major dispute unresolved.
practice.explanation: "In fact" contrasts the popular view with the historian's: the treaty is praised (hailed) as a triumph but was actually empty (hollow), leaving disputes unresolved. "Derided as a triumph" makes no sense.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

The museum guide was so ___ that the hour-long tour felt like ten minutes.
practice.explanation: A tour that seems to fly by needs a guide who holds attention: engaging and captivating. "Tedious" and "monotonous" are a matched pair but have the wrong meaning.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

Despite the forecast's dire warnings, the storm proved ___, causing little more than a few downed branches.
practice.explanation: "Despite" the warnings, the storm did little damage, so it was innocuous or harmless. "Catastrophic" and "devastating" match each other but contradict the minor damage.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

The professor's explanation was admirably ___, conveying in two sentences what the textbook took two pages to say.
practice.explanation: Two sentences versus two pages points to brevity: succinct and concise. "Verbose" and "prolix" are synonyms meaning wordy, the opposite of what the sentence needs.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

Long considered ___, the theory has gained new respectability after several independent labs replicated its key prediction.
practice.explanation: The theory gained respectability only recently, so it was once doubted: dubious or questionable. "Orthodox" and "conventional" would mean it was already accepted.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

The startup's founder was notoriously ___, changing the company's strategy so often that employees stopped taking announcements seriously.
practice.explanation: Frequent, unpredictable changes describe someone mercurial or capricious. "Steadfast" and "resolute" are a pair meaning firm, the opposite.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

Rather than ___ the critics, the director thanked them publicly and incorporated several of their suggestions into the final cut.
practice.explanation: "Rather than" contrasts the blank with thanking and using suggestions, so the blank means reject: rebuff or dismiss. "Heed" and "embrace" describe what the director actually did.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

The negotiator's ___ manner (calm, patient, never raising her voice) helped defuse even the most heated sessions.
practice.explanation: The parenthetical defines the blank as calm and patient: imperturbable and unflappable. "Volatile" and "irascible" form a pair meaning easily angered.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

Though his prose is often described as ___, a careful reader discovers that its apparent simplicity conceals intricate patterns of allusion.
practice.explanation: The blank matches "apparent simplicity," so it means simple: artless or unadorned. "Ornate" and "baroque" are synonyms but describe elaborate prose.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

The auditor's report was ___, cataloguing every minor discrepancy with a thoroughness that some managers found exhausting.
practice.explanation: Cataloguing every minor discrepancy is extremely careful work: punctilious or meticulous. "Cursory" and "perfunctory" mean hasty and minimal, the opposite.

practice.prompt:
Select the pair of words that, when either is used to complete the sentence, produces sentences that fit the meaning of the whole and are alike in meaning.

Many readers found the essay's argument ___: its premises were sound, but the conclusion did not follow from them.
practice.explanation: An argument whose conclusion does not follow from sound premises is logically flawed but may look plausible: specious or fallacious. "Cogent" and "compelling" describe a strong argument.

practice.passage: Art historians once treated the workshops of Renaissance painters as factories for a single master's vision: apprentices ground pigments and painted backgrounds, while the master supplied everything of artistic consequence. Technical analysis has complicated that picture. Infrared imaging of several altarpieces reveals underdrawings in more than one hand, sometimes with revisions that the master appears to have accepted rather than corrected. Such evidence does not mean that apprentices were secret geniuses, but it does suggest that the finished works emerged from negotiation more than dictation.
practice.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that apprentices were more talented than the masters they served
describe how infrared imaging technology works
defend the traditional view of Renaissance workshops
explain how new evidence has challenged a traditional view of how certain paintings were produced
practice.explanation: The passage presents the old view, then imaging evidence that complicates it. The author explicitly denies that apprentices were "secret geniuses," so the second choice is wrong.

practice.passage: Art historians once treated the workshops of Renaissance painters as factories for a single master's vision: apprentices ground pigments and painted backgrounds, while the master supplied everything of artistic consequence. Technical analysis has complicated that picture. Infrared imaging of several altarpieces reveals underdrawings in more than one hand, sometimes with revisions that the master appears to have accepted rather than corrected. Such evidence does not mean that apprentices were secret geniuses, but it does suggest that the finished works emerged from negotiation more than dictation.
practice.prompt: The author mentions revisions that "the master appears to have accepted rather than corrected" most likely in order to
options: show that masters rarely reviewed their apprentices' work
suggest that apprentices were secretly better artists than their masters
support the claim that the master did not exercise complete control over the finished work
explain why underdrawings are visible under infrared light
practice.explanation: Accepted revisions by other hands show that apprentices influenced the final work, supporting "negotiation more than dictation." The detail implies the master did review the work, so the second choice is wrong.

practice.passage: Tardigrades, microscopic animals found in moss and soil worldwide, can survive near-complete dehydration by entering a state called anhydrobiosis, in which metabolism nearly stops. For years, researchers assumed that tardigrades, like brine shrimp and some nematodes, relied on the sugar trehalose, which forms a glassy matrix that protects cell structures as water disappears. Yet many tardigrade species accumulate little or no trehalose. Researchers have since identified a family of tardigrade-specific proteins that are disordered, lacking a fixed three-dimensional shape, in water but that appear to form a protective glassy state as the cell dries. When the genes for these proteins were suppressed, tardigrades survived drying far less often; when the proteins were produced in yeast and bacteria, those organisms tolerated drying better. The findings do not mean that trehalose plays no role in any tardigrade, but they suggest that the animals arrived at a similar physical solution, vitrification, by a largely different molecular route.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, why did researchers come to question the trehalose explanation for tardigrades?
options: Many tardigrade species accumulate little or no trehalose.
Trehalose was found to damage cell structures.
Brine shrimp were shown not to use trehalose.
Tardigrades were found to stay metabolically active when dry.
practice.explanation: The passage says "many tardigrade species accumulate little or no trehalose." It never says trehalose fails in brine shrimp; it says the opposite.

practice.prompt: The experiments with yeast and bacteria are mentioned primarily to
options: demonstrate that yeast and bacteria naturally produce the proteins
prove that trehalose plays no role in any tardigrade
explain how the proteins lose their three-dimensional shape
show that the proteins can increase drying tolerance even outside tardigrades
practice.explanation: Producing the proteins in other organisms improved their drying tolerance, which shows the proteins themselves have a protective effect. The passage specifically says trehalose may still play a role in some tardigrades.

practice.prompt: The passage suggests which of the following about trehalose and the tardigrade-specific proteins?
options: The proteins work by breaking down trehalose.
Trehalose is ineffective in all animals.
Both are thought to protect cells by forming a glassy state as water is lost.
The proteins have a rigid structure that trehalose lacks.
practice.explanation: Trehalose "forms a glassy matrix," and the proteins "form a protective glassy state," which is the "similar physical solution, vitrification." The proteins are described as disordered, not rigid.

For years, researchers assumed that tardigrades, like brine shrimp and some nematodes, relied on the sugar trehalose, which forms a glassy matrix that protects cell structures as water disappears. Yet many tardigrade species accumulate little or no trehalose. The findings do not mean that trehalose plays no role in any tardigrade, but they suggest that the animals arrived at a similar physical solution, vitrification, by a largely different molecular route.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, would most seriously weaken the conclusion that the proteins are important for tardigrades' survival of drying?
options: Some nematodes accumulate large amounts of trehalose.
Tardigrades whose genes for the proteins were suppressed also became ill and died more often even when kept moist.
The proteins have been found in every tardigrade species studied so far.
Yeast producing the proteins also tolerated freezing better.
practice.explanation: If suppression made tardigrades generally sick, their lower survival of drying may not be due to losing protection against drying, which undercuts the key experiment. Nematodes' use of trehalose is irrelevant to tardigrades.

practice.passage: A city replaced all of its incandescent streetlights with LED fixtures last year. Since then, the city's electricity costs for street lighting have fallen by 40 percent. The city's energy director concludes that converting the lights in municipal buildings to LEDs will produce similar savings on the buildings' electricity costs.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the energy director's conclusion?
options: LED fixtures generally last longer than incandescent bulbs.
Several nearby cities have also converted their streetlights to LEDs.
Lighting accounts for only a small fraction of electricity use in the municipal buildings, most of which goes to heating, cooling, and computers.
The price of LED fixtures has fallen in recent years.
practice.explanation: A 40 percent cut in lighting costs produces a much smaller cut in total building costs if lighting is a small share of use. The falling price of LEDs, if anything, supports the plan.

practice.passage: After Ridgeway College's library extended its weekend hours, the number of students visiting the library on weekends rose by 30 percent. Therefore, the extended hours caused students to spend more total time studying.
practice.prompt: The argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: The library is the only building on campus open on weekends.
Students who came during the new weekend hours did not simply move study time they would otherwise have spent elsewhere.
Most students prefer to study on weekends rather than weekdays.
Library staff supported the change in hours.
practice.explanation: If students only shifted study time from dorms or weekdays to the library, total study time would not rise, so the conclusion needs this assumption. The other choices are not required for the conclusion to hold.

practice.passage: In a region where foxes are the main predator of rabbits, a disease sharply reduced the fox population. Two years later, however, the rabbit population was smaller than it had been before the disease.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, best explains the outcome described?
options: After the foxes declined, the rabbit population grew rapidly, exhausted its food supply, and then crashed.
The disease that affected the foxes cannot infect rabbits.
Foxes in the region also eat mice and voles.
Rabbits in the region breed several times a year.
practice.explanation: Fewer predators let rabbits boom, and the resulting overgrazing led to starvation, explaining a population below its starting level. Rapid breeding alone would predict more rabbits, not fewer.

practice.passage: Every applicant who scored above 90 on the exam was offered an interview. Some applicants who were offered an interview did not accept a position. No applicant who failed to submit references was offered an interview.
practice.prompt: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Some applicants who scored above 90 did not accept a position.
Every applicant who submitted references was offered an interview.
No applicant who scored 90 or below was offered an interview.
Every applicant who scored above 90 on the exam submitted references.
practice.explanation: Scoring above 90 guarantees an interview, and anyone interviewed must have submitted references, so high scorers submitted references. The third choice reverses a conditional, and the second may be false because the applicants who declined could all have scored 90 or below.

practice.passage: Economists have long noted that workers who move from rural areas to cities earn more, on average, than those who stay. A straightforward reading attributes the gap to the city itself: denser labor markets match workers to jobs more efficiently and spread knowledge quickly. Recent studies that follow the same individuals over time complicate this account. Part of the gap reflects selection, since those who move tend to differ from those who stay in education, ambition, or prior earnings. But the studies also find that a worker's earnings continue to rise the longer she remains in a city, and that much of this gain persists if she later returns to a smaller town. This pattern suggests that cities do more than reward existing skills; they help workers acquire new ones.
practice.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: evaluating explanations for the earnings advantage of workers who move to cities
arguing that rural workers should move to cities
describing the history of rural migration
criticizing economists for ignoring selection effects
practice.explanation: The passage weighs the city-effect explanation against selection and then offers a skill-building interpretation. It never advises workers to move.

practice.passage: Economists have long noted that workers who move from rural areas to cities earn more, on average, than those who stay. A straightforward reading attributes the gap to the city itself: denser labor markets match workers to jobs more efficiently and spread knowledge quickly. Recent studies that follow the same individuals over time complicate this account. Part of the gap reflects selection, since those who move tend to differ from those who stay in education, ambition, or prior earnings. But the studies also find that a worker's earnings continue to rise the longer she remains in a city, and that much of this gain persists if she later returns to a smaller town. This pattern suggests that cities do more than reward existing skills; they help workers acquire new ones.
practice.prompt: The author mentions that much of the earnings gain "persists if she later returns to a smaller town" in order to
options: show that small towns pay more than cities
support the view that working in a city helps people develop lasting skills
argue that selection explains the entire earnings gap
suggest that workers often regret moving to cities
practice.explanation: If the gain stays after leaving, it reflects something the worker acquired, such as skills, not just the city's pay level. The detail works against the idea that selection explains everything.

practice.passage: Economists have long noted that workers who move from rural areas to cities earn more, on average, than those who stay. A straightforward reading attributes the gap to the city itself: denser labor markets match workers to jobs more efficiently and spread knowledge quickly. Recent studies that follow the same individuals over time complicate this account. Part of the gap reflects selection, since those who move tend to differ from those who stay in education, ambition, or prior earnings. But the studies also find that a worker's earnings continue to rise the longer she remains in a city, and that much of this gain persists if she later returns to a smaller town. This pattern suggests that cities do more than reward existing skills; they help workers acquire new ones.
practice.prompt: It can be inferred that the "straightforward reading" described in the passage
options: has been entirely disproved by recent studies
attributes the earnings gap mainly to differences in education
does not account for the possibility that movers differ systematically from those who stay
is based on studies that follow the same individuals over time
practice.explanation: The straightforward reading credits the city alone, and the newer studies add that "part of the gap reflects selection," which the old reading ignored. "Entirely disproved" is too strong, since the passage says the studies only complicate it.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

Quantity A: 3/5 + 1/4
Quantity B: 0.85
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: 3/5 + 1/4 = 0.60 + 0.25 = 0.85, so the quantities are equal.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

Quantity A: (-3)^4
Quantity B: -3^4
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: (-3)^4 = 81, while -3^4 means -(3^4) = -81. The exponent applies before the negative sign unless parentheses are used.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

A circle has radius 3.
Quantity A: the circumference of the circle
Quantity B: 18
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: Circumference = 2π(3) = 6π, about 18.85, which is greater than 18. Using π = 3 would wrongly suggest equality.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

Data set: 3, 8, 1, 9, 4
Quantity A: the median of the data set
Quantity B: the mean of the data set
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: Sorted: 1, 3, 4, 8, 9, so the median is 4. The mean is 25/5 = 5, which is greater.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

x^2 = 16
Quantity A: x
Quantity B: 4
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: x could be 4 (equal) or -4 (B greater), so the relationship cannot be determined.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

Quantity A: 30% of 70
Quantity B: 70% of 30
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: Both equal 0.3 x 70 = 0.7 x 30 = 21, because multiplication is commutative.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

0 < x < 1
Quantity A: x^2
Quantity B: √x
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: For values between 0 and 1, squaring makes a number smaller and taking a square root makes it larger, so √x > x^2. For example, x = 0.25 gives 0.0625 versus 0.5.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

A rectangle has a perimeter of 20.
Quantity A: the area of the rectangle
Quantity B: 30
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: With length plus width equal to 10, the largest possible area is 5 x 5 = 25, which is less than 30. So B is always greater.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

Quantity A: the number of ways to choose 3 people from a group of 7
Quantity B: the number of distinct arrangements of the letters in the word LEVEL
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: 7C3 = 35. LEVEL has 5 letters with L and E each repeated twice, so 5!/(2!2!) = 30. A is greater.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

x and y are integers, x > y, and xy = 12.
Quantity A: x + y
Quantity B: 7
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: Pairs include (4, 3) with sum 7, (6, 2) with sum 8, and (-3, -4) with sum -7. A can be equal to, greater than, or less than B.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

n is a positive integer.
Quantity A: the remainder when 7^n is divided by 5
Quantity B: 4
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: Remainders of 7^n divided by 5 cycle through 2, 4, 3, 1. When n = 2 the quantities are equal; otherwise B is greater. So the relationship cannot be determined.

practice.prompt:
Compare Quantity A and Quantity B.

Quantity A: the area of a square whose diagonal has length 10
Quantity B: the area of a right triangle whose legs each have length 10
options: The relationship cannot be determined from the information given
practice.explanation: A square with diagonal d has area d^2/2 = 50. The triangle's area is (10 x 10)/2 = 50. Treating the diagonal as a side would wrongly give 100.

practice.prompt: If 3/4 of a number is 27, what is 2/3 of the number?
practice.explanation: The number is 27 / (3/4) = 36, and 2/3 of 36 is 24. The answer 18 takes 2/3 of 27 instead of the original number.

practice.prompt: If 4x - 7 = 2x + 9, what is the value of x^2?
practice.explanation: 2x = 16, so x = 8 and x^2 = 64. The answer 8 is x itself, not x^2.

practice.prompt: What is the area of the triangle with vertices (0, 0), (6, 0), and (2, 5)?
practice.explanation: The base along the x-axis is 6 and the height is the y-coordinate 5, so the area is (6 x 5)/2 = 15. The answer 30 forgets to divide by 2.

practice.prompt: A class of 20 students has a mean score of 70, and a class of 30 students has a mean score of 80. What is the mean score of all 50 students?
practice.explanation: Total = 20(70) + 30(80) = 1,400 + 2,400 = 3,800, and 3,800 / 50 = 76. The answer 75 averages the two means without weighting by class size.

practice.prompt: A store discounts an item by 30%, and a coupon then takes 20% off the discounted price. The final price is what percent of the original price?
practice.explanation: 0.70 x 0.80 = 0.56, so 56%. Adding the discounts to 50% off ignores that the second discount applies to a smaller price.

practice.prompt: If x + 1/x = 5, what is the value of x^2 + 1/x^2?
practice.explanation: Squaring gives x^2 + 2 + 1/x^2 = 25, so x^2 + 1/x^2 = 23. The answer 25 forgets the middle term.

practice.prompt: A right circular cylinder has radius 3 and volume 72π. What is its total surface area?
practice.explanation: Height = 72π / (9π) = 8. Surface area = 2π(3)^2 + 2π(3)(8) = 18π + 48π = 66π. The answer 48π is the lateral area only.

practice.prompt: A bag contains 4 red and 6 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are the same color?
practice.explanation: (4C2 + 6C2)/10C2 = (6 + 15)/45 = 7/15. The answer 13/25 is the with-replacement probability, and 8/15 is the probability of different colors.

practice.prompt: In an arithmetic sequence, the 3rd term is 11 and the 8th term is 31. What is the 20th term?
practice.explanation: Five steps raise the term by 20, so d = 4 and the first term is 11 - 8 = 3. The 20th term is 3 + 19(4) = 79. The answer 83 uses 20 steps instead of 19.

practice.prompt: How many positive divisors does 360 have?
If 2^(x+3) - 2^x = 112, what is the value of x?
practice.explanation: Factor: 2^x(2^3 - 1) = 7 x 2^x = 112, so 2^x = 16 and x = 4. The answer 16 is 2^x rather than x.

practice.prompt: A rectangle is inscribed in a circle of radius 5. If one side of the rectangle has length 6, what is the area of the rectangle?
practice.explanation: The rectangle's diagonal is a diameter, 10. The other side is √(100 - 36) = 8, so the area is 48. The answer 60 multiplies 6 by the diameter.

practice.prompt: How many integers from 1 to 200, inclusive, are divisible by 3 or by 5 but not by both?
practice.explanation: There are 66 multiples of 3, 40 multiples of 5, and 13 multiples of 15. Excluding the overlap from both groups gives 66 + 40 - 2(13) = 80. The answer 93 counts the multiples of 15 once.

practice.prompt: A recipe uses sugar and flour in the ratio 2 : 5 by volume. If the recipe uses 21 cups of sugar and flour combined, how many cups of flour does it use?
practice.explanation: The ratio has 7 parts, each worth 21 / 7 = 3 cups, so flour is 5 x 3 = 15 cups. Answering 6 gives the sugar instead.

practice.prompt: If f(x) = 3x - 2 and g(x) = x^2 + 1, what is the value of f(g(2))?
practice.explanation: g(2) = 5, and f(5) = 15 - 2 = 13. Reversing the order, g(f(2)) = 17, is a common mistake.

practice.prompt: A committee of 2 men and 2 women is to be chosen from 5 men and 4 women. How many different committees are possible?
practice.explanation: 5C2 x 4C2 = 10 x 6 = 60. Choosing 4 people from 9 (126) ignores the 2-and-2 requirement.

practice.prompt: A bag contains red and blue chips in the ratio 3 : 5. After 18 red chips are added, the ratio of red to blue chips is 3 : 2. How many blue chips are in the bag?
practice.explanation: Let red = 3k and blue = 5k. Then (3k + 18)/(5k) = 3/2 gives 6k + 36 = 15k, so k = 4 and there are 20 blue chips.

practice.prompt: What is the units digit of 3^47?
practice.explanation: Units digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1. Since 47 divided by 4 leaves remainder 3, the units digit is the third in the cycle, 7.

practice.prompt: The two roots of x^2 - 10x + k = 0 differ by 4. What is the value of k?
practice.explanation: The roots sum to 10 and differ by 4, so they are 7 and 3. Their product, k, is 21.

practice.passage:
Enrollment in four online courses
Course | 2024 | 2025
A | 1,200 | 1,500
B | 800 | 760
C | 2,000 | 2,600
D | 500 | 700
practice.prompt: Which course had the greatest percent increase in enrollment from 2024 to 2025?
practice.explanation: Percent changes: A 25%, B -5%, C 30%, D 40%. Course C had the largest increase in number of students (600) but not the largest percent increase.

practice.passage:
Enrollment in four online courses
Course | 2024 | 2025
A | 1,200 | 1,500
B | 800 | 760
C | 2,000 | 2,600
D | 500 | 700
practice.prompt: Total enrollment in 2025 was approximately what percent greater than total enrollment in 2024?
practice.explanation: Totals are 4,500 and 5,560, an increase of 1,060, and 1,060 / 4,500 is about 23.6%, roughly 24%. Dividing by the 2025 total gives about 19%.

practice.passage:
Enrollment in four online courses
Course | 2024 | 2025
A | 1,200 | 1,500
B | 800 | 760
C | 2,000 | 2,600
D | 500 | 700
practice.prompt: In 2025, Course C accounted for approximately what percent of total enrollment in the four courses?
practice.explanation: 2,600 / 5,560 is about 46.8%, roughly 47%. The answer 44% is Course C's share in 2024 (2,000 / 4,500).

practice.passage:
Enrollment in four online courses
Course | 2024 | 2025
A | 1,200 | 1,500
B | 800 | 760
C | 2,000 | 2,600
D | 500 | 700
practice.prompt: If Course B's enrollment continues to decrease by the same percent each year as it did from 2024 to 2025, in what year will its enrollment first fall below 600?
practice.explanation: B falls 5% a year: 760(0.95)^n gives about 722 (2026), 686 (2027), 652 (2028), 619 (2029) and 588 (2030). Assuming a linear drop of 40 a year would suggest 2029 (600, not below it).
