lessons.title: GMAT Focus Edition: structure, order and the review tool
lessons.body: The GMAT Focus Edition has three 45-minute sections: Quantitative Reasoning (21 questions), Verbal Reasoning (23) and Data Insights (20), for 2 hours 15 minutes in total, with one optional 10-minute break. There is no essay. You choose the section order, so put your strongest section first if you need confidence, or your weakest first if you tire quickly; test both orders in official practice exams. Each section is computer-adaptive at the question level, and unanswered questions reduce your score significantly, so finish every section. A distinctive feature is the Question Review and Edit tool: you can bookmark questions and change up to three answers per section at the end, so reserve a few minutes. Pacing: about 2 minutes 8 seconds per Quant question, 1 minute 57 seconds per Verbal, and 2 minutes 15 seconds per Data Insights question. Total scores run from 205 to 805, with section scores from 60 to 90. Scores are valid for five years. Mini-example: if a question has consumed three minutes, bookmark it, guess, and move on.

lessons.title: Quant: number properties and smart shortcuts
lessons.body: The Quant section is problem solving only, covering arithmetic and algebra, with no calculator, so efficiency matters. Know number properties cold: even x anything = even; odd x odd = odd; the product of two consecutive integers, n(n + 1), is always even; a number is divisible by 3 if its digit sum is. For word problems, translate carefully and look for invariants. Average speed for a round trip is total distance divided by total time, never the average of the two speeds. Example: 120 km out at 60 km/h takes 2 hours, back at 40 km/h takes 3 hours, so the average is 240 / 5 = 48 km/h, not 50. For mixture problems, track the quantity that does not change: adding water to 20 liters of 30% acid keeps 6 liters of acid, so reaching 20% needs a total of 30 liters, meaning 10 liters of water. When answer choices are far apart, estimate. When they contain variables, pick simple numbers and test each choice.

lessons.title: Verbal: critical reasoning and reading comprehension
lessons.body: Critical reasoning gives a short argument and asks you to strengthen it, weaken it, find an assumption, or explain a discrepancy. Always break the argument into a conclusion and its evidence, then find the gap between them. Most arguments assume that the cause they name is the only cause, or that a sample represents the whole group. To weaken, choose the option that widens the gap, often an alternative cause. To find an assumption, use the negation test: negate the option, and if the argument falls apart, that option is required. Mini-example: "Sales rose after our ad campaign, so the campaign worked." Assumption: nothing else, such as a competitor closing, caused the rise. For reading comprehension, read for structure: what is the main point, and what job does each paragraph do? Correct answers are supported by specific lines; wrong ones are too broad, too extreme, or out of scope. Spend about two to three minutes on the passage and then move through the questions quickly.

lessons.title: Data Insights: data sufficiency and reading tables
lessons.body: Data Insights mixes data sufficiency with table analysis, graphics interpretation, multi-source reasoning and two-part analysis, and an on-screen calculator is available. Data sufficiency asks whether each statement alone, or both together, give enough information to answer the question; you do not need the actual value. Work in fixed order: test statement 1 alone, then statement 2 alone, and combine only if neither works alone. For yes/no questions, a statement is sufficient if it always gives yes or always gives no. Mini-example: "Is x positive?" (1) x squared = 9 gives x = 3 or -3, so not sufficient. (2) x cubed = 27 gives x = 3, so sufficient. For tables and graphs, read titles, units and scales before calculating, and estimate before using the calculator. In multi-source questions, note which tab holds which data. The most common error is answering from the wrong row or using a total instead of a subgroup, so restate the exact question before you compute.

lessons.title: Section order, pacing and the review tool in practice
lessons.body:
The GMAT Focus Edition has three sections of 45 minutes each: Quantitative Reasoning (21 questions), Verbal Reasoning (23 questions) and Data Insights (20 questions). There is no essay and no geometry. You pick the order of the three sections at the start of the exam, and you may take one optional 10-minute break. Each section is adaptive at the question level, so the next question depends on how you answered the current one.

Choosing an order. Use your official practice exams to test at least two orders. Many test takers put their strongest section first to build confidence; others put their weakest first while they are fresh. Data Insights is often the most tiring because it mixes math and reading, so think about where it sits relative to your break.

Pacing. The averages are about 2 minutes 8 seconds per Quant question, 1 minute 57 seconds per Verbal question and 2 minutes 15 seconds per Data Insights question. Set checkpoints: in Quant, aim to finish question 7 by minute 15 and question 14 by minute 30. If you are behind, make a quick educated guess on a question that looks long and move on. Unanswered questions at the end are penalized heavily, so always finish the section.

The Question Review and Edit tool. You can bookmark any question while you work. When you reach the end of a section with time left, you can review bookmarked questions and change up to three answers in that section. Use it deliberately: bookmark only questions where you made a guess between two choices, and keep two or three minutes at the end for them. Do not reserve too much time, since changing answers is limited.

Scoring. The total score runs from 205 to 805, and each section is scored from 60 to 90. All three sections count equally toward the total. Scores remain valid for five years, and the official score report includes performance insights by topic and question type that help you plan a retake.

Mini-example: in Verbal, you reach question 18 with 8 minutes left for 6 questions. That is about 80 seconds each, so skim a long passage question quickly, answer, bookmark, and keep moving.

lessons.title: Problem Solving: arithmetic and algebra without a calculator
lessons.body:
Quantitative Reasoning on the GMAT Focus Edition contains only Problem Solving questions on arithmetic and algebra, with five answer choices and no calculator. The math level is modest; the challenge is speed and accuracy under pressure.

Arithmetic essentials. Percents: a 20 percent discount and a 20 percent profit on cost are based on different amounts, so always ask "percent of what?" Successive changes multiply. Ratios: if boys to girls is 4 : 5 with 36 members, each part is 36 / 9 = 4. Averages: total = average x count; the average of evenly spaced numbers is the middle value. Rates: distance = rate x time; work rates add (and a draining pipe subtracts). Mixtures: write a weighted-average equation in dollars or amounts of the substance.

Number properties. Prime factorization answers questions about divisors, perfect squares and least common multiples. For a perfect square, every prime exponent must be even, so the smallest n making 120n a square is 2 x 3 x 5 = 30. Remainders: if n leaves remainder 4 when divided by 6, then 5n leaves the same remainder as 5 x 4 = 20, which is 2.

Algebra essentials. Linear equations and systems, quadratics (factor or complete the square), inequalities (flip when multiplying by a negative), absolute value (split into two cases), and sequences defined by a rule. Recognize special products: x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y).

Strategies. Backsolve when the answer choices are numbers: start with the middle choice. Pick numbers when the answer choices contain variables or percents of an unknown amount; for percent problems, 100 is a convenient starting value. Estimate when the choices are far apart. Avoid long calculations: if your setup needs more than about 90 seconds of arithmetic, look for a shortcut.

Mini-example: 7 consecutive odd integers average 25. The middle one is 25, so they run from 19 to 31, and the product of the smallest and largest is 589. No need to write all seven numbers.

lessons.title: Critical Reasoning: a method for every question type
lessons.body:
Critical Reasoning questions present a short argument or set of facts and ask you to analyze it. They make up roughly half of the Verbal Reasoning section, alongside Reading Comprehension.

A four-step method:
1. Read the question stem first so you know your task: weaken, strengthen, assumption, evaluate, inference, explain a discrepancy, flaw, or the role of a statement.
2. Break the argument into conclusion and evidence. Conclusions often follow words like therefore, so, thus or concludes.
3. Predict the gap. What must be true for the evidence to prove the conclusion? Common gaps include another cause of the result, an unrepresentative sample, a comparison that is not like-for-like, and a plan that ignores costs or side effects.
4. Eliminate choices that are out of scope, too extreme, or that address a different conclusion.

By type:
Weaken: choose a fact that makes the gap wider, often an alternative explanation. Strengthen: choose a fact that closes the gap or removes an alternative.
Assumption: use the negation test. Negate the choice; if the argument falls apart, that choice is the required assumption.
Evaluate: choose the question whose answer would either strengthen or weaken the argument, depending on the answer.
Inference: the correct answer must follow from the statements. Diagram conditionals and do not reverse them: "all A are B" does not mean "all B are A."
Explain a discrepancy: choose a fact that allows both surprising statements to be true at once.
Role of a statement: in passages with two highlighted portions, label each as evidence, conclusion, an opposing view, or background.
Flaw: name the mistake, such as confusing correlation with causation or reversing cause and effect.

Mini-example: a city cut bus fares in half and fare revenue rose. This seems paradoxical until you learn that ridership more than doubled: half the price times more than double the riders gives more revenue.

Time: aim for about 2 minutes per Critical Reasoning question. If two choices remain, compare them directly against the conclusion, not against the evidence.

lessons.title: Reading Comprehension: mapping GMAT passages
lessons.body:
Reading Comprehension passages on the GMAT are usually 200 to 350 words on business, social science, natural science or humanities topics, each followed by three or four questions. You do not need outside knowledge, and the test does not reward speed-reading every detail.

Build a passage map. As you read, write a few words per paragraph describing its role: "P1: economists like surge pricing; consumers don't. P2: reference-price theory explains it. P3: firms reframe; critics vs. defenders." Note the author's tone: is the author neutral, supportive, or critical? Mark contrast words such as however, yet, but and recently, because GMAT passages are built around a shift from one view to another.

Question types:
Main idea or primary purpose: the right answer covers the whole passage. Watch the verb: "explain," "argue," "challenge," "describe." A choice that fits only one paragraph is too narrow.
Detail: go back to the text. The correct answer often paraphrases a sentence, so match meaning rather than words.
Inference: the answer must be supported by the passage, not merely possible. Extreme words such as "always," "entirely" or "proves" are warning signs.
Function: ask why the author included a detail; usually to support, illustrate or qualify a nearby claim.
Application and strengthen or weaken: apply the passage's reasoning to a new situation or evaluate which fact would affect a claim made in the passage.

Common traps. Choices that use the passage's exact words but distort the meaning; choices that attribute one group's opinion to another (critics versus defenders); and choices that are true in the real world but not stated in the passage.

Pacing: spend about 2 to 3 minutes reading and mapping, then about 1 to 1.5 minutes per question. If the first question for a passage is hard, the time you put into the map pays off on the next ones.

Mini-example: in a passage about coral bleaching, skeptics argue that heat-tolerant corals grow slowly. They would agree that surviving warming does not guarantee a reef persists, because slow growth may not keep pace with erosion.

lessons.title: Data Sufficiency: the AD/BCE method
lessons.body:
Data Sufficiency appears in the Data Insights section. Each question asks a question and gives two statements. You decide whether the information is enough to answer the question, not what the answer is. The five answer choices are always the same:
(A) Statement (1) alone is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not.
(B) Statement (2) alone is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not.
(C) Both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is.
(D) Each statement alone is sufficient.
(E) The statements together are not sufficient.

The AD/BCE method. Evaluate statement (1) alone. If it is sufficient, the answer is A or D; then check statement (2) alone to choose between them. If (1) is not sufficient, the answer is B, C or E; check (2) alone, and if it is not sufficient either, combine the statements. Never carry information from statement (1) into your analysis of statement (2) alone.

Value versus yes/no questions. For "What is x?" a statement is sufficient only if it gives exactly one value. For "Is x > y?" a statement is sufficient if the answer is always yes or always no. A consistent "no" is sufficient.

Test cases. To show insufficiency, find two allowed cases that give different answers. Try positive and negative numbers, zero, fractions, and integers versus non-integers when the question allows them. Read the conditions in the question stem carefully: "x is a positive integer" removes many cases.

Common traps. Assuming that a quadratic gives one value (x^2 = 25 gives 5 or -5). Assuming that two equations always solve for two variables (they may be multiples of each other). Forgetting that statements that look weak alone, such as "n^2 + n is even," may tell you nothing because the expression is always even.

Mini-example: What is the remainder when n is divided by 12? (1) n leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4. (2) n leaves remainder 2 when divided by 3. Each alone allows several remainders, but together they force n = 11 more than a multiple of 12, so the answer is C.

lessons.title: Data Insights beyond DS: tables, graphics, two-part and multi-source
lessons.body:
Data Insights has 20 questions in 45 minutes and is the only section with an on-screen calculator. Besides Data Sufficiency, it uses four formats. In the real exam several of them use special screens (sortable tables, drop-down menus, tabs); the practice items in this app present the same reasoning as standard multiple-choice questions.

Table Analysis. You get a sortable table and several statements to mark as true or false, yes or no. Before calculating, read the column headings and units. Sort mentally by the column the question asks about. Many statements ask about rates or shares, so compute ratios such as returns divided by orders rather than comparing raw counts.

Graphics Interpretation. A chart is followed by sentences with drop-down blanks. Read the axis labels, scale and legend first. Percent change questions are common: (new - old)/old. Distinguish between the largest absolute change and the largest percent change.

Two-Part Analysis. You choose one answer for each of two columns from a shared list, and the two parts are often linked, such as a pair of values that satisfy an equation, or an assumption and a weakener for one argument. Solve the more constrained part first, then test the remaining part. Both parts must be right to earn credit.

Multi-Source Reasoning. Information is spread across two or three tabs, such as an email, a table and a policy memo. Skim every tab once and write one line about each. Questions often require combining a rule from one tab with numbers from another; for example, a vendor-selection rule that depends on both cost and on-time rate. Expect three questions per set.

Calculator tips. Use it for multi-step arithmetic, but estimate first so you notice a typing slip. Do not use it for simple steps that waste time.

Pacing. Aim for about 2 minutes 15 seconds per question on average. Multi-Source Reasoning sets take longer at the start because of reading, then speed up.

Mini-example: a site had 61,000 visitors in May and 70,000 in June. If July grows by the same percent (about 14.75 percent) and 4 percent of visitors sign up, July sign-ups are about 80,300 x 0.04, roughly 3,200.

practice.prompt: Pens are sold at 3 for $2.40. At this rate, how much do 15 pens cost?
practice.explanation: One pen costs $2.40 / 3 = $0.80, so 15 pens cost 15 x $0.80 = $12.00. Equivalently, 15 pens is 5 groups of 3, and 5 x $2.40 = $12.00.

practice.prompt: How many liters of water must be added to 20 liters of a 30% acid solution to make a 20% acid solution?
practice.explanation: Acid stays at 0.30 x 20 = 6 liters. For 20% concentration, total volume = 6 / 0.20 = 30 liters, so add 10 liters of water.

practice.prompt: If n is an integer, which of the following must be even?
practice.explanation: n^2 + n = n(n + 1), the product of consecutive integers, one of which is even. The others depend on whether n is odd or even.

practice.prompt: A car travels 120 km at 60 km/h and returns the same 120 km at 40 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole trip?
practice.explanation: Total distance 240 km; total time 2 + 3 = 5 hours; average speed = 240 / 5 = 48 km/h. 50 is the trap of averaging the speeds.

practice.prompt: Company spokesperson: "Since we introduced flexible working hours, employee turnover has dropped by a third. Therefore, flexible hours have improved employee retention." The argument assumes which of the following?
options: Turnover at competing firms has risen.
Most employees prefer to work in the morning.
No other change during the same period, such as higher salaries, accounts for the drop in turnover.
practice.explanation: The conclusion attributes the drop to flexible hours; it requires that another cause did not produce it. Negate the option ("a pay rise caused the drop") and the argument collapses.

practice.prompt: A town's new bike-lane network was followed by a 15% fall in downtown car traffic, so the council concludes the bike lanes reduced car use. Which of the following, if true, most weakens the conclusion?
options: Bike-lane usage has grown each month since opening.
Several nearby towns plan to build bike lanes.
During the same period a major downtown employer relocated outside town, removing thousands of daily commuters.
practice.explanation: An alternative explanation (fewer commuters) could account for the traffic drop, weakening the causal claim.

practice.passage: Economists once assumed that consumers respond to price changes in a consistent way. Behavioral researchers have since shown that the framing of a price matters: shoppers often react more strongly to a surcharge than to an equivalent lost discount, even when the final cost is identical. Some economists argue these effects are small in markets where buyers make repeated purchases and learn over time. Others counter that firms deliberately design prices to exploit framing, so the effects persist.
practice.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: arguing that repeated purchases eliminate all framing effects.
describing a finding about price framing and a debate over its significance.
practice.explanation: The passage presents the framing finding, then two opposing views about how much it matters. It does not prove a broad claim or take a side.

practice.passage: Economists once assumed that consumers respond to price changes in a consistent way. Behavioral researchers have since shown that the framing of a price matters: shoppers often react more strongly to a surcharge than to an equivalent lost discount, even when the final cost is identical. Some economists argue these effects are small in markets where buyers make repeated purchases and learn over time. Others counter that firms deliberately design prices to exploit framing, so the effects persist.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, why might some economists consider framing effects small?
options: Buyers who purchase repeatedly may learn over time.
Discounts are more common than surcharges.
practice.explanation: The third sentence states the effects may be small where buyers make repeated purchases and learn.

practice.passage: Units sold (thousands) by region: North 120; South 80; East 150; West 50.
practice.prompt: What percentage of total units were sold in the East region?

practice.passage: Units sold (thousands) by region: North 120; South 80; East 150; West 50.
practice.prompt: If South's sales increased by 25% and all other regions stayed the same, South's share of the new total would be closest to
practice.explanation: South becomes 80 x 1.25 = 100; new total = 420; 100 / 420 is about 23.8%, closest to 24%.

practice.prompt: Machine A makes 40 widgets per hour and Machine B makes 60 widgets per hour. Working together at these rates, how many hours do they need to make 500 widgets?
practice.explanation: Combined rate = 100 widgets per hour, so 500 / 100 = 5 hours.

practice.passage: A company's annual revenue: 2024: $80 million; 2025: $100 million; 2026: $130 million.
practice.prompt: By what percent did revenue grow from 2025 to 2026?
Notebooks cost $3.20 each. If Maria buys 7 notebooks and pays with a $50 bill, how much change should she receive?
practice.explanation: 7 x $3.20 = $22.40, and $50 - $22.40 = $27.60. The answer $22.40 is the cost, not the change.

practice.prompt: If 3(y + 4) = 2y - 5, what is the value of y?
practice.explanation: 3y + 12 = 2y - 5, so y = -17. The answer -9 comes from writing 3(y + 4) as 3y + 4.

practice.prompt: The ratio of boys to girls in a club is 4 : 5. If the club has 36 members, how many are girls?
practice.explanation: There are 9 parts, each worth 4 members, so girls = 5 x 4 = 20. The answer 16 is the number of boys.

practice.prompt: The average of 12, 15, x, and 21 is 17. What is x?
practice.explanation: The total must be 4 x 17 = 68, and 12 + 15 + 21 = 48, so x = 20.

practice.prompt: If a = 2b and b = 3c, what is a/c?
practice.explanation: a = 2(3c) = 6c, so a/c = 6. Adding the coefficients to get 5 is a common slip.

practice.prompt: The price of a $250 item increases by 8%. What is the new price?
practice.explanation: 8% of 250 is 20, so the new price is $270. The answer $258 adds 8 dollars instead of 8 percent.

practice.prompt: Which of the following fractions is greatest?
practice.explanation: As decimals: 4/9 = 0.444, 3/7 = 0.429, 5/12 = 0.417, 2/5 = 0.400. Cross-multiplying 4/9 and 3/7 gives 28 > 27, confirming 4/9.

practice.prompt: If x^2 - 5x = 14 and x > 0, what is x?
practice.explanation: x^2 - 5x - 14 = (x - 7)(x + 2) = 0, so x = 7 or -2, and only 7 is positive. The answer 2 comes from a sign error in factoring.

practice.prompt: A train travels 300 kilometers in 2.5 hours. At the same speed, how many minutes does it take to travel 84 kilometers?
practice.explanation: Speed = 120 km per hour, which is 2 km per minute, so 84 km takes 42 minutes.

practice.prompt: If 1/x + 1/y = 1/4 and x = 12, what is y?
practice.explanation: 1/y = 1/4 - 1/12 = 2/12 = 1/6, so y = 6. The answer 8 subtracts 12 - 4 directly.

practice.prompt: How many pounds of coffee worth $6 per pound must be mixed with 20 pounds of coffee worth $9 per pound to make a blend worth $7 per pound?
practice.explanation: 6x + 9(20) = 7(x + 20) gives 6x + 180 = 7x + 140, so x = 40. The blend price is closer to $6, so more of the cheap coffee is needed.

practice.prompt: An investment of $5,000 earns 4% interest compounded annually. How much interest does it earn in 2 years?
practice.explanation: 5,000(1.04)^2 = 5,408, so the interest is $408. The answer $400 is simple interest.

practice.prompt: For what value of c does x^2 + 6x + c = 0 have exactly one real solution?
practice.explanation: One solution requires the discriminant 36 - 4c = 0, so c = 9, giving (x + 3)^2. The answer 36 forgets the factor of 4.

practice.prompt: What is the smallest positive integer n such that 120n is a perfect square?
practice.explanation: 120 = 2^3 x 3 x 5. Each exponent must become even, so n = 2 x 3 x 5 = 30, giving 3,600 = 60^2.

practice.prompt: What is the sum of all values of x that satisfy |2x - 3| = 7?
practice.explanation: 2x - 3 = 7 gives x = 5, and 2x - 3 = -7 gives x = -2. Their sum is 3. Answering 5 ignores the negative case.

practice.prompt: Machine A produces 300 units in 5 hours. Machines A and B working together produce 300 units in 3 hours. How many hours would machine B alone take to produce 300 units?
practice.explanation: A makes 60 units per hour and together they make 100, so B makes 40 per hour and needs 300 / 40 = 7.5 hours. The answer 2 subtracts the times.

practice.prompt: How many integers x satisfy -3 < 2x + 1 ≤ 9?
practice.explanation: Subtract 1 and divide by 2: -2 < x ≤ 4, so x = -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, which is 6 integers. Including -2 gives 7.

practice.prompt: A merchant sells an item at a 20% discount off the list price and still makes a 20% profit on her cost. If the cost is $60, what is the list price?
practice.explanation: The selling price is 1.2 x 60 = $72, which is 80% of the list price, so the list price is 72 / 0.8 = $90. The answer $86.40 adds 20% to $72 instead of dividing by 0.8.

practice.prompt: If x and y are positive, x^2 - y^2 = 48, and x + y = 12, what is x?
practice.explanation: x^2 - y^2 = (x - y)(x + y), so x - y = 4. Adding to x + y = 12 gives x = 8. The answer 4 is x - y.

practice.prompt: When the positive integer n is divided by 6, the remainder is 4. What is the remainder when 5n is divided by 6?
practice.explanation: n = 6k + 4, so 5n = 30k + 20, and 20 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 6. Test: n = 4 gives 5n = 20, remainder 2.

practice.prompt: The average of 7 consecutive odd integers is 25. What is the product of the smallest and largest of these integers?
practice.explanation: The middle integer is 25, so the integers run from 19 to 31, and 19 x 31 = 589. The answer 625 is 25^2.

practice.prompt: A sequence is defined by a_1 = 3 and a_n = 2a_(n-1) - 1 for n ≥ 2. What is a_6?
practice.explanation: The terms are 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65. The answer 33 is a_5, and 129 is a_7.

practice.prompt: How many four-digit positive integers have four different digits, all of which are odd?
practice.explanation: There are 5 odd digits; choosing 4 different ones in order gives 5 x 4 x 3 x 2 = 120. The answer 625 allows repeated digits.

practice.prompt: Pipe A can fill an empty tank in 6 hours, and pipe B can empty a full tank in 9 hours. If both pipes are opened when the tank is empty, how many hours will it take to fill the tank?
practice.explanation: The net rate is 1/6 - 1/9 = 1/18 of the tank per hour, so it takes 18 hours. The answer 3.6 adds the rates as if both pipes were filling.

practice.passage: Bakery owner: Since we introduced our new sourdough loaf, it has outsold our wheat loaf every week. Clearly, our customers prefer sourdough to wheat.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the owner's conclusion?
options: The two loaves have been sold at the same price and displayed equally prominently.
The sourdough loaf takes longer to bake than the wheat loaf.
Several other bakeries in town also sell sourdough.
Some customers buy both kinds of loaf.
practice.explanation: Equal price and display rule out other reasons for higher sourdough sales, supporting a real preference. Baking time does not affect what customers prefer.

practice.passage: Last year the town installed speed cameras along Route 9. Over the following year, the number of accidents on Route 9 fell by 30 percent. The town council concludes that the cameras reduced accidents.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the council's conclusion?
options: During the same year, Route 9 was closed for three months for repaving, and its traffic was diverted to other roads.
Speed cameras are expensive to install and maintain.
Some drivers on Route 9 received more than one speeding ticket.
Neighboring towns have also considered installing speed cameras.
practice.explanation: With the road closed for a quarter of the year, fewer accidents could simply reflect less traffic, an alternative explanation. Cost does not affect whether the cameras reduced accidents.

practice.passage: Sales representative: Our firm should advertise on the Main Street Business podcast. Sixty percent of its listeners own small businesses, and small-business owners are exactly the customers we want to reach.
practice.prompt: The sales representative's argument depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: No competing firm advertises on the podcast.
Every listener to the podcast owns a business.
The cost of advertising on the podcast is not so high that it outweighs the likely benefit of reaching these listeners.
The podcast is the most popular business podcast in the country.
practice.explanation: If the ads cost more than the business they bring in, the recommendation fails, so the argument needs this assumption (negation test). The argument does not require that every listener owns a business; 60 percent is enough.

practice.passage: Last year a city cut its bus fares in half. Over the following year, the city's total revenue from bus fares increased.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, best explains the increase in fare revenue?
options: The city's cost of operating buses fell during the same period.
After the fare cut, the number of bus riders more than doubled.
Most regular riders use monthly passes whose prices did not change.
Some riders switched from buses to bicycles during the period.
practice.explanation: Half the fare times more than twice the riders yields more revenue. Lower operating costs affect profit, not fare revenue, and unchanged pass prices would explain stable revenue, not higher revenue.

practice.passage: A school district found that students who ate the free school breakfast scored higher on standardized tests than students who did not. The district concludes that eating the breakfast improves test scores.
practice.prompt: Which of the following would be most useful to know in evaluating the district's conclusion?
options: Whether the breakfast menu changes from week to week
Whether other districts offer free lunch as well as breakfast
Whether test scores in the district have risen over the past decade
Whether students who eat the free breakfast differ from those who do not in other ways that affect test scores, such as attendance
practice.explanation: If breakfast eaters already attend more or differ in other ways, those differences, not breakfast, might explain higher scores; if not, the conclusion is stronger. The menu's variety does not bear on cause and effect.

practice.passage: All of the firm's senior analysts hold an MBA. Some employees who hold an MBA work part-time. No part-time employee is eligible for the annual bonus.
practice.prompt: If the statements above are true, which of the following must also be true?
options: Some senior analysts are not eligible for the annual bonus.
Every employee who is eligible for the bonus holds an MBA.
Some employees who hold an MBA are not eligible for the annual bonus.
practice.explanation: Some MBA holders work part-time, and no part-time employee is eligible, so those MBA holders are ineligible. The part-time MBA holders need not be senior analysts, so the second choice may be false.

practice.passage: To reduce traffic congestion downtown, the city plans to double the fees at all downtown parking garages and meters.

Whether parking fees in other cities are higher than in this city

practice.passage: A survey found that 80 percent of people who use the Calmly meditation app every day report feeling less stressed than they did a year ago. Therefore, using Calmly reduces stress.
practice.prompt: Which of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the reasoning?
options: It relies on a survey with too few respondents to be reliable.
It assumes that stress cannot be measured.
It fails to consider that people whose stress was falling may have been more likely to keep using the app every day.
It treats a claim about one app as a claim about all meditation apps.
practice.explanation: The survey includes only daily users, and people who felt better may have been the ones who kept using the app, so the causation could run the other way or reflect selection. Nothing indicates the sample was small.

practice.passage: To cut costs, a grocery retailer plans to replace most of its cashiers with self-checkout machines, saving the wages those cashiers are paid.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most strongly suggests that the plan will not reduce the retailer's costs?
options: At stores that adopted self-checkout, losses from unscanned items rose by more than the wages saved.
Some customers prefer to be served by a cashier.
Self-checkout machines take up less floor space than staffed lanes.
The retailer's competitors have not yet adopted self-checkout.
practice.explanation: If added theft and errors exceed the wage savings, total costs rise. Customer preference may affect sales but does not directly show that costs will fail to fall.

practice.passage: Charred seeds of a domesticated variety of barley were found at an archaeological site dated to about 9,000 years ago. The researchers conclude that the site's inhabitants farmed barley.
practice.prompt: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the researchers' conclusion?
options: Barley is one of the oldest cultivated grains in the world.
Charred seeds are more likely to survive for thousands of years than uncharred seeds.
Grinding stones and storage pits at the site are of types associated with processing grain, and no wild barley grew within 200 kilometers at that time.
Other sites in the region contain charred seeds of wild wheat.
practice.explanation: Grain-processing tools show local handling of grain, and the absence of wild barley nearby rules out gathering, so local farming becomes more likely. Seed preservation explains why seeds survived, not where they came from.

practice.passage: Last year 40 percent of the e-readers lent by the Lakeview library were returned damaged. The library director proposes requiring a $50 deposit, refunded when a device is returned undamaged, and concludes that the deposit will substantially reduce damage.
practice.prompt: The director's conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: Most borrowers can afford a $50 deposit.
A substantial portion of the damage results from borrowers' carelessness, which a financial incentive could influence, rather than from normal wear or manufacturing defects.
The e-readers cost the library more than $50 each to replace.
Other libraries that require deposits have reported less damage.
practice.explanation: If damage comes mainly from wear or defects, a deposit cannot change it, so the plan depends on carelessness being a large factor. Affordability is not required: if borrowers could not pay, fewer devices would be lent and damaged anyway.

practice.passage:
When ride-hailing companies introduced surge pricing, which automatically raises fares when demand outstrips the supply of drivers, economists largely applauded. Higher prices, they argued, would ration scarce rides to those who valued them most while drawing more drivers onto the road. Consumer reaction was harsher. Riders who paid triple fares during a snowstorm often described the practice as gouging, and several companies capped surge multipliers during emergencies.

Behavioral research helps explain the gap between the two views. People judge prices against a reference point, typically the price they are used to paying, and they treat increases justified by a seller's higher costs as fair while viewing increases driven only by heightened demand as exploitation. Under this framework, surge pricing is perceived as unfair precisely because it ties the price to demand rather than to cost.

Some firms have responded by changing how prices are framed rather than how they are set. A fare that rises during peak hours can be presented as a discount during off-peak hours, or the higher price can be explained in terms of driver pay. Critics see such reframing as manipulation; defenders reply that it simply aligns consumers' perceptions with a market reality that benefits them by keeping rides available.
practice.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to
options: argue that surge pricing should be banned during emergencies
compare the pricing strategies of different ride-hailing companies
show that consumers' reference prices are usually accurate
explain why a pricing practice favored by economists has drawn consumer resentment and describe how firms have responded
practice.explanation: The passage covers economists' support, consumer anger, a behavioral explanation, and firms' reframing. It reports caps during emergencies but never argues for a ban.

practice.passage:
Reef-building corals depend on symbiotic algae that live within their tissues and supply most of their energy through photosynthesis. When water temperatures rise even 1 to 2 degrees Celsius above the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership breaks down: the algae are expelled, the coral turns white, and unless conditions improve, it may starve. Because ocean temperatures are projected to keep rising, many researchers once assumed that bleaching would eliminate most reefs within decades.

That forecast has been complicated by the discovery that heat tolerance varies. Some corals host algal strains that remain functional at higher temperatures, and corals that survive one bleaching event sometimes bleach less severely in the next. Researchers have therefore proposed "assisted evolution," breeding heat-tolerant corals or inoculating corals with tolerant algae, to accelerate adaptation.

Skeptics caution that tolerance often comes at a cost. Corals hosting the most heat-tolerant algae tend to grow more slowly, because those algae transfer less energy to their hosts. A reef composed of tolerant but slow-growing corals may survive warming yet fail to keep pace with erosion and storm damage.
practice.prompt: According to the passage, coral bleaching occurs when
options: corals grow too slowly to repair storm damage
algae transfer too much energy to their hosts
ocean temperatures fall below the usual summer maximum
corals expel their symbiotic algae under prolonged heat stress
practice.explanation: The first paragraph says sustained temperatures above the usual maximum cause the algae to be expelled and the coral to turn white. Slow growth is a separate concern raised by skeptics.

practice.passage: Historians of the nineteenth-century novel have often assumed that serial publication, which released a novel in weekly or monthly installments, encouraged loose, episodic plotting, since authors wrote under deadline and could not revise earlier parts once printed. Yet a closer look at authors' working notes complicates this view. Several serial novelists kept detailed plans that mapped major revelations months in advance, and some used reader letters to gauge which subplots to expand. Serialization, on this account, did not so much prevent careful design as change its nature: authors planned structurally while improvising locally, adjusting pace and emphasis in response to an audience whose reactions arrived before the book was finished.
practice.prompt: The passage is primarily concerned with
options: describing the economics of nineteenth-century publishing
arguing that serialized novels were superior to novels published whole
explaining why authors stopped publishing in installments
challenging an assumption about how a publication format affected the construction of novels
practice.explanation: The passage presents the assumption that serialization led to loose plotting and then evidence that complicates it. It never claims serialized novels were superior.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

What is the value of x?

(1) 3x + 2 = 17
(2) x^2 = 25
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: Statement (1) gives x = 5, a single value. Statement (2) allows x = 5 or x = -5, so it is not sufficient.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

A store sold 120 items on Monday. How many items did it sell on Tuesday?

(1) The store sold 25% more items on Tuesday than on Monday.
(2) The store sold a total of 270 items on Monday and Tuesday combined.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: Statement (1) gives 1.25 x 120 = 150. Statement (2) gives 270 - 120 = 150. Each is sufficient alone.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

If n is an integer, is n even?

(1) n^2 + n is even.
(2) 3n is even.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: n^2 + n = n(n + 1) is the product of consecutive integers and is always even, so (1) tells us nothing. If 3n is even, n must be even because 3 is odd, so (2) is sufficient.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

What is the price of one pen?

(1) Three pens and two notebooks cost $12.
(2) Two pens and one notebook cost $7.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: Each statement alone has two unknowns. Together, 3p + 2n = 12 and 2p + n = 7 give p = 2, so both together are sufficient.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Is x > y?

(1) x - y > -2
(2) x + y > 0
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: x = 2, y = 1 satisfies both statements with x > y, but x = 0, y = 1 also satisfies both (0 - 1 = -1 > -2 and 0 + 1 > 0) with x < y. Even together the statements are not sufficient.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

If k is a positive integer, is k divisible by 6?

(1) k^2 is divisible by 12.
(2) k is divisible by 4.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: If k^2 is divisible by 12 = 2^2 x 3, then k must contain the primes 2 and 3, so k is divisible by 6: (1) is sufficient. Under (2), k = 4 is not divisible by 6 but k = 12 is.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

What is the remainder when the positive integer n is divided by 12?

(1) When n is divided by 4, the remainder is 3.
(2) When n is divided by 3, the remainder is 2.
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: Under (1), n could be 3 or 7 (remainders 3 and 7). Under (2), n could be 2 or 5. Together, n must be 11, 23, 35, ..., which always leave remainder 11, so both together are sufficient.

practice.prompt:
Data Sufficiency: decide whether the data given in the statements are sufficient to answer the question.

Is |x| < 1?

(1) x^3 < x
(2) x^2 < x
options: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are not sufficient.
practice.explanation: x^3 < x holds for 0 < x < 1 (yes) and for x < -1 (no), so (1) is not sufficient. x^2 < x holds only for 0 < x < 1, so (2) always gives yes.

practice.prompt: Two-Part Analysis: Train A leaves a station at 9:00 a.m. traveling at 60 miles per hour. Train B leaves the same station at 10:00 a.m. on a parallel track in the same direction at 80 miles per hour. Select the time at which Train B catches up with Train A (part 1) and their distance from the station at that moment (part 2).
practice.explanation: At 10:00, Train A is 60 miles ahead, and B closes the gap at 20 mph, taking 3 hours, so 1:00 p.m. B has then traveled 80 x 3 = 240 miles. The answer 180 miles uses only A's three hours after 10:00.

practice.prompt: Two-Part Analysis: a chemist mixes a 10% salt solution with a 30% salt solution to make 50 liters of a 22% salt solution. Select the amount of 10% solution (part 1) and the amount of 30% solution (part 2).
practice.explanation: 0.10a + 0.30(50 - a) = 11 gives 15 - 0.2a = 11, so a = 20 and the 30% amount is 30. Since 22% is closer to 30% than to 10%, more of the stronger solution is needed.

practice.prompt: If the company ships 30,000 packages next year, what will Vendor Q's total charge be?
practice.explanation: Q charges 20,000 x $4 = $80,000 plus 10,000 x $2 = $20,000, for $100,000. The answer $110,000 is Vendor P's charge, and $120,000 applies $4 to every package.

practice.prompt: If the company expects to ship 30,000 packages, which vendor does the selection rule require, and why?

practice.prompt: At what annual number of packages would the two vendors' total charges be equal?
